gei-coverb.title_tr: 给 (gěi) as a Coverb: 'to/for' (给我打电话)
gei-coverb.intro_tr: 给[gěi] is one of the most useful small words in Chinese because it does two different jobs: it is a full VERB meaning 'to give' (我给你一本书 'I give you a book'), and it is a COVERB (a preposition-like word placed before a verb) meaning 'to/for someone', marking who receives the action or benefits from it, as in 给我打电话[gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà] 'call me'. As a coverb, 给 + person always goes BEFORE the main verb, unlike English 'to me/for me' which usually comes after. 给 is essential with communication verbs (打电话, 写信, 发短信) and giving/service verbs (买, 做, 介绍, 解释). Beginners often confuse 给 with 对[duì] and 跟[gēn] — this sheet compares them clearly. 给 can also appear informally as a passive marker (similar to 被[bèi]), which is worth recognizing even though it is a more advanced use.

tables.caption_tr: The Two Faces of 给[gěi]: Main Verb vs. Coverb
rows: 我给你钱。 [Wǒ gěi nǐ qián.]
把书给我。 [Bǎ shū gěi wǒ.]
他给我打电话。 [Tā gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà.]
我给她买了礼物。 [Wǒ gěi tā mǎi le lǐwù.]
I bought a gift for her.
衣服给雨淋湿了。 [Yīfu gěi yǔ lín shī le.]
The clothes got soaked by the rain.

tables.caption_tr: 给[gěi] + Verb: Common Collocations (recipient always BEFORE the verb)
rows: 我给妈妈打电话。 [Wǒ gěi māma dǎ diànhuà.] — I call mom.
给 + 人 + 写信/发短信
write a letter / send a text to someone
给我发短信。 [Gěi wǒ fā duǎnxìn.] — Text me.
给 + 人 + 做饭/做菜
他给我们做饭。 [Tā gěi wǒmen zuò fàn.] — He cooks for us.
妈妈给我买了新鞋。 [Māma gěi wǒ mǎi le xīn xié.] — Mom bought me new shoes.
我给你介绍一下。 [Wǒ gěi nǐ jièshào yíxià.] — Let me introduce (this) to you.
老师给我们解释了语法。 [Lǎoshī gěi wǒmen jiěshì le yǔfǎ.] — The teacher explained the grammar to us.
他给老板道歉了。 [Tā gěi lǎobǎn dàoqiàn le.] — He apologized to the boss.
给 + 人 + 提意见/提建议
请给我提意见。 [Qǐng gěi wǒ tí yìjiàn.] — Please give me feedback.

tables.caption_tr: Word Order: 给 Before the Verb vs. After the Verb
rows: Before the verb (coverb use — most common, works with almost any verb)
我给他寄了一个包裹。 [Wǒ gěi tā jì le yí gè bāoguǒ.]
Neutral, standard word order — always safe to use.
After the verb (only with a small set of 'transfer' verbs: 给, 寄, 送, 还, 交, 卖)
我寄了一个包裹给他。 [Wǒ jì le yí gè bāoguǒ gěi tā.]
Emphasizes the destination/final recipient; sounds slightly more formal or emphatic.
Only after the verb (does NOT work before)
S + V(送/还/卖...) + O + 给 + Person
他把车卖给了我。 [Tā bǎ chē mài gěi le wǒ.]
*我给他卖了车 sounds odd — 卖给 is treated almost as one word.
他送我一本书。 [Tā sòng wǒ yì běn shū.]
Some verbs (送, 给, 教, 问, 借) can drop 给 entirely and take two objects directly.

tables.caption_tr: 给[gěi] vs 对[duì] vs 跟[gēn]: Don't Mix Them Up
rows: to/for (recipient or beneficiary of an action)
Someone RECEIVES the action or BENEFITS from it
他给我买了咖啡。 [Tā gěi wǒ mǎi le kāfēi.] — He bought me coffee.
对 would sound like 'towards me' with no transfer; 跟 would sound like 'together with me' (doing it jointly).
toward/regarding (attitude, direction of feeling or effect)
Expressing an attitude, effect, or facing something
他对我很好。 [Tā duì wǒ hěn hǎo.] — He is nice to me.
给 here would wrongly imply he 'gives' niceness like an object being handed over.
Doing something together / interacting with someone
我跟他说了这件事。 [Wǒ gēn tā shuō le zhè jiàn shì.] — I talked with him about this.
给 would frame it as 'telling for his benefit' rather than a mutual conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Negation and Question Forms with 给[gěi]
rows: Negation (未来/习惯, not yet done)
我不给他打电话。 [Wǒ bù gěi tā dǎ diànhuà.]
我没给他打电话。 [Wǒ méi gěi tā dǎ diànhuà.]
你给他打电话吗？ [Nǐ gěi tā dǎ diànhuà ma?]
你给不给他打电话？ [Nǐ gěi bu gěi tā dǎ diànhuà?]
Are you calling him or not?
你给她写信了没有？ [Nǐ gěi tā xiě xìn le méiyǒu?]
Have you written to her yet?

tables.caption_tr: Fixed Expressions Built on 给[gěi]
rows: to leave an impression on someone
他给我留下了好印象。 [Tā gěi wǒ liúxià le hǎo yìnxiàng.] — He left a good impression on me.
对不起，给你添麻烦了。 [Duìbuqǐ, gěi nǐ tiān máfan le.] — Sorry to trouble you.
请给我一个面子。 [Qǐng gěi wǒ yí gè miànzi.] — Please do me this favor (save my face).
这个办法真给力！ [Zhège bànfǎ zhēn gěilì!] — This method really works well!
这给公司造成了损失。 [Zhè gěi gōngsī zàochéng le sǔnshī.] — This caused a loss for the company.

examples.target: 给我打电话。
examples.reading: Gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà.
examples.translation_tr: Give me a call. (给 marks the recipient of the action 打电话)

examples.target: 妈妈给我做了晚饭。
examples.reading: Māma gěi wǒ zuò le wǎnfàn.
examples.translation_tr: Mom made dinner for me. (给 = 'for', beneficiary)

examples.target: 我给他写了一封信。
examples.reading: Wǒ gěi tā xiě le yì fēng xìn.
examples.translation_tr: I wrote him a letter. (给 + recipient before the verb)

examples.target: 请把这本书给我。
examples.reading: Qǐng bǎ zhè běn shū gěi wǒ.
examples.translation_tr: Please give this book to me. (here 给 is the main VERB 'to give', not a coverb)

examples.target: 他给我介绍了一个朋友。
examples.reading: Tā gěi wǒ jièshào le yí gè péngyou.
examples.translation_tr: He introduced a friend to me.

examples.target: 我不给他打电话了。
examples.reading: Wǒ bù gěi tā dǎ diànhuà le.
examples.translation_tr: I'm not going to call him anymore. (negation: 不 goes before 给)

examples.target: 这件事给我留下了很深的印象。
examples.reading: Zhè jiàn shì gěi wǒ liúxià le hěn shēn de yìnxiàng.
examples.translation_tr: This matter left a deep impression on me. (fixed expression 给...留下印象)

examples.target: 杯子给他打破了。
examples.reading: Bēizi gěi tā dǎpò le.
examples.translation_tr: The cup got broken by him. (colloquial passive use of 给, similar to 被— more advanced, good to recognize early)

cong-dao.intro_tr: 从...到... (cóng...dào...) is one of the most common paired prepositions in Chinese, used to mark a range with a clear starting point and ending point. 从 (cóng) introduces where something begins, and 到 (dào) introduces where it ends — together they translate to English "from... to...". This pattern is extremely flexible: it can describe distance between places, a time span, a sequence of pages or steps, or even an abstract range like a price interval or a stage of life. Either part can also be used alone (从 = "from", 到 = "to/arrive at") without the other, but when combined they form a tight matched pair that cannot be split by other prepositions. Word order is fixed: the whole 从...到... phrase acts as an adverbial and must come BEFORE the main verb, just like other prepositional phrases in Chinese.

tables.caption_tr: Core Structure: 从 (cóng) + Start Point + 到 (dào) + End Point
rows: marks the STARTING point of a range (place, time, sequence)
marks the ENDING point of a range (place, time, sequence)
marks the FULL range, start to end, in one phrase
从北京到上海[cóng Běijīng dào Shànghǎi]
can be used without 到 to just mean 'from/since'
can be used without 从 as a verb 'to arrive at' or preposition 'until'

tables.caption_tr: 从...到... Used With Different Types of Range
rows: cóng jiǔ diǎn dào shíyī diǎn
cóng dì yī kè dào dì shí kè
cóng shí kuài dào wǔshí kuài
from childhood to adulthood ('from small to big')

tables.caption_tr: Word Order: Where 从...到... Goes in a Sentence
rows: 我从八点到十点学习。[Wǒ cóng bā diǎn dào shí diǎn xuéxí.]
The whole phrase acts as an adverbial modifying the verb; it CANNOT go after the verb
As the subject of 很/是 sentences (distance/duration)
从我家到学校很近。[Cóng wǒ jiā dào xuéxiào hěn jìn.]
Common pattern for describing distance: 'From A to B is (adj).'
从头到尾都很精彩。[Cóng tóu dào wěi dōu hěn jīngcǎi.]
都 (dōu) after the phrase emphasizes 'the entire range, without exception'
Question form with 多长时间/多远
从...到...要 + 多长时间/多远?
从这儿到那儿要多远?[Cóng zhèr dào nàr yào duō yuǎn?]
要 (yào) means 'it takes/requires' before the question word

tables.caption_tr: 从...到... vs Similar Prepositions: Common Mistakes
rows: 从...到... states a FULL range between two points; 离 only states the DISTANCE/relationship between two points, no verb of motion implied
我家离学校很近。[Wǒ jiā lí xuéxiào hěn jìn.] (my home is close to school)
我家从学校很近。(✗ 从 cannot replace 离 in this static-distance pattern)
Even though 到 can stand alone, once you use 从 you should generally also use 到 (or another end-marker) to complete the pair
从九点到十一点上课。[Cóng jiǔ diǎn dào shíyí diǎn shàngkè.]
从九点上课到。(✗ wrong word order, 到 stranded)
从...到... must precede the verb like other coverbs/prepositional phrases, not follow it
他从北京到上海坐火车。[Tā cóng Běijīng dào Shànghǎi zuò huǒchē.]
他坐火车从北京到上海。(✗ unnatural word order)
到 as a resultative complement vs 到 in 从...到...
到 can also attach directly after a verb as a complement (走到, 跑到, 送到) meaning 'do X until arriving/reaching'; this is different from the preposition 到 in the 从...到... frame
他走到学校了。[Tā zǒu dào xuéxiào le.] (he walked to school / walked and arrived)

examples.target: 我从北京坐飞机到上海。
examples.reading: Wǒ cóng Běijīng zuò fēijī dào Shànghǎi.
examples.translation_tr: I take a flight from Beijing to Shanghai.

examples.target: 我们从八点上课到十二点。
examples.reading: Wǒmen cóng bā diǎn shàngkè dào shí'èr diǎn.
examples.translation_tr: We have class from 8 o'clock to 12 o'clock.

examples.target: 从我家到学校很近。
examples.reading: Cóng wǒ jiā dào xuéxiào hěn jìn.
examples.translation_tr: It's very close from my house to school.

examples.target: 这本书从第一页到最后一页都很有意思。
examples.reading: Zhè běn shū cóng dì yī yè dào zuìhòu yí yè dōu hěn yǒu yìsi.
examples.translation_tr: This book is interesting from the first page to the last page.

examples.target: 他从小到大都喜欢音乐。
examples.reading: Tā cóng xiǎo dào dà dōu xǐhuan yīnyuè.
examples.translation_tr: He has liked music from childhood to adulthood.

examples.target: 从星期一到星期五我都要上班。
examples.reading: Cóng xīngqīyī dào xīngqīwǔ wǒ dōu yào shàngbān.
examples.translation_tr: I have to work from Monday to Friday.

examples.target: 这件衣服从一百块到三百块都有。
examples.reading: Zhè jiàn yīfu cóng yìbǎi kuài dào sānbǎi kuài dōu yǒu.
examples.translation_tr: This clothing item ranges from 100 to 300 yuan (in price).

examples.target: 从这儿到火车站要多长时间?
examples.reading: Cóng zhèr dào huǒchēzhàn yào duō cháng shíjiān?
examples.translation_tr: How long does it take from here to the train station?

li-distance.intro_tr: 离 [lí] is a preposition that expresses the distance between two points, either in space (how far one place is from another) or in time (how long until an event happens). The basic pattern is A + 离 [lí] + B + [description of distance], where A and B are the two reference points and the description can be an adjective like 远 [yuǎn] 'far' / 近 [jìn] 'near', or an exact measurement with 有 [yǒu]. Crucially, 离 [lí] is static — it simply states a relationship between two fixed points and does NOT describe movement, so it is very different from 从...到 [cóng...dào] 'from...to', which marks the start and end of a journey or action. Zero-level learners often mix up 离 [lí], 从 [cóng], and 在 [zài]; the tables below clarify exactly when each one is used. 离 [lí] also appears without a spatial subject A when talking about time remaining until something, e.g. 离考试还有三天 [lí kǎoshì hái yǒu sān tiān] 'there are still three days until the exam'.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Sentence Pattern: A + 离 [lí] + B + Distance Description
rows: A is very far from B
My home is very far from school.
The supermarket is very near my home.
A + 离[lí] + B + 有[yǒu] + distance
The company is 500 meters from the subway station.
A + 离[lí] + B + 不远[bùyuǎn]/不近[bùjìn]
A is not far / not close to B
The hospital is not far from here.
There are still three days until the exam.
离[lí] + Event + 只有[zhǐyǒu] + Time + 了
There is only [short time] left until [event]
There are only two days left until the holiday.
footnotes_tr: When 离[lí] introduces a time expression (rather than a place), the subject A is often omitted because it's understood as 'now' — compare 离考试还有三天 (no A needed) with 我家离学校很远 (A = 我家 required).

tables.caption_tr: Common Words Used After 离[lí] to Describe Distance
rows: 这儿[zhèr]离[lí]机场[jīchǎng]很远[hěnyuǎn]。 (It's far from here to the airport.)
邮局[yóujú]离[lí]公司[gōngsī]很近[hěnjìn]。 (The post office is very close to the company.)
你家[nǐjiā]离[lí]学校[xuéxiào]多远[duōyuǎn]? (How far is your home from school?)
这儿[zhèr]离[lí]车站[chēzhàn]有[yǒu]一公里[yìgōnglǐ]。 (It's one kilometer from here to the station.)
离[lí]过年[guònián]还有[háiyǒu]一个月[yíge yuè]。 (There is still one month until New Year.)
离[lí]下课[xiàkè]只有[zhǐyǒu]五分钟[wǔfēnzhōng]了。 (There are only five minutes left until class ends.)

tables.caption_tr: 离[lí] vs 从...到[cóng...dào] vs 在[zài]: Do Not Confuse These Three
rows: states the static distance/relationship between two points
Just describes how far apart two things are; nobody is going anywhere.
marks the starting point and ending point of a route, action, or time span
Describes travelling or a process moving from A to B.
Gives an absolute location, not a distance relationship between two points.
footnotes_tr: A useful test: if you can insert an exact travel time or measured distance after the phrase (离 X 很远 / 有 500 米), you need 离[lí]; if the sentence describes going somewhere, use 从...到[cóng...dào]; if it just answers 'where is it', use 在[zài].

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with 离[lí]
rows: 我从学校很远。 (wǒ cóng xuéxiào hěn yuǎn)
从[cóng] cannot be used alone to state a static distance — it needs a matching 到[dào] and normally describes movement. Use 离[lí] for 'far from'.
我家离学校去。 (wǒjiā lí xuéxiào qù)
离[lí] cannot be followed by a movement verb like 去[qù]; if movement is involved, switch to 从...到[cóng...dào] or 从 + place + verb.
Don't mix 远[yuǎn]/近[jìn] (used for physical distance) with 还有 + time (used for time remaining) in the same phrase — pick the pattern that matches whether you're describing space or time.
在[zài] states a location, it cannot directly connect two places to show distance — 离[lí] is required for that comparison.

examples.target: 我家离学校很远。
examples.reading: Wǒ jiā lí xuéxiào hěn yuǎn.
examples.translation_tr: My home is far from the school.
examples.note_tr: Basic pattern: A 离 B + 很远 (very far).

examples.target: 银行离这儿不远。
examples.reading: Yínháng lí zhèr bù yuǎn.
examples.translation_tr: The bank isn't far from here.
examples.note_tr: 这儿[zhèr] 'here' is a common B-point in daily speech.

examples.target: 你家离公司远不远?
examples.reading: Nǐ jiā lí gōngsī yuǎn bu yuǎn?
examples.translation_tr: Is your home far from the company or not?
examples.note_tr: V不V question form using the adjective 远[yuǎn].

examples.target: 离上课还有十分钟。
examples.reading: Lí shàngkè hái yǒu shí fēnzhōng.
examples.translation_tr: There are still ten minutes until class starts.
examples.note_tr: Time-distance use: no subject A needed before 离 when talking about 'until now'.

examples.target: 这儿离火车站只有两公里。
examples.reading: Zhèr lí huǒchēzhàn zhǐ yǒu liǎng gōnglǐ.
examples.translation_tr: It's only two kilometers from here to the train station.
examples.note_tr: 只有[zhǐyǒu] emphasizes that the distance is small.

examples.target: 离春节没有几天了。
examples.reading: Lí Chūnjié méiyǒu jǐ tiān le.
examples.translation_tr: There are only a few days left until Spring Festival.
examples.note_tr: 没有几天了[méiyǒu jǐ tiān le] = 'not many days left', a very common set phrase.

examples.target: 学校离我家不太近。
examples.reading: Xuéxiào lí wǒ jiā bú tài jìn.
examples.translation_tr: The school isn't too close to my home.
examples.note_tr: 近[jìn] 'near' is the opposite of 远[yuǎn] 'far'.

examples.target: 现在离下班还有一个小时。
examples.reading: Xiànzài lí xiàbān hái yǒu yí ge xiǎoshí.
examples.translation_tr: There is still one hour left until we get off work.
examples.note_tr: 还有 + 一个小时[yí ge xiǎoshí] shows remaining time before an event.

ba-suggestion.intro_tr: 吧 [ba] is a sentence-final particle with two closely related core jobs: (1) making a suggestion or proposal, like English "Let's..." or "Why don't you...", and (2) expressing a guess or assumption that invites the listener to confirm it, like English "...right?" or "I guess...". It is also used to soften commands, requests, and orders so they sound more polite or less abrupt, and it appears in several fixed expressions such as 好吧 [hǎo ba] "okay, fine." Unlike 吗 [ma], which asks a genuine yes/no question with no assumption, 吧 always signals that the speaker already leans toward an answer or is proposing something, so it invites agreement rather than pure information. 吧 sits at the very end of the sentence, after everything else including 了 [le].

tables.caption_tr: Core Functions of 吧 [ba]
rows: 你是老师吧？[Nǐ shì lǎoshī ba?]
Go ahead and sit. / Please sit.
好吧，我去。[Hǎo ba, wǒ qù.]
Let's just leave it at that.

tables.caption_tr: Suggestion Pattern in Detail
rows: Suggestion to listener (You should... / Go ahead and...)

tables.caption_tr: Conjecture Pattern (Making a Guess That Seeks Confirmation)
rows: Dàgài shì tā dǎ de ba.
It was probably him who called, I think.
有 + Number + Measure Word + 吧 (guessing a quantity)
Zhège bāo yǒu shí jīn ba?
This bag weighs about ten jin, right?

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of Sentence-Final Particles: 吧 vs 吗 vs 呢 vs 啊
rows: 你是学生吗？[Nǐ shì xuésheng ma?]
Speaker has no idea what the answer is.
你是学生吧？[Nǐ shì xuésheng ba?]
你呢？[Nǐ ne?] / 他在睡觉呢。
Often means 'and what about...?' or marks ongoing action.
太好了啊！[Tài hǎo le a!]
Adds emphasis or warmth, not agreement-seeking.

tables.caption_tr: Common Fixed Expressions with 吧
rows: Let's go / Come on, let's move
Come on, don't be like that
Forget it / Just let it go

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with 吧
rows: Using 吧 for a totally open information question
吧 always implies the speaker already has a guess; it cannot be used when the speaker has no idea at all
你叫什么名字吧？(wrong) → 你叫什么名字？(use no particle, or 吗 is not needed for wh-questions either)
Placing 吧 in the middle of the sentence
吧 must always be the very last element of the sentence
我们吧走。(wrong) → 我们走吧。(correct)
Combining 吧 and 吗 in the same clause
Redundant and ungrammatical, since they mark different, incompatible speaker attitudes
你是学生吧吗？(wrong) → 你是学生吧？or 你是学生吗？(pick one)
Using 吧 to express strong certainty
吧 always carries some tentativeness or invites confirmation, so it weakens certainty
他一定是老师吧。(odd) → 他一定是老师。(certain statement, no 吧)

examples.target: 我们去吃饭吧。
examples.reading: Wǒmen qù chīfàn ba.
examples.translation_tr: Let's go eat.
examples.note_tr: Suggestion pattern: 我们 + V + 吧.

examples.target: 你累了吧？
examples.reading: Nǐ lèi le ba?
examples.translation_tr: You're tired, aren't you?
examples.note_tr: Conjecture: speaker guesses based on appearance, seeks confirmation.

examples.target: 坐吧，别客气。
examples.reading: Zuò ba, bié kèqi.
examples.translation_tr: Go ahead and sit, don't be so polite.
examples.note_tr: Softened invitation/command, friendlier than a bare imperative.

examples.target: 这个电影很有意思吧？
examples.reading: Zhège diànyǐng hěn yǒuyìsi ba?
examples.translation_tr: This movie is interesting, isn't it?
examples.note_tr: Speaker already believes it's interesting and wants agreement.

examples.target: 好吧，我知道了。
examples.reading: Hǎo ba, wǒ zhīdào le.
examples.translation_tr: Fine, I understand.
examples.note_tr: Fixed expression 好吧 shows reluctant agreement.

examples.target: 明天你有空吧？
examples.reading: Míngtiān nǐ yǒu kòng ba?
examples.translation_tr: You're free tomorrow, right?
examples.note_tr: Polite way to ask, assuming the answer is probably yes.

examples.target: 别哭了吧。
examples.reading: Bié kū le ba.
examples.translation_tr: Please stop crying.
examples.note_tr: 吧 softens the negative command 别哭了, making it gentler.

examples.target: 咱们走吧，要迟到了。
examples.reading: Zánmen zǒu ba, yào chídào le.
examples.translation_tr: Let's go, we're going to be late.
examples.note_tr: 咱们 (inclusive 'we') + 吧 is a very common way to propose immediate action.

measure-words-common.title_tr: Common Measure Words (本, 张, 杯, 件, 只...)
measure-words-common.intro_tr: In Chinese, whenever you count a noun with a number (or point to it with 这/那/哪/几), you almost always need a measure word (量词 [liàngcí]) placed between the number and the noun — you cannot say "three book" as *三书[sān shū]. Different nouns take different measure words depending on their shape, category, or fixed convention, much like English "a piece of paper" or "a cup of tea." The all-purpose default is 个[gè], which technically works for most nouns when you forget the specific one, but native speakers strongly expect the correct specific measure word. Remember that 二[èr] always becomes 两[liǎng] when a measure word follows it (两本书[liǎng běn shū], not 二本书). This page collects the most frequent HSK2-level measure words so you can look them up quickly.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Sentence Patterns with Measure Words
rows: 两只小猫 [liǎng zhī xiǎo māo]
这些/那些 + Noun (no MW, plural)
footnotes_tr: Use 两 [liǎng], not 二 [èr], whenever a number directly precedes a measure word: 两本书 [liǎng běn shū], not 二本书.
些 [xiē] ('some/several') replaces a specific measure word when talking about an unspecified plural amount.

tables.caption_tr: Comprehensive List of Common Measure Words
rows: General default; people, generic objects when no specific MW is known
Flat objects (paper, tables, tickets, photos, beds)
Most animals; also one of a paired body part (eye, hand)
Clothing (upper body/general garments), matters, affairs, items
Long, thin, flexible objects (fish, rivers, roads, pants, dogs)
Objects with a handle (chairs, umbrellas, knives)
Long, thin, stick-like objects (pens, cigarettes, flowers)
Machines and appliances (computers, TVs, washing machines)
Large, solid, immovable structures (mountains, buildings, bridges)
Chunks or pieces of something; also colloquial for money (yuan)
footnotes_tr: The number 一 [yī] changes tone depending on the tone of the syllable that follows it, whether that syllable is the measure word or (rarely) the noun itself: yì before 1st/2nd/3rd-tone syllables (yì zhāng, yì tiáo), yí before 4th-tone syllables (yí gè, yí jiàn).
个 [gè] is usually pronounced with a light/neutral tone in casual speech, even though its citation tone is 4th (gè).

tables.caption_tr: Measure Words Grouped by Shape / Semantic Category
rows: 一张纸, 一张桌子, 一张床, 一张照片
一条路, 一条河, 一条裤子, 一条鱼
一本书, 一本杂志, 一本词典

tables.caption_tr: Common Confusions and Mistakes to Avoid
rows: 个 vs a specific measure word
个 is a safe generic fallback, but native speakers expect the specific MW once you know it
一个书 [yí gè shū] (understandable, but not natural)

只 [zhī] is for animals, never for people
两 vs 二 before a measure word
Use 两 [liǎng], not 二 [èr], directly before any measure word

件 [jiàn] is for upper-body/general garments; 条 [tiáo] is for long items like pants and skirts
一件衬衫 / 一条裤子

张 [zhāng] is for a single flat sheet; 本 [běn] is for a bound volume
只 vs 双 for shoes
只 [zhī] counts one single shoe; 双 [shuāng] counts a matching pair
一双鞋 (a pair) / 一只鞋 (a single shoe)
Mixing them up changes the meaning

ordinal-di.intro_tr: In Chinese, plain numbers like 一 [yī], 二 [èr], 三 [sān] are cardinal numbers ("one, two, three") and cannot express order by themselves. To turn a cardinal number into an ordinal number ("first, second, third"), you simply attach the prefix 第 [dì] directly before the number: 第一 [dìyī] "first", 第二 [dì'èr] "second", 第三 [dìsān] "third". This is one of the simplest grammar points in Chinese — there is no irregular counting system like English "first/second/third" vs. "fourth/fifth..."; every ordinal is built the same way, all the way up to any number. The resulting 第+Number unit behaves like an adjective/determiner and is usually followed by a measure word and then a noun, though the measure word is often dropped before certain common nouns (天 "day", 次 "time", 年 "year"). The question word for "which number in a sequence" is 第几 [dì jǐ].

tables.caption_tr: Cardinal Numbers → Ordinal Numbers with 第 (dì)
footnotes_tr: The prefix 第 [dì] itself never changes — you simply add it before ANY cardinal number, no matter how large.
The tone of 一 in 第一 stays first tone (yī); it does NOT shift to yí or yì the way 一 sometimes does before other syllables.

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Structure: 第 + Number + Measure Word + Noun
footnotes_tr: The measure word (个, 本, 只, etc.) must match the noun, just like in normal counting.
Certain nouns that already function like counting units (天, 年, 次, 课, 名, 页) attach directly to the number without a separate measure word.

tables.caption_tr: Asking 'Which Number?' with 第几 (dì jǐ)
rows: 我排第一。[Wǒ pái dì yī.]
Which floor do you live on?
Zhè shì nǐ dì jǐ cì lái?
How many times has this been that you've come? (lit. which numbered time)
footnotes_tr: 第几 replaces the unknown number in the 第+Number pattern, just like 几 replaces an unknown small number in normal counting.

tables.caption_tr: Key Rules and Common Pitfalls
rows: Always use 二 [èr], never 两 [liǎng]
Unlike in plain counting (where 两 replaces 二 before measure words), ordinals always keep 二.
第二个孩子 [dì èr gè háizi] 'the second child' — never 第两个孩子
In 第一, the number 一 stays first tone (yī); it does not undergo the usual tone sandhi to yí/yì.
Cardinal numbers alone cannot show order
A bare number + noun only counts a quantity; you must add 第 to show sequence/rank.
三本书 [sān běn shū] 'three books' ≠ 第三本书 [dì sān běn shū] 'the third book'
Measure word often dropped before time/unit nouns
With nouns like 天, 年, 次, 遍, 课, 页, 名 the measure word is skipped entirely.
第一次 [dì yī cì], 第二天 [dì èr tiān], 第五课 [dì wǔ kè]
第 is never used for approximate amounts
第 marks an exact position in a sequence, not an estimated quantity — for 'about the third' use context words like 大概 separately.
大概是第三个 [dàgài shì dì sān ge] 'it's probably the third one'

tables.caption_tr: Common Fixed Expressions with 第
rows: first / number one (also used to mean 'most important')
first place (in a ranking or competition)
which number (in a sequence) — question word
third party (often used for 'the other person' in an affair)

ba-construction-basic.title_tr: 把 (bǎ) Construction Basics: Moving the Object Before the Verb
ba-construction-basic.intro_tr: The 把 (bǎ) construction is one of the most distinctive patterns in Chinese: instead of the usual Subject-Verb-Object order, the object is pulled forward and placed right after 把, resulting in Subject + 把 + Object + Verb + [Something Else]. It is used when the speaker wants to emphasize what HAPPENED TO a specific, already-known object — typically that it was moved, changed, finished, or disposed of in some way. Because 把 highlights a result or disposal, the bare verb almost never stands alone at the end; it needs a completion marker (like 了), a complement, or a reduplicated form after it. This page covers the basic word order and the minimum "something after the verb" rule; the full list of complement types and stricter exceptions are covered in the separate Full Scope lesson.

tables.caption_tr: Basic formula of the 把 construction
rows: Fixed marker word, introduces the object
Must be something specific / already known (definite), not a random/general noun
The action performed on the object
REQUIRED: 了[le], a complement (result/direction/degree), a reduplicated verb, or another object — the verb cannot stand alone at the end

tables.caption_tr: Normal SVO order vs. 把 order (same meaning)
rows: 我 吃 了 那个 苹果。 [Wǒ chī le nàge píngguǒ.]
我 把 那个 苹果 吃 了。 [Wǒ bǎ nàge píngguǒ chī le.]
他 关上 了 门。 [Tā guānshàng le mén.]
他 把 门 关上 了。 [Tā bǎ mén guānshàng le.]
我 写 错 了 这个 字。 [Wǒ xiě cuò le zhège zì.]
我 把 这个 字 写 错 了。 [Wǒ bǎ zhège zì xiě cuò le.]
她 放 好 了 东西。 [Tā fàng hǎo le dōngxi.]
她 把 东西 放 好 了。 [Tā bǎ dōngxi fàng hǎo le.]
She put the things away properly.

tables.caption_tr: What can follow the verb (the verb can never stand alone)
rows: 我把饭吃了。 [Wǒ bǎ fàn chī le.] — I ate up the food.
关 上 [guān shàng], 写 错 [xiě cuò]
请把窗户关上。 [Qǐng bǎ chuānghu guān shàng.] — Please close the window.
拿 走 [ná zǒu], 带 来 [dài lái]
他把书拿走了。 [Tā bǎ shū ná zǒu le.] — He took the book away.
洗 一 洗 [xǐ yi xǐ], 看 一 看 [kàn yi kàn]
把这件事想一想。 [Bǎ zhè jiàn shì xiǎng yi xiǎng.] — Think this matter over.
放 在 桌子 上 [fàng zài zhuōzi shàng]
我把书放在桌子上。 [Wǒ bǎ shū fàng zài zhuōzi shàng.] — I put the book on the table.

tables.caption_tr: When to use 把 vs. when NOT to use it
rows: The object is specific/definite (you both know which one)
把那本书还给我。 [Bǎ nà běn shū huán gěi wǒ.] — Give that book back to me.
The object is indefinite/general (e.g. 一本书, any book) — 把 sounds wrong here
The action changes, moves, or disposes of the object with a clear result
把桌子擦干净。 [Bǎ zhuōzi cā gānjìng.] — Wipe the table clean.
The verb has no result/complement at all, e.g. plain verbs like 喜欢[xǐhuan], 是[shì], 有[yǒu], 知道[zhīdào] — these never take 把
You want to emphasize 'what happened to X'
把门开开。 [Bǎ mén kāikāi.] — Open the door.
The sentence is simply descriptive with no disposal meaning, e.g. 我喜欢这本书 (not 我把这本书喜欢)

tables.caption_tr: Negation and modal words with 把 (placed BEFORE 把, never between 把 and the object)
rows: 我没把作业做完。 [Wǒ méi bǎ zuòyè zuò wán.]
不 + 把 (rare, mostly in conditionals/habits)
你不把话说清楚,我不走。 [Nǐ bù bǎ huà shuō qīngchu, wǒ bù zǒu.]
If you don't explain clearly, I won't leave.
别把手机忘在家里。 [Bié bǎ shǒujī wàng zài jiālǐ.]
Don't forget your phone at home.
能/可以/应该 + 把 (modal verb)
你应该把房间打扫干净。 [Nǐ yīnggāi bǎ fángjiān dǎsǎo gānjìng.]
You should clean the room thoroughly.

bei-passive-basic.intro_tr: The 被[bèi] passive turns the normal Subject-Verb-Object sentence around so that the person or thing AFFECTED by an action becomes the grammatical subject, while the doer (agent) is optional and introduced with 被[bèi]. Unlike English "was/were + verb", Chinese 被[bèi] almost always signals that something bad, unexpected, or notably significant happened to the subject — it is NOT used for neutral, everyday passive statements the way English uses "is made of" or "is spoken here". Crucially, a bare verb almost never follows 被[bèi]; you must add something after the verb (了[le], a result complement, a duration, a complement of degree, etc.) to show the outcome — "被打" alone sounds incomplete, but "被打了" or "被打疼了" is correct. This page covers the skeleton formula, agent omission, negation/modal placement, and the most common beginner mistakes.

tables.caption_tr: Basic 被[bèi] Passive Formula
rows: Affected Subject + 被[bèi] + Agent + Verb + (Complement/了[le]/etc.)
我的书被他借走了。[Wǒ de shū bèi tā jiè zǒu le.]
My book was taken/borrowed by him.
车被偷了。[Chē bèi tōu le.]
Affected Subject + Modal + 被[bèi] + (Agent) + Verb + Complement
这件事可能会被发现。[Zhè jiàn shì kěnéng huì bèi fāxiàn.]
Affected Subject + 没(有)[méi(yǒu)] + 被[bèi] + (Agent) + Verb + Complement
我没被老师批评。[Wǒ méi bèi lǎoshī pīpíng.]
I wasn't criticized by the teacher.

tables.caption_tr: 被[bèi] vs. 叫[jiào] vs. 让[ràng]: Colloquial Passive Markers
rows: Neutral, most common, works in writing & speech
Yes — 车被撞坏了。[Chē bèi zhuàng huài le.]
书被(小明)拿走了。[Shū bèi (Xiǎomíng) ná zǒu le.] — 'The book got taken away (by Xiaoming).'
衣服叫雨淋湿了。[Yīfu jiào yǔ lín shī le.] — 'The clothes got soaked by the rain.'
钱包让小偷偷走了。[Qiánbāo ràng xiǎotōu tōu zǒu le.] — 'The wallet got stolen by a thief.'

tables.caption_tr: What Must Follow the Verb After 被[bèi] (No Bare Verbs!)
rows: 杯子被打破了。[Bēizi bèi dǎ pò le.]
衣服被弄脏了。[Yīfu bèi nòng zāng le.]
'弄脏[nòng zāng]' = 'made dirty' — shows the outcome.
钱被拿走了。[Qián bèi ná zǒu le.]
'走[zǒu]' shows the money was taken away.
他被关了三天。[Tā bèi guān le sān tiān.]
Shows how long the state lasted.
Incomplete — sounds unfinished; native speakers expect an outcome word.

tables.caption_tr: Negation and Modal Verb Placement
rows: 他没被发现。[Tā méi bèi fāxiàn.]
✗ 他被没发现。(negation placed after 被 is wrong)
这种事不会被原谅。[Zhè zhǒng shì bú huì bèi yuánliàng.]
不[bù] alone (without a modal) rarely negates a completed 被 event; 没[méi] is far more common
Modal verbs (会[huì], 可能[kěnéng], 应该[yīnggāi])
他可能被骗了。[Tā kěnéng bèi piàn le.]
✗ 他被可能骗了。(modal placed after 被 is wrong)
他已经被通知了。[Tā yǐjīng bèi tōngzhī le.]
✗ 他被已经通知了。(adverb placed after 被 is wrong)

tables.caption_tr: Common Beginner Mistakes
rows: Using 被[bèi] for neutral/positive passive facts
✗ 这本书被写在1990年。[Zhè běn shū bèi xiě zài yī jiǔ jiǔ líng nián.]
这本书是1990年写的。[Zhè běn shū shì yī jiǔ jiǔ líng nián xiě de.]
被[bèi] implies something unfortunate or notable happened TO the subject; neutral facts use 是...的[shì...de] or plain statements instead.
他被打了。[Tā bèi dǎ le.] / 他被打疼了。[Tā bèi dǎ téng le.]
A completion marker or result complement is required after the verb.
Forgetting the affected item must be definite/specific
✗ 被他打了一个人。[Bèi tā dǎ le yí rén.]
那个人被他打了。[Nà ge rén bèi tā dǎ le.]
The 被[bèi]-subject must be a known, specific item — it comes first, not introduced with 一个[yí ge] as if new information.
✗ 他被没批评。[Tā bèi méi pīpíng.]
他没被批评。[Tā méi bèi pīpíng.]
Negation and modal verbs always precede 被[bèi], never follow it.

shi-de-construction.title_tr: 是...的 Construction (Emphasizing Time / Place / Manner of a Past Action)
shi-de-construction.intro_tr: The 是...的 construction is used to put extra emphasis on a specific detail — such as the time, place, manner, means of transport, or the person involved — of an action that has ALREADY taken place and that both the speaker and listener already know happened. Unlike 了, which simply announces that an action occurred, 是...的 spotlights the circumstances surrounding an already-known past event. 是 is placed right before the emphasized detail, and 的 appears at the end of the clause (or right before/after the object, depending on the object type). In relaxed spoken Chinese, 是 is very often dropped in affirmative sentences, but 的 can never be omitted, and 是 must stay in negative sentences (不是...的).

tables.caption_tr: Core Structure: Affirmative, Negative, and Question Forms
rows: Subject + 是 + [emphasized element] + Verb (+Object) + 的
我是昨天来的。[Wǒ shì zuótiān lái de.]
Subject + 不是 + [emphasized element] + Verb (+Object) + 的
我不是昨天来的。[Wǒ bú shì zuótiān lái de.]
你是昨天来的吗?[Nǐ shì zuótiān lái de ma?]
Subject + 是不是 + [element] + Verb + 的?
你是不是昨天来的?[Nǐ shì bu shì zuótiān lái de?]
Is it (the case) that you came yesterday?
Subject + 是 + [question word] + Verb + 的?
你是什么时候来的?[Nǐ shì shénme shíhou lái de?]

tables.caption_tr: What Can Be Emphasized with 是...的
rows: 我是昨天来的。[Wǒ shì zuótiān lái de.]
我是在中国学的汉语。[Wǒ shì zài Zhōngguó xué de Hànyǔ.]
他是骑自行车来的。[Tā shì qí zìxíngchē lái de.]
我是跟朋友一起去的。[Wǒ shì gēn péngyou yìqǐ qù de.]
我是来学习的。[Wǒ shì lái xuéxí de.]

tables.caption_tr: Word Order When There Is an Object
rows: 的 goes at the very end of the clause
我是昨天来的。[Wǒ shì zuótiān lái de.] — I came yesterday.
的 MUST come AFTER the pronoun object
我是在图书馆看见他的。[Wǒ shì zài túshūguǎn kànjiàn tā de.] — I saw him at the library. (NOT 看见的他)
的 may go before OR after the object; placing it before the object is more common
我是在超市买的水果。 / 我是在超市买水果的。[Wǒ shì zài chāoshì mǎi de shuǐguǒ. / Wǒ shì zài chāoshì mǎi shuǐguǒ de.] — I bought fruit at the supermarket.

tables.caption_tr: 是...的 vs. 了 — Key Contrast
rows: The circumstances (time, place, manner, agent) of a completed action
That an action happened or a change occurred
Speaker and listener already know/assume the action happened
The action may be new or unexpected information
你是什么时候到的?[Nǐ shì shénme shíhou dào de?] 'When did you arrive?' (arrival already known)
你到了吗?[Nǐ dào le ma?] 'Have you arrived?' (asking if it happened at all)
No — only refers to a specific, already-completed past action
了 mainly marks completion/change, not future events either, but it does not require prior shared knowledge

tables.caption_tr: Dropping 是 in Casual Speech
rows: 我是昨天来的。[Wǒ shì zuótiān lái de.]
我昨天来的。[Wǒ zuótiān lái de.]
是 is often dropped; 的 always stays
我不是昨天来的。[Wǒ bú shì zuótiān lái de.]
不是 can never be shortened or dropped

tables.caption_tr: Common Question Words Paired with 是...的
rows: 你是什么时候出生的?[Nǐ shì shénme shíhou chūshēng de?] — When were you born?
你是在哪儿学的汉语?[Nǐ shì zài nǎr xué de Hànyǔ?] — Where did you learn Chinese?
你是怎么去的?[Nǐ shì zěnme qù de?] — How did you go?
你是跟谁一起来的?[Nǐ shì gēn shéi yìqǐ lái de?] — Who did you come with?
你是为什么来中国的?[Nǐ shì wèishénme lái Zhōngguó de?] — Why did you come to China?

examples.target: 你是什么时候来的?
examples.reading: Nǐ shì shénme shíhou lái de?
examples.translation_tr: When did you come? (emphasis: assumes you already arrived, asking about the time)

examples.target: 我是昨天来的。
examples.reading: Wǒ shì zuótiān lái de.
examples.translation_tr: I came yesterday.
examples.note_tr: In casual speech 是 can be dropped: 我昨天来的。The 的 can never be dropped.

examples.target: 他是坐飞机来的。
examples.reading: Tā shì zuò fēijī lái de.

examples.translation_tr: We met in Beijing. (emphasis: the place)

examples.translation_tr: I borrowed this book at the library.
examples.note_tr: Noun object placed after 的; 我是在图书馆借这本书的 is also correct.

examples.target: 我不是坐火车来的。

examples.target: 这件衣服是在网上买的。

examples.note_tr: The topic (衣服) is placed at the front; no object remains after the verb, so 的 sits at the very end.

topic-comment.intro_tr: Chinese is often described as a "topic-prominent" language: instead of always starting a sentence with the grammatical subject (as English does), Chinese frequently opens with the TOPIC — the thing being talked about — and then adds a COMMENT that says something about it. The topic can be the object, a time expression, a place, or even a whole item whose part is discussed next. A classic example is 那本书我看过 [Nà běn shū wǒ kàn guò] — literally "That book, I have read," where the object 那本书 (normally after the verb in SVO order) has been moved to the very front. The key rule: a fronted topic must refer to something specific/definite (already known to the listener), not to something indefinite or brand-new. This structure is extremely common in natural spoken and written Chinese, so recognizing it is essential even though English rarely uses it this way.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure: SVO vs. Topic-Comment
rows: 我看过那本书。 [Wǒ kàn guò nà běn shū.]
那本书我看过。 [Nà běn shū wǒ kàn guò.]
那本书看过了。 [Nà běn shū kàn guò le.]
中文,我学过。 [Zhōngwén, wǒ xué guò.]
footnotes_tr: The comment often contains a 'gap' where the topic would normally sit as an object — that gap is understood, not repeated with a pronoun in most cases.

tables.caption_tr: What Can Become the Topic?
rows: Zhè běn shū wǒ kàn guò.
Jīntiān de zuòyè wǒ zuò wán le.
Běijīng wǒ qù guò liǎng cì.
Whole-part topic (whole first, part commented on)
Zhè jiàn yīfu yánsè hěn hǎokàn.
This piece of clothing, the color is very nice.
(Of) fruit, apples I like the most.

tables.caption_tr: Definiteness Requirement: Why Not Every Object Can Front
rows: 那本书我看过。 [Nà běn shū wǒ kàn guò.]
'That book' is a specific, identifiable book.
'A book' (any book) is not specific enough to be a topic; keep it in SVO: 我看过一本书。
苹果我最喜欢吃。 [Píngguǒ wǒ zuì xǐhuan chī.]
Here 'apples' as a whole category is treated as a known topic, not one indefinite item.
Question words like 什么 stay in normal object position: 我喜欢什么?
footnotes_tr: A useful test: if you can naturally say 'As for ___' or 'Speaking of ___' in English before the phrase, it likely works as a Chinese topic.

tables.caption_tr: Topic-Comment vs. 把 (bǎ) Sentence: Key Differences
rows: Object moves to the very front of the sentence
Object stays after 把, before the verb, subject stays first
No — bare verb + 了/过 is fine
Yes — verb almost always needs a result/complement (完, 好, 到, etc.)
Shifting emphasis / discussing something already mentioned
Emphasizing what HAPPENED TO the object / disposal of object
过 (experience) or 了 (completion), often optional
了 or a resultative complement is nearly obligatory
No, 把 needs a clear agent doing the action

tables.caption_tr: Common Learner Mistakes
rows: Fronting an indefinite object: *一个苹果我吃了。
Indefinite 'an apple' cannot be a topic; only definite/known things can front.
Adding an extra pronoun after the verb: *那本书我看过它。
那本书我看过。 (no extra pronoun needed)
The topic already fills the object gap; repeating it with 它 is redundant and unnatural.
Forgetting aspect marker when needed: *这个电影我看。 (meant 'I have watched it')
这个电影我看过。 / 这个电影我看了。
Without 了/过 the sentence reads as a general/habitual statement, not a completed or experienced action.
Fronting a question word as topic: *谁我认识。
我认识谁?/ 我谁都认识。
Question words cannot serve as sentence topics; they must stay in their normal grammatical slot or use special patterns like 谁都.

examples.reading: Nà běn shū wǒ kàn guò.
examples.translation_tr: That book, I have read (it). [book = topic, placed before the subject 我]

examples.reading: Zhège wèntí wǒ bù zhīdào.
examples.translation_tr: This question, I don't know (the answer to it).

examples.target: 中文,我已经学了三年了。
examples.reading: Zhōngwén, wǒ yǐjīng xué le sān nián le.
examples.translation_tr: Chinese, I have already studied (it) for three years.

examples.target: 昨天的电影,你看了吗?
examples.reading: Zuótiān de diànyǐng, nǐ kàn le ma?
examples.translation_tr: Yesterday's movie, did you watch (it)?

examples.target: 这件事我们以后再谈。
examples.reading: Zhè jiàn shì wǒmen yǐhòu zài tán.
examples.translation_tr: This matter, we'll discuss (it) later.

examples.target: 苹果我最喜欢吃。
examples.reading: Píngguǒ wǒ zuì xǐhuan chī.
examples.translation_tr: Apples, I like eating (them) the most.

examples.target: 那个人我认识。
examples.reading: Nàge rén wǒ rènshi.
examples.translation_tr: That person, I know (them).

examples.target: 他的名字我忘了。
examples.reading: Tā de míngzi wǒ wàng le.
examples.translation_tr: His name, I've forgotten (it).

resultative-complements.title_tr: Resultative Complements (完, 好, 到, 见, 懂, 错)
resultative-complements.intro_tr: Resultative complements (结果补语) are single-syllable words placed directly after a verb to state the outcome of an action, not merely that the action took place. Where English often leaves the result implied ("I ate" vs. "I finished eating"), Chinese requires a Verb + Complement pattern to make the result explicit — whether an action was completed, succeeded, was perceived, understood, or done incorrectly. This page covers the six most common resultative complements tested at HSK3: 完[wán] (finish/use up), 好[hǎo] (completed satisfactorily), 到[dào] (successfully reach/achieve), 见[jiàn] (perceive by the senses), 懂[dǒng] (understand/comprehend), and 错[cuò] (do incorrectly). Negation always uses 没(有) before the verb — never 不 — and drops 了; most of these complements can also form "potential complements" by inserting 得 (can) or 不 (cannot) between the verb and the complement.

tables.caption_tr: The Six Core Resultative Complements
rows: 吃, 喝, 做, 看, 写, 说
做, 准备, 写, 说, 商量
找, 买, 收, 想, 听, 得
看, 听, 闻, 梦
看, 听, 写, 说, 做, 买

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Patterns: Affirmative, Negative, and Question Forms
rows: 没(有) + V + Complement — no 了
我没找到钥匙。[Wǒ méi zhǎodào yàoshi.]
你吃完了吗?[Nǐ chīwán le ma?]
你吃完了没有?[Nǐ chīwán le méiyǒu?]
Have you finished eating or not?

tables.caption_tr: Potential Complement Forms (inserting 得 / 不 for 'can / cannot')
footnotes_tr: 错 almost never forms a potential complement (avoid 看得错/看不错); it is used only as a plain resultative complement, e.g. 看错, 写错.
The potential complement form (V+得/不+Complement) is a separate, more advanced pattern — see the Potential Complements topic for full details.

tables.caption_tr: Common Verb + Complement Combinations
Easily Confused: 到 vs 见 vs 懂
rows: marks that the action successfully reached its goal (implies effort/intention)
Pairs with goal-directed verbs: 找, 买, 收, 想, 得
marks passive or incidental sensory perception
Used only with sense verbs: 看, 听, 闻, 梦
marks comprehension of meaning/content, not just perception
Used only with 听 and 看 when the point is understanding, not merely noticing
both mean 'see/notice' and are often interchangeable
看到消息[kàndào xiāoxi] — 'saw the message'
看到 has broader use (news, information, abstract content); 看见 is stricter about literal visual sight

examples.target: 我吃完饭了。
examples.reading: Wǒ chīwán fàn le.
examples.translation_tr: I have finished eating.
examples.note_tr: 完 shows the eating action reached full completion.

examples.target: 你听懂了吗?
examples.reading: Nǐ tīngdǒng le ma?
examples.translation_tr: Did you understand (what was said)?
examples.note_tr: 懂 checks comprehension, not just whether you physically heard the sound.

examples.target: 我没找到我的手机。
examples.reading: Wǒ méi zhǎodào wǒ de shǒujī.
examples.translation_tr: I couldn't find my phone.
examples.note_tr: Negation uses 没(有) before the verb; 了 is dropped in the negative form.

examples.target: 我在公园里看见了他。
examples.reading: Wǒ zài gōngyuán lǐ kànjiàn le tā.
examples.translation_tr: I saw him in the park.
examples.note_tr: 见 marks an incidental sensory perception, not a deliberate search.

examples.target: 你写错字了。
examples.reading: Nǐ xiěcuò zì le.
examples.translation_tr: You wrote the character wrong.
examples.note_tr: 错 attaches directly to the verb of writing to flag an error in the result.

examples.target: 这本书我还没看完。
examples.reading: Zhè běn shū wǒ hái méi kànwán.
examples.translation_tr: I haven't finished reading this book yet.
examples.note_tr: 还没 + V + 完 is the standard way to say 'not yet finished'.

examples.target: 作业做好了吗?
examples.reading: Zuòyè zuòhǎo le ma?
examples.translation_tr: Is the homework done?
examples.note_tr: 好 here means 'completed satisfactorily / ready', not 'good'.

examples.target: 我听不懂老师说的话。
examples.reading: Wǒ tīngbudǒng lǎoshī shuō de huà.
examples.translation_tr: I can't understand what the teacher says.
examples.note_tr: This is the potential complement form: V + 不 + Complement expresses inability.

directional-complements-compound.title_tr: Compound Directional Complements (起来, 下去, 出来...)
directional-complements-compound.intro_tr: Compound directional complements combine a direction word (上, 下, 进, 出, 回, 过, 起) with 来 or 去 to show both the direction of motion and whether it moves toward the speaker (来) or away from the speaker (去). They attach directly after a main verb, e.g. 走进来[zǒu jìnlai] "walk in (this way)" or 站起来[zhàn qǐlai] "stand up". Besides literal physical motion, most of these compounds also carry extended, figurative meanings — 起来[qǐlai] can mean "start doing something" or "recall", 下去[xiàqu] can mean "continue", and 出来[chūlai] can mean "recognize/figure out". Where the object goes in the sentence depends on whether it is a place word or an ordinary thing. This page lays out the full 12-form paradigm, the word-order rules, the potential (得/不) form, and the most common figurative meanings and verb pairings.

tables.caption_tr: The 12 Compound Directional Complements (Direction + 来/去)
footnotes_tr: The second syllable 来/去 is usually pronounced in the neutral tone when it follows a direction word: 起来[qǐlai], 出去[chūqu], etc.
起去 is not a word in Modern Chinese — only 起来 exists.

tables.caption_tr: Placing the Object: Place Words vs. Ordinary Things
rows: Place word (教室, 家, 楼上...)
Verb + Direction + Place + 来/去 (the place word MUST sit between the direction word and 来/去)
他走进教室来了。[Tā zǒu jìn jiàoshì lái le.] — He walked into the classroom.
Verb + Direction + Object + 来/去 (object inserted before 来/去)
他拿出一本书来。[Tā ná chū yì běn shū lái.] — He took out a book.
他买回来一件毛衣。[Tā mǎi huílai yí jiàn máoyī.] — He bought back a sweater.
把 + Object + Verb + Direction + 来/去
请把书拿出来。[Qǐng bǎ shū ná chūlai.] — Please take the book out.
footnotes_tr: Place-word placement is a fixed rule with no exceptions; ordinary-object placement is more flexible and both patterns are common in speech.

tables.caption_tr: Potential Form: Verb + 得/不 + Direction + 来/去
rows: 拿得出来[ná de chūlai] — can manage to take (it) out
拿不出来[ná bu chūlai] — cannot take (it) out
走得进去[zǒu de jìnqù] — able to walk in
想不起来[xiǎng bu qǐlai] — can't recall / can't remember
footnotes_tr: This is the same 得/不 insertion pattern used for simple resultative complements — insert 得 for 'can' and 不 for 'cannot' right after the verb.

tables.caption_tr: Common Figurative (Extended) Meanings
rows: 1) start doing an action; 2) come together / add up; 3) recall something
他笑起来了。[Tā xiào qǐlai le.] — He started laughing. / 想起来[xiǎngqǐlai] — to recall
请你说下去。[Qǐng nǐ shuō xiàqu.] — Please keep talking.
something becomes identifiable / perceivable through the senses
我听出来了他的声音。[Wǒ tīng chūlai le tā de shēngyīn.] — I recognized his voice by hearing it.
to recover, return to a normal state; to manage / cope
他昏倒后又醒过来了。[Tā hūndǎo hòu yòu xǐng guòlai le.] — After fainting, he came around again.
to manage to do something (usually in the potential form)
这道题我答不上来。[Zhè dào tí wǒ dá bu shànglai.] — I can't come up with an answer to this question.
footnotes_tr: These figurative meanings are extremely common; native speakers use them at least as often as the literal, physical-motion meanings.

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used Verb + Compound Directional Complement Pairs

examples.target: 他站起来了。
examples.reading: Tā zhàn qǐlai le.
examples.translation_tr: He stood up.
examples.note_tr: 起来 here shows upward motion of the body — a very common everyday use.

examples.target: 请把书拿出来。
examples.reading: Qǐng bǎ shū ná chūlai.
examples.translation_tr: Please take the book out.
examples.note_tr: With 把, the object comes before the verb, and the whole compound complement 出来 follows the verb.

examples.target: 他走进教室来了。
examples.reading: Tā zǒu jìn jiàoshì lái le.
examples.translation_tr: He walked into the classroom (toward the speaker).
examples.note_tr: 教室 is a place word, so it MUST be inserted between 进 and 来.

examples.target: 我想起来他的名字了。
examples.reading: Wǒ xiǎngqǐlai tā de míngzi le.
examples.translation_tr: I remembered his name.
examples.note_tr: Figurative use of 起来 with 想: 'to recall'.

examples.target: 请你说下去,别停。
examples.reading: Qǐng nǐ shuō xiàqu, bié tíng.
examples.translation_tr: Please keep talking, don't stop.
examples.note_tr: Figurative 下去: continuing an action already in progress.

examples.target: 他从楼上跑下来了。
examples.reading: Tā cóng lóushàng pǎo xiàlai le.
examples.translation_tr: He ran down from upstairs.
examples.note_tr: Literal downward motion toward the speaker.

examples.target: 这个字我认不出来。
examples.reading: Zhège zì wǒ rèn bu chūlai.
examples.translation_tr: I can't recognize this character.
examples.note_tr: Potential form (negative) with figurative 出来: something becoming identifiable.

examples.target: 他昏倒后又醒过来了。
examples.reading: Tā hūndǎo hòu yòu xǐng guòlai le.
examples.translation_tr: After fainting, he came around again.
examples.note_tr: Figurative 过来: to recover / return to a normal state.

duration-complement.title_tr: Duration Complement (时量补语): 学了三年汉语
duration-complement.intro_tr: The duration complement (时量补语) states how long an action or state has lasted, and it is placed AFTER the verb — this is the opposite of English, where "for three years" comes at the end of the whole sentence but in Chinese it sits right next to the verb it measures. The basic shape is Verb + 了/过 + Duration, and if there is also an object, Chinese normally either repeats the verb (V + O + V + Duration) or inserts 的 before the object (V + 了 + Duration + 的 + O). Pronoun objects (我, 你, 他...) behave differently: they go directly after the verb, before the duration word, with no repetition and no 的. Whether you add a sentence-final 了 changes the meaning from "did it for X time (possibly finished)" to "have been doing it for X time (still ongoing)". A special group of "point" verbs (结婚, 毕业, 死, 来, 到, 认识...) that describe an instant rather than an ongoing action use duration to mean "time since that instant happened," not "how long the action itself lasted."

tables.caption_tr: Basic Duration Complement Structure (no object)
rows: Wǒ shuì le bā ge xiǎoshí.
Wǒ shuì le bā ge xiǎoshí le.
I have slept for eight hours (and may still be sleeping / it's been 8 hrs so far)
Wǒ xué guo sān nián gāngqín.
I once studied piano for three years. (past experience, now stopped)
Question: V + 了 + 多长时间/多久
Nǐ děng le duō cháng shíjiān?

tables.caption_tr: Word Order When There Is an Object
rows: Regular noun object (Option A: repeat verb)
Wǒ xué Hànyǔ xué le sān nián.
Regular noun object (Option B: 的 insertion)
V + 了 + Duration + 的 + O
Wǒ xué le sān nián de Hànyǔ.
Tā děng le wǒ bàn ge xiǎoshí.
住在 + Place + V + 了 + Duration
Wǒ zhù zài Shànghǎi zhù le shí nián.

tables.caption_tr: Common Duration (Time-Span) Words
rows: two years (note: 两 not 二 before measure words)

tables.caption_tr: Negative Duration Sentences ('haven't done X for a duration')
rows: Tā sān tiān méi shuìjiào le.
He hasn't slept in three days.
Duration + 没(有) + V + O + 了
Wǒ liǎng ge xīngqī méi chī ròu le.
I haven't eaten meat in two weeks.
Duration always comes BEFORE 没, unlike the positive form where duration comes after V
Tā yì nián méi huí jiā le.
He hasn't gone home in a year.

tables.caption_tr: Meaning Shift: Sentence-Final 了 (ongoing vs finished)
rows: V + 了 + Duration (no final 了)
I waited 30 minutes. (the waiting is over)
V + 了 + Duration + 了 (final 了 added)
Wǒ děng le sānshí fēnzhōng le.
I have been waiting for 30 minutes (and I'm still waiting now).
Wǒ zài Běijīng zhù guo liǎng nián.
I lived in Beijing for two years at some point in the past (not now).

tables.caption_tr: Point-in-Time Verbs (瞬间动词): Duration Means 'Time Since', Not 'How Long the Action Lasted'
rows: It has been three years since they got married. (NOT 'they married for 3 years')
It has been two years since I graduated.
Tā sǐ le shí nián le.
It has been ten years since he died.
Tā lái Běijīng sān ge yuè le.
It has been three months since he came to Beijing.
Wǒ rènshi tā wǔ nián le.
I have known him for five years. (pronoun object, so it goes right after the verb)

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes to Avoid
rows: Duration cannot go before the verb in a positive sentence — it must follow the verb.
我学了三年汉语。 / 我学了三年的汉语。
Pronoun objects go directly after the verb and BEFORE the duration, not the reverse.
他等了我三年。 (pronoun before duration)
In negative sentences, the duration must come BEFORE 没, not after it.

结婚 is a point-in-time verb — it already happened at one instant, so 了 does not attach directly to it the way it does to durative verbs like 学/等/住; still, native usage often allows 他们结婚三年了 without the first 了.

examples.target: 我学了三年汉语。
examples.reading: Wǒ xué le sān nián Hànyǔ.
examples.translation_tr: I studied Chinese for three years. (may or may not still be studying)

examples.target: 我学汉语学了三年了。
examples.reading: Wǒ xué Hànyǔ xué le sān nián le.
examples.translation_tr: I have been studying Chinese for three years. (and I'm still studying it now)

examples.target: 他等了我半个小时。
examples.reading: Tā děng le wǒ bàn ge xiǎoshí.
examples.translation_tr: He waited for me for half an hour. (pronoun object 我 goes before the duration)

examples.target: 我看了两个小时的电视。
examples.reading: Wǒ kàn le liǎng ge xiǎoshí de diànshì.
examples.translation_tr: I watched TV for two hours.

examples.target: 他三天没睡觉了。
examples.reading: Tā sān tiān méi shuìjiào le.
examples.translation_tr: He hasn't slept in three days. (negative: duration comes before 没 + verb)

examples.target: 他们结婚三年了。
examples.reading: Tāmen jiéhūn sān nián le.
examples.translation_tr: They have been married for three years. (结婚 is a point-in-time verb, so no 了 right after the verb)

examples.target: 我住在北京住了五年。
examples.reading: Wǒ zhù zài Běijīng zhù le wǔ nián.
examples.translation_tr: I have lived in Beijing for five years. (verb repeated because the first slot is filled by the place phrase)

examples.target: 你等了多长时间?
examples.reading: Nǐ děng le duō cháng shíjiān?
examples.translation_tr: How long did you wait?

frequency-complement.intro_tr: A frequency complement tells you HOW MANY TIMES an action happens — it is a number + measure word placed right after the verb (and after 了/过 if present). Chinese has three common frequency measure words: 次[cì] (the all-purpose "time(s)"), 遍[biàn] (a "time(s)" that stresses the whole process from beginning to end, like reading a whole book), and 趟[tàng] (a "time(s)" used only for trips/journeys with verbs like 去[qù] and 来[lái]). Where the frequency complement sits in the sentence depends on what kind of object the verb has: ordinary nouns go after the complement, pronouns must go before it, and place names can go either way. Getting the right measure word and the right word order is the two things you need to master here.

tables.caption_tr: The Three Frequency Measure Words at a Glance
rows: generic "time(s)" — the default, safe choice for almost any repeatable action
看[kàn], 说[shuō], 去[qù], 来[lái], 见[jiàn], 找[zhǎo], 吃[chī], 买[mǎi]
看了三次[kànle sān cì] — watched it 3 times
"time(s)" that emphasizes the ENTIRE process from start to finish (not just a glance)
看[kàn], 读[dú], 写[xiě], 念[niàn], 讲[jiǎng], 想[xiǎng]
看了三遍[kànle sān biàn] — read it 3 times, cover to cover each time
one round trip; a journey/errand to a place and (usually) back
去[qù], 来[lái], 跑[pǎo], 走[zǒu]
去了一趟[qùle yí tàng] — made one trip there
footnotes_tr: 趟[tàng] can ONLY be used with movement verbs — never say 看一趟 or 说一趟.
遍[biàn] vs 次[cì] with the same verb: 看一次电影 just means "watched a movie once" (no emphasis on completeness), while 看一遍课文 means "read the text through once, all of it".

tables.caption_tr: Word Order: Where Does the Frequency Complement Go?
rows: 我去过两次。[wǒ qùguo liǎng cì.] — I've been (there) twice.
我看了三次电影。[wǒ kànle sān cì diànyǐng.] — I watched movies 3 times.
Frequency complement comes BEFORE a plain noun object.
我找过他两次。[wǒ zhǎoguo tā liǎng cì.] — I've looked for him twice.
Frequency complement MUST come AFTER a pronoun object — never before it.
Subject + V + (了/过) + Frequency + Place  OR  Subject + V + (了/过) + Place + Frequency
我去过两次北京。 / 我去过北京两次。[wǒ qùguo liǎng cì Běijīng. / wǒ qùguo Běijīng liǎng cì.]
Both orders are correct and equally natural with place names.
footnotes_tr: The aspect particle 了[le] or 过[guo] always attaches directly to the verb, immediately before the frequency complement — not after it.

tables.caption_tr: Sample Sentence Patterns Across Different Numbers
rows: 每次都很有意思。[měi cì dōu hěn yǒu yìsi.]
每遍都不一样。[měi biàn dōu bù yíyàng.]
每趟都很累。[měi tàng dōu hěn lèi.]
footnotes_tr: Use 两[liǎng], not 二[èr], before a measure word: 两次, 两遍, 两趟 — never 二次 in normal speech.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with Frequency Complements
rows: ✓ 我看了他三次。[wǒ kànle tā sān cì.]
A pronoun object must come BEFORE the frequency complement, not after.
✓ 我去了一趟。[wǒ qùle yí tàng.]
了[le] attaches right after the verb, before the frequency complement — it does not go at the very end here.
✓ 我说一次中文 / 说了一遍。[wǒ shuōle yí cì Zhōngwén / shuōle yí biàn.]
趟[tàng] is only for movement/trips (去/来); it cannot be used with 说[shuō].
✓ 我看了两遍这本书。[wǒ kànle liǎng biàn zhè běn shū.]
For reading a book cover to cover, use 遍[biàn] (whole process), not 趟[tàng].
✓ 他找过我两次。[tā zhǎoguo wǒ liǎng cì.]
Same pronoun-before-frequency rule: 我 (a pronoun) must precede 两次.

examples.target: 我去过三次北京。
examples.reading: wǒ qùguo sān cì Běijīng.
examples.translation_tr: I have been to Beijing three times.

examples.target: 我去了一趟超市。

examples.target: 请你再说一遍。

examples.translation_tr: Please say it one more time (the whole thing).

examples.target: 我见过他两次。
examples.reading: wǒ jiànguo tā liǎng cì.
examples.translation_tr: I have met him twice.

examples.target: 医生一天要来看病人两次。

examples.target: 妈妈去了一趟医院。
examples.reading: māma qùle yí tàng yīyuàn.
examples.translation_tr: Mom made a trip to the hospital.

de-adverbial.intro_tr: 地 (de) is a grammatical particle that turns the word or phrase before it into an adverbial modifier describing HOW an action is performed — much like the "-ly" ending in English (quick → quickly), except it's placed before the verb instead of being attached to the adjective. The basic pattern is [Adjective/Descriptive Phrase] + 地 + [Verb]. 地 is one of three particles pronounced identically as "de" in speech (的, 得, 地), but each has a completely different grammatical job and a different character in writing — 地 is specifically the one that links a modifier to a following verb. Whether 地 is required, optional, or forbidden depends heavily on the length and type of the modifying word, which is why this topic has several sub-rules worth memorizing as tables rather than a single formula.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Formation Pattern: [Modifier] + 地 + [Verb Phrase]
rows: yí bù yí bù de zǒu

tables.caption_tr: Is 地 Required, Optional, or Dropped? — Rules by Modifier Type
rows: "Hurry up!" — 快地走 sounds unnatural in speech
"work conscientiously" — both with and without 地 are acceptable, 地 is more common in writing
"dance joyfully" — 地 is almost never dropped here

tables.caption_tr: Distinguishing the Three "de" Particles (same sound, different characters and jobs)
rows: marks an adverbial modifier of a verb (manner)
marks a complement describing the result or degree of an action

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used AABB Reduplications That Must Take 地
Common Learner Errors with 地
rows: Monosyllabic adjectives like 快 normally drop 地 before the verb in everyday speech
This sentence needs the complement particle 得, not 地 — don't mix them up
Disyllabic adjectives usually keep 地 before the verb in written or careful style
yí bù yí bù de zǒu
Repeated / parallel structures require 地 before the verb

tables.caption_tr: True Adverbs (副词) Never Take 地 — They Attach Directly to the Verb

de-three-way.title_tr: 的 / 得 / 地 Comparison (The Three "de" Particles)
de-three-way.intro_tr: In Mandarin, three different characters — 的, 得, and 地 — are all pronounced "de" (neutral tone) as grammatical particles, which is exactly why English-speaking beginners mix them up constantly. Even though they sound identical, each one has a completely different job and appears in a different position in the sentence: 的 connects a modifier to a following NOUN (showing possession or description), 地 connects a modifier to a following VERB (turning an adjective into an adverb), and 得 connects a VERB or ADJECTIVE to a following complement (describing degree, result, or manner AFTER the action). The single most useful trick for beginners is to look at what comes right after the "de": if it's a noun, use 的; if it's a verb (and the "de" comes before it), use 地; if the "de" comes right after a verb or adjective (i.e., something follows describing how well/fast/etc.), use 得. This page lays out every pattern, position rule, and common mix-up in table form so you can check at a glance.

tables.caption_tr: Quick Overview: The Three de's at a Glance
rows: Marks possession or describes a NOUN
我的书 [wǒ de shū] — my book
Turns an adjective into an ADVERB before a VERB
慢慢地走 [mànmàn de zǒu] — walk slowly
Introduces a COMPLEMENT after a verb or adjective (degree/result/manner)
跑得快 [pǎo de kuài] — run fast

tables.caption_tr: 的 (de) in Detail — Before a Noun
rows: 我买的衣服 [wǒ mǎi de yīfu]

tables.caption_tr: 地 (de) in Detail — Before a Verb
rows: 高高兴兴地说 [gāogāoxìngxìng de shuō]
快走 [kuài zǒu] or 快地走 [kuài de zǒu]
Most single-syllable adjectives (快, 慢 as single char, 好) can modify a verb directly WITHOUT 地, but 2-syllable adjectives almost always need 地.

tables.caption_tr: 得 (de) in Detail — After a Verb or Adjective
rows: Verb + 得 + Adjective (often with 很)
Degree complement: how well/fast/etc. an action is done
他跑得很快。[Tā pǎo de hěn kuài.] — He runs very fast.
Describes the result or quality of the action
她说得很好。[Tā shuō de hěn hǎo.] — She speaks very well.
高兴得跳起来 [gāoxìng de tiào qǐlai] — so happy (that he) jumped up
Verb + 得 + 不 + Verb (potential form)
听得懂 [tīng de dǒng] — can understand (by listening)
得 NEVER goes before a noun and NEVER goes before a verb — it always comes right after a verb or adjective.

tables.caption_tr: Decision Guide: Which "de" Do I Need?
rows: 的 — e.g. 我的狗 [wǒ de gǒu] my dog
A verb, and the "de" is describing HOW that action happens
地 — e.g. 认真地写 [rènzhēn de xiě] write carefully
A verb or adjective, and something AFTER describes the result/degree
得 — e.g. 写得好 [xiě de hǎo] write well
的 = noun-glue, 地 = verb-glue (before), 得 = result-glue (after)
Memorize the 3 positions, not just the sound

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes for Beginners
rows: 他很好地说汉语。 (using 地 after the verb)
他汉语说得很好。 [Tā Hànyǔ shuō de hěn hǎo.]
The evaluation of HOW he speaks comes AFTER the verb, so it needs 得, not 地
这是我的书。 [Zhè shì wǒ de shū.]
Possession before a noun always uses 的, never 得
她高兴的笑了。 (using 的 before a verb)
她高兴地笑了。 [Tā gāoxìng de xiào le.]
高兴 modifies the verb 笑 (how she laughed), so it needs 地, not 的
跑地很快 (using 地 after the verb)
跑得很快 [pǎo de hěn kuài]
A complement describing the result/degree after a verb always uses 得

tables.caption_tr: Watch Out: 的, 得, 地 Have Other Pronunciations Too (Not as Particles)
rows: 我得走了。 [Wǒ děi zǒu le.]
I have to go (need to / must)
As a structural grammar particle (the topic of this page), all three are ALWAYS read as the neutral tone "de".

examples.target: 这是我的书。
examples.reading: Zhè shì wǒ de shū.
examples.translation_tr: This is my book. (的 marks possession: my + 的 + noun)

examples.target: 他慢慢地走进教室。
examples.reading: Tā mànmàn de zǒu jìn jiàoshì.
examples.translation_tr: He walked into the classroom slowly. (地 marks the adverb describing how he walked)

examples.target: 她说得很好。
examples.reading: Tā shuō de hěn hǎo.
examples.translation_tr: She speaks (it) very well. (得 introduces a complement describing how well she speaks)

examples.target: 漂亮的花在桌子上。
examples.reading: Piàoliang de huā zài zhuōzi shàng.
examples.translation_tr: The beautiful flower is on the table. (的 links the adjective 漂亮 to the noun 花)

examples.target: 我们高兴地唱歌。
examples.reading: Wǒmen gāoxìng de chàng gē.
examples.translation_tr: We sang songs happily. (地 turns the adjective 高兴 into an adverb before the verb 唱歌)

examples.target: 他跑得很快。
examples.reading: Tā pǎo de hěn kuài.
examples.translation_tr: He runs very fast. (得 attaches the degree complement 很快 after the verb 跑)

examples.target: 这是谁的手机?
examples.reading: Zhè shì shéi de shǒujī?
examples.translation_tr: Whose phone is this? (的 marks possession in a question)

examples.target: 你写得对不对?
examples.reading: Nǐ xiě de duì bú duì?
examples.translation_tr: Is what you wrote correct or not? (得 introduces a complement evaluating the result of writing)

a-particle.intro_tr: 啊[a] is a sentence-final mood particle (语气词[yǔqìcí]) used almost entirely in spoken Chinese to color a sentence with emotion — surprise, admiration, complaint, urgency, or simply friendliness. It carries no meaning of its own and never changes the grammatical structure of a sentence; it only softens or intensifies the tone. A key feature that trips up beginners is that 啊 changes its pronunciation (and sometimes its written character) depending on the sound that comes right before it — this is called 音变[yīnbiàn], 'sound change'. Because it is so tone-dependent, 啊 is best learned by listening to native speech, but the rules below cover the patterns you will meet at HSK3 level. Compare it with 吗[ma] (yes/no question), 呢[ne] (follow-up question), and 吧[ba] (suggestion/guess) — all four particles can appear at the end of a sentence but each does a different emotional/grammatical job.

tables.caption_tr: Sound-change (音变[yīnbiàn]) rules: how 啊[a] is pronounced (and often written) after different preceding sounds
column_headers: Preceding sound (last sound of previous syllable)
rows: a, o, e, i, ü (vowel endings)
好大呀![Hǎo dà ya!] — So big!
快走哇![Kuài zǒu wa!] — Go quickly!
真甜哪![Zhēn tián na!] — So sweet!
你别太忙啊![Nǐ bié tài máng a!] — Don't be too busy!
ra (rare, informal, often just left as 啊)
Any other sound (default, no clear change)
你去啊?[Nǐ qù a?] — Are you going?
footnotes_tr: In writing, many textbooks and native speakers simply keep 啊 regardless of the sound change and let pronunciation do the work — you are not wrong to always write 啊, but recognizing 呀/哇/哪 in reading is important.
This sound change only affects PRONUNCIATION triggered by the immediately preceding syllable's final sound, not the meaning of 啊 itself.

tables.caption_tr: The four main functions of 啊[a] in a sentence
rows: 太漂亮了啊![Tài piàoliang le a!]
你叫什么名字啊?[Nǐ jiào shénme míngzi a?]
Emphasizes each item one by one
书啊、笔啊、本子啊,都在书包里。[Shū a, bǐ a, běnzi a, dōu zài shūbāo lǐ.]
Books, pens, notebooks — they're all in the bag.

tables.caption_tr: 啊[a] compared with the other common sentence-final particles
rows: Emotional coloring: exclamation, softening, listing, urging
No (only if a question word/structure is already present)
真好吃啊![Zhēn hǎochī a!] — So delicious!
Turns a statement into a yes/no question
你好吗?[Nǐ hǎo ma?] — Are you well?
我很好,你呢?[Wǒ hěn hǎo, nǐ ne?] — I'm fine, and you?
No, but softens tone of a statement/command
走吧![Zǒu ba!] — Let's go! / 你累了吧?[Nǐ lèi le ba?] — You're tired, right?
Marks completed action or a new state of affairs
下雨了![Xià yǔ le!] — It's raining now! (new situation)
footnotes_tr: 啊 can actually combine with 了 or follow a 吗/呢-question in casual speech to add extra feeling, e.g. 下雨了啊![Xià yǔ le a!] 'Oh, it's raining!' — here 啊 adds surprise on top of 了's state-change meaning.
Unlike 吗, 啊 by itself never creates a yes/no question — it only makes an already-formed question or statement sound warmer or more emotional.

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed conversational patterns using 啊[a]
rows: A: 你是老师吗?B: 是啊!
A: 这是你的书吧?B: 对啊!
'Who is it?' — very common everyday question
小心啊,别摔倒啊![Xiǎoxīn a, bié shuāidǎo a!]
快来啊,大家都在等你![Kuài lái a, dàjiā dōu zài děng nǐ!]

examples.target: 今天的天气真好啊!
examples.reading: Jīntiān de tiānqì zhēn hǎo a!
examples.translation_tr: The weather today is really nice!  (啊 adds an exclamatory, admiring tone)

examples.target: 你怎么才来啊?
examples.reading: Nǐ zěnme cái lái ya?
examples.translation_tr: Why are you only arriving now? (啊→呀 after the 'ai' vowel; softens a mildly complaining question)

examples.target: 这个蛋糕真甜啊!
examples.reading: Zhège dàngāo zhēn tián na!
examples.translation_tr: This cake is really sweet! (啊→哪 after 'n' in 甜[tián])

examples.target: 快跑啊!
examples.reading: Kuài pǎo wa!
examples.translation_tr: Run, quick! (啊→哇 after the 'ao' vowel; urgent warning)

examples.target: 你要买什么啊?
examples.reading: Nǐ yào mǎi shénme a?
examples.translation_tr: What do you want to buy? (friendly, casual tone softening a question — no sound change needed after 'e')

examples.target: 水果啊、蔬菜啊、肉啊,冰箱里什么都有。
examples.reading: Shuǐguǒ a, shūcài a, ròu a, bīngxiāng lǐ shénme dōu yǒu.
examples.translation_tr: Fruit, vegetables, meat — the fridge has everything. (啊 marks each item in a list for emphasis)

examples.target: A: 谁啊?  B: 是我啊!
examples.reading: A: Shéi a?  B: Shì wǒ a!
examples.translation_tr: A: Who is it? B: It's me! (啊 gives a natural, conversational ring to both the question and the answer)

examples.target: 小心啊,路很滑!
examples.reading: Xiǎoxīn a, lù hěn huá!
examples.translation_tr: Be careful, the road is very slippery! (啊 softens the warning/imperative, making it sound caring rather than harsh)

dui-coverb.intro_tr: 对 (duì) is one of the most frequent coverbs (co-verbs act like prepositions) in Mandarin, used to introduce the person, thing, or topic that a feeling, attitude, action, or evaluation is directed toward. Typical translations include "toward," "to," "about," or "for," depending on context. The single most important rule for beginners: the phrase "对 + Object" always comes BEFORE the main verb or adjective, never after it like an English preposition phrase would. 对 also appears in several very common fixed expressions (对不起 "sorry," 对了 "by the way," 对啊 "right/exactly") and, separately, functions as a standalone adjective meaning "correct." This page focuses on 对 as a coverb; for its more formal/written cousins see 对于 and 关于.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure & Word Order
rows: 他对我很好。[Tā duì wǒ hěn hǎo.] — He is very good to me.
我对音乐很了解。[Wǒ duì yīnyuè hěn liǎojiě.] — I know a lot about music.
Subject + 不 + 对 + Object + Adj/VP
Negation goes BEFORE 对, not after
他不对我说实话。[Tā bú duì wǒ shuō shíhuà.] — He doesn't tell me the truth.
As for O.../From O's point of view
对我来说，这很难。[Duì wǒ láishuō, zhè hěn nán.] — For me, this is difficult.
我对历史感兴趣。[Wǒ duì lìshǐ gǎn xìngqù.] — I'm interested in history.

tables.caption_tr: Common Collocations: 对 + Target + Predicate
rows: 她对绘画感兴趣。[Tā duì huìhuà gǎn xìngqù.]
睡觉对健康有帮助。[Shuìjiào duì jiànkāng yǒu bāngzhù.]
多喝水对身体有好处。[Duō hē shuǐ duì shēntǐ yǒu hǎochù.]
抽烟对身体不好。[Chōuyān duì shēntǐ bù hǎo.]
她对朋友很好。[Tā duì péngyou hěn hǎo.]
时间对我们很重要。[Shíjiān duì wǒmen hěn zhòngyào.]
老板对结果很满意。[Lǎobǎn duì jiéguǒ hěn mǎnyì.]
医生要对病人负责。[Yīshēng yào duì bìngrén fùzé.]
他对中国文化很了解。[Tā duì Zhōngguó wénhuà hěn liǎojiě.]
别对我这么客气。[Bié duì wǒ zhème kèqi.]
父母对孩子很严格。[Fùmǔ duì háizi hěn yángé.]

tables.caption_tr: 对 vs. Similar Coverbs — Which One to Use
rows: toward / to / about (general attitude, feeling, effect, evaluation)
我对你没有意见。[Wǒ duì nǐ méiyǒu yìjiàn.] — I have no complaints about you.
regarding / with respect to (more formal, often sentence-initial)
written/formal register; cannot be used with feeling verbs like 好/客气
对于这个问题，大家意见不同。[Duìyú zhège wèntí, dàjiā yìjiàn bùtóng.]
about / concerning (topic of a book, talk, discussion)
introduces a TOPIC, not a target of feeling; often sentence-initial or after 一本书/一个报告 etc.
这是一本关于历史的书。[Zhè shì yì běn guānyú lìshǐ de shū.]
我跟他一起去。[Wǒ gēn tā yìqǐ qù.] — I'll go with him.
marks the receiver of giving/calling/sending etc.
我给你打电话。[Wǒ gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.] — I'll call you.
toward (direction, often formal — asking, learning, facing)
physical or abstract direction, more formal than 对
他向我道歉。[Tā xiàng wǒ dàoqiàn.] — He apologized to me.

tables.caption_tr: Fixed Expressions Containing 对 (Not Following the Coverb Pattern)
rows: That's right! / Oh, by the way...
Used to correct oneself or introduce a new topic
对 is part of a compound verb here, not a coverb
Formal coverb-like verb, different from plain 对

tables.caption_tr: Negation, Questions & Common Mistakes
rows: S + 不 + 对 + O + Adj/VP
我不对他生气。[Wǒ bú duì tā shēngqì.] — I'm not angry at him.
不 must go BEFORE 对, never between 对 and the object
S + 对 + O + Adj/VP + 吗？
你对中国菜感兴趣吗？[Nǐ duì Zhōngguó cài gǎn xìngqù ma?]
Standard 吗 question, 对-phrase stays before the predicate
should be: 我对他很好。[Wǒ duì tā hěn hǎo.]
Learners often place 对+O after the adjective by analogy with English 'good to him' — this is incorrect in Chinese
对 alone after 是/说得 = 'correct'
你说得对。[Nǐ shuō de duì.] — What you said is correct.
Here 对 is NOT a coverb; it's a stand-alone adjective meaning 'right/correct'
S + 对 + O + 没有兴趣 / 不感兴趣
我对足球没有兴趣。[Wǒ duì zúqiú méiyǒu xìngqù.]
没有 or 不 negates 感兴趣, both placed after 对+O, before the verb phrase itself

examples.target: 我对中国历史很感兴趣。
examples.reading: Wǒ duì Zhōngguó lìshǐ hěn gǎn xìngqù.
examples.translation_tr: I am very interested in Chinese history. (对 introduces the topic of interest, placed BEFORE the verb 感兴趣)

examples.target: 运动对身体有好处。
examples.reading: Yùndòng duì shēntǐ yǒu hǎochù.
examples.translation_tr: Exercise is good for the body. (对 + target + 有好处 = 'good for...')

examples.target: 他对我很好。
examples.reading: Tā duì wǒ hěn hǎo.
examples.translation_tr: He is very good to me. (对 + person + 很 + adjective = attitude/treatment toward someone)

examples.target: 这件事对公司很重要。
examples.reading: Zhè jiàn shì duì gōngsī hěn zhòngyào.
examples.translation_tr: This matter is very important to the company.

examples.target: 对不起，我迟到了。
examples.reading: Duìbuqǐ, wǒ chídào le.
examples.translation_tr: Sorry, I'm late. (fixed expression, does not follow the S+对+O pattern)

examples.target: 对我来说，学汉语不容易。
examples.reading: Duì wǒ láishuō, xué Hànyǔ bù róngyì.
examples.translation_tr: For me, learning Chinese is not easy. (对...来说 = 'as for..., from...'s point of view')

examples.target: 老师对学生很严格。

examples.target: 我对这个问题不太了解。

examples.translation_tr: I don't understand this problem very well. (negation 不 goes before the main predicate, not before 对)

geng-comparative.intro_tr: 更[gèng] is an adverb meaning "even more" or "still more" — it intensifies an adjective or verb by pushing an existing quality or action a step further, rather than describing an absolute high degree like 很[hěn] or 最[zuì] do. It always sits directly in front of the adjective or verb it modifies (never after) and is extremely common in comparative sentences built with 比[bǐ], where it signals that the difference is being pushed further ("A is even more X than B"). Unlike 最[zuì] (which marks the single highest degree, "the most"), 更[gèng] is always relative — it compares to a previous state, a rival, or an implicit baseline ("compared to that, this is even more..."). In formal writing, 更[gèng] is often replaced or reinforced by its two-syllable cousin 更加[gèngjiā]. Because 更[gèng] is a pure adverb, it can never attach directly to a noun and can never be preceded by 不[bù] to mean "less" — negation works differently, as shown in the tables below.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Position of 更[gèng] in a Sentence
rows: She is even better at cooking.
Zhè gèng shì yí ge hǎo jīhuì.
This is even more of a good opportunity.
Not grammatical — 更 cannot modify a bare noun.

tables.caption_tr: 更[gèng] in Comparative Sentences with 比[bǐ]: A 比 B 更 + Adjective
rows: A + 比 + B + 更 + Adj
Today is even colder than yesterday.
A + 比 + B + 更 + Verb Phrase
Tā bǐ wǒ gèng liǎojiě qíngkuàng.
He understands the situation even better than I do.
A + 比 + B + 更 + Adj + Amount (optional)
这个比那个更贵一点儿。
Zhège bǐ nàge gèng guì yìdiǎnr.
This one is even a bit more expensive than that one.
没有 + Noun + 比 + Noun + 更 + Adj + 的了
没有比健康更重要的了。
Méiyǒu bǐ jiànkāng gèng zhòngyào de le.
Nothing is more important than health. (superlative use)

tables.caption_tr: Degree Adverbs at a Glance: 很 vs 太 vs 最 vs 更 vs 非常
rows: 'quite / very' (often just a neutral link, no strong emphasis)
他很高。 Tā hěn gāo. — He is tall.
他非常高。 Tā fēicháng gāo. — He is extremely tall.
他太高了！Tā tài gāo le! — He is SO tall!
'the most' (single highest point, no comparison word needed)
他最高。 Tā zuì gāo. — He is the tallest.
他更高。 Tā gèng gāo. — He is even taller (than before/than someone).

tables.caption_tr: 更[gèng] vs 还[hái]: Two Ways to Say 'Even More'
rows: 'even more' — but also carries 'still / additionally' nuances
Neutral, works in speech and writing
A 比 B 更 + Adj (very common, neutral)
A 比 B 还 + Adj (adds a stronger note of surprise/unexpectedness)
他比我更聪明。 Tā bǐ wǒ gèng cōngming. — He is even smarter than me. (plain statement)
他比我还聪明！ Tā bǐ wǒ hái cōngming! — He is even smarter than ME! (surprised tone)
Also means 'still' in general: 他还在睡觉。 (He is still sleeping.)

tables.caption_tr: 更[gèng] vs 更加[gèngjiā]: Casual vs Formal Register
rows: Neutral, everyday spoken and written Chinese
Shēnghuó gèng hǎo le. — Life has gotten even better.
More formal, common in writing, essays, news
Jīngjì gèngjiā fādá le. — The economy has become even more developed.

tables.caption_tr: Common Collocations with 更[gèng]
Negation and Special Patterns with 更[gèng]
rows: Wrong — 不更 does not mean 'less good'. Use 不如 or 没有...那么 instead: 这个不如那个好 (This one isn't as good as that one).
Tā gèng bù xǐhuan hē kāfēi le.
'更' comes before the negation — meaning 'even less/even more not...'
Méiyǒu bǐ zhè gèng jiǎndān de le.
Fixed pattern meaning 'nothing is more ... than this' — a superlative built from a comparative.
天气越来越热，比昨天更热。
Tiānqì yuè lái yuè rè, bǐ zuótiān gèng rè.
越来越 shows a trend over time; 更 pinpoints a specific comparison point within that trend.
