bi-comparison-extended.title_tr: Extended 比[bǐ] Comparisons (比...更 / 多了 / 一点儿)
bi-comparison-extended.intro_tr: This page extends the basic 比[bǐ] comparison (A 比 B + Adjective) by adding precision: how MUCH more or less one thing is compared to another. You can intensify the comparison with 更[gèng] or 还[hái] ('even more'), soften it with 一点儿[yìdiǎnr] or 一些[yìxiē] ('a little more'), emphasize a big gap with 多了[duō le] or 得多[de duō] ('much more'), or state an exact difference with a number + measure word (比...大三岁). All of these attachments go in fixed positions relative to the adjective, and mixing up the word order — or adding 很/太 incorrectly — is the most common learner mistake with this pattern.

tables.caption_tr: Core extended patterns with 比[bǐ]
rows: 他比我高。[Tā bǐ wǒ gāo.] — He is taller than me.
A + 比 + B + 更 + Adj
A is even more [Adj] than B
他比我更高。[Tā bǐ wǒ gèng gāo.] — He is even taller than me.
A + 比 + B + 还 + Adj
A is even more [Adj] than B (often w/ surprise)
他比我还高。[Tā bǐ wǒ hái gāo.] — He's even taller than me (surprisingly).
A + 比 + B + Adj + 一点儿/(一)些
A is a little more [Adj] than B
他比我高一点儿。[Tā bǐ wǒ gāo yìdiǎnr.] — He's a little taller than me.
A + 比 + B + Adj + 多了
A is much more [Adj] than B
他比我高多了。[Tā bǐ wǒ gāo duō le.] — He's much taller than me.
A + 比 + B + Adj + 得多
A is much more [Adj] than B
他比我高得多。[Tā bǐ wǒ gāo de duō.] — He's much taller than me.
A + 比 + B + Adj + Number + Measure Word
A is exactly [amount] more [Adj] than B
他比我高五厘米。[Tā bǐ wǒ gāo wǔ límǐ.] — He's 5cm taller than me.

tables.caption_tr: Degree modifiers: where they attach and what they mean
rows: No — mutually exclusive with an exact number
Like 更, often adds mild surprise/emphasis
Same as 一点儿, slightly more formal/written

tables.caption_tr: Negative and question forms
rows: A is not more [Adj] than B (does NOT mean 'A is less')
我不比他高。[Wǒ bù bǐ tā gāo.] — I'm not taller than him.
A + 没有 + B + (那么/这么) + Adj
A is not as [Adj] as B (clearer 'less than' meaning)
我没有他那么高。[Wǒ méiyǒu tā nàme gāo.] — I'm not as tall as him.
A + 比 + B + Adj + 吗?
他比你高吗?[Tā bǐ nǐ gāo ma?] — Is he taller than you?
A + 比 + B + Adj + 多少?
By how much is A more [Adj] than B?
他比你高多少?[Tā bǐ nǐ gāo duōshao?] — By how much is he taller than you?

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes with extended 比[bǐ] sentences
rows: Using 很/太 before the adjective
他比我高。/ 他比我更高。
很 and 太 clash with the comparative meaning of 比; use 更/还 instead if you need intensity.
Putting 一点儿 before the adjective
Degree complements (一点儿, 多了, 得多, numbers) always follow the adjective, never precede it.
他比我高多了。 OR 他比我更高。
更/还 (before Adj) and 多了/得多/一点儿 (after Adj) are usually not combined together in one sentence.
Using 不比 to mean 'less than'
我不比他高 (intended: I am shorter than him)
我没有他高。/ 我比他矮。
不比 only negates the comparison ('not necessarily more'); it doesn't assert the opposite direction.
Forgetting the measure word with numbers
An exact quantity comparison needs a measure word (岁, 厘米, 公斤, 块, 分钟...) after the number.

examples.target: 今天比昨天更冷。
examples.reading: Jīntiān bǐ zuótiān gèng lěng.
examples.translation_tr: Today is even colder than yesterday.
examples.note_tr: 更 adds emphasis to an already-understood comparison.

examples.target: 这本书比那本书还贵。
examples.reading: Zhè běn shū bǐ nà běn shū hái guì.

examples.target: 我姐姐比我大三岁。

examples.translation_tr: My older sister is three years older than me.
examples.note_tr: An exact quantity (三岁) placed after the adjective states a precise difference.

examples.target: 今年的雨比去年多得多。
examples.reading: Jīnnián de yǔ bǐ qùnián duō de duō.
examples.translation_tr: This year's rainfall is much greater than last year's.
examples.note_tr: 得多 is interchangeable with 多了 for 'much more/much...er', but 得多 sounds slightly more written/formal.

examples.target: 这个方法不比那个好。
examples.reading: Zhège fāngfǎ bù bǐ nàge hǎo.
examples.translation_tr: This method is not better than that one.
examples.note_tr: 不比 negates the comparison itself — it means 'not necessarily better', not 'worse'.

examples.reading: Tā pǎo de bǐ wǒ kuài yìxiē.
examples.translation_tr: He runs a bit faster than me.
examples.note_tr: 一些 is interchangeable with 一点儿 for small differences; here it combines with the 得-complement structure (跑得...).

gen-yiyang.intro_tr: The pattern 跟[gēn]...一样[yíyàng] is the standard way to say that two people, things, or situations are "the same as" one another. 跟[gēn] here functions like the preposition "with/as," while 一样[yíyàng] literally means "one kind/the same," and together they form a bridge linking the two items being equated. The pattern is extremely flexible: use it alone to say two things are simply identical, add an adjective after 一样[yíyàng] to compare a specific quality (height, age, price, etc.), or add a verb phrase to say someone does something "just like" someone else. To negate it, put 不[bù] directly before 一样[yíyàng] (never before the adjective), and to ask a yes/no question, simply add 吗[ma] at the end. Because this structure states pure equality rather than a difference in degree, it works alongside — but differently from — comparison patterns like 比[bǐ] (unequal comparison) and 有[yǒu]...那么[nàme] (degree comparison in negatives/questions).

tables.caption_tr: Core Sentence Patterns with 跟[gēn]...一样[yíyàng]
rows: 我跟他一样。[Wǒ gēn tā yíyàng.]
I am the same as him.
A + 跟 + B + 一样 + Adj
我跟他一样高。[Wǒ gēn tā yíyàng gāo.]
I am as tall as him.
A + 跟 + B + 不一样
我跟他不一样。[Wǒ gēn tā bù yíyàng.]
A + 跟 + B + 不一样 + Adj
我跟他不一样高。[Wǒ gēn tā bù yíyàng gāo.]
He and I are not the same height.
A + 跟 + B + 一样 (+ Adj) + 吗?
你跟他一样大吗?[Nǐ gēn tā yíyàng dà ma?]
Are you the same age as him?
A + 跟 + B + 一样 + Verb Phrase
我跟你一样喜欢中文。[Wǒ gēn nǐ yíyàng xǐhuan Zhōngwén.]
I like Chinese just like you do.

tables.caption_tr: Choosing the Linking Word: 跟[gēn] vs 和[hé] vs 与[yǔ]
rows: 我跟你一样。[Wǒ gēn nǐ yíyàng.]
我和你一样。[Wǒ hé nǐ yíyàng.]
Fully interchangeable with 跟[gēn]; slightly more common in writing.
我与你一样。[Wǒ yǔ nǐ yíyàng.]
Used in essays, news, and formal writing; rare in casual speech.

tables.caption_tr: 跟[gēn]...一样[yíyàng] vs Other Comparison Structures
rows: State that two things are the same.
A跟B不一样。[A gēn B bù yíyàng.]
Show one side exceeds the other in degree.
A有B那么高吗?[A yǒu B nàme gāo ma?]
Ask or deny whether A reaches B's degree.
A没有B那么高。[A méiyǒu B nàme gāo.]
Negative degree comparison (A falls short of B).
Emphasize resemblance in appearance or manner, often more vivid/figurative than 跟...一样.

tables.caption_tr: Degree Adverbs Commonly Placed Before 一样[yíyàng]
rows: 这幅画跟原作完全一样。[Zhè fú huà gēn yuánzuò wánquán yíyàng.] — This painting is completely identical to the original.
这两个字不太一样。[Zhè liǎng gè zì bú tài yíyàng.] — These two characters aren't quite the same.
我们的想法差不多一样。[Wǒmen de xiǎngfǎ chàbuduō yíyàng.] — Our ideas are almost the same.
这两只猫几乎一样。[Zhè liǎng zhī māo jīhū yíyàng.] — These two cats are nearly identical.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes to Avoid
rows: ✓ 我跟他一样高。[Wǒ gēn tā yíyàng gāo.]
Never insert 是[shì] before the adjective; the adjective attaches directly after 一样.
✓ 我跟他一样高。[Wǒ gēn tā yíyàng gāo.]
Word order is fixed: 跟 + B must come before 一样, not after.
✓ 我跟他完全一样。[Wǒ gēn tā wánquán yíyàng.] / 我跟他不太一样。[Wǒ gēn tā bú tài yíyàng.]
一样 is not modified by 很[hěn]; use 完全[wánquán] or 不太[bú tài] instead.
✓ 我跟他不一样高。[Wǒ gēn tā bù yíyàng gāo.] / 我没有他那么高。[Wǒ méiyǒu tā nàme gāo.]
To negate a degree comparison, negate 一样 itself (or switch to 没有...那么), not the adjective.

examples.reading: Wǒ gēn nǐ yíyàng gāo.
examples.translation_tr: I am as tall as you.

yidianr-youdianr.title_tr: 一点儿 vs 有点儿: The "a little / a bit" Difference
yidianr-youdianr.intro_tr: 一点儿[yìdiǎnr] and 有点儿[yǒudiǎnr] both translate as "a little / a bit" in English, but they behave completely differently in a sentence, and beginners mix them up constantly. 一点儿[yìdiǎnr] always comes AFTER an adjective or verb (Adj/V + 一点儿), and it is neutral or even friendly in tone — it softens requests, expresses a small quantity of something, or marks a small comparative difference. 有点儿[yǒudiǎnr] always comes BEFORE an adjective (有点儿 + Adj), and it almost always carries a negative or undesirable nuance — the speaker is complaining, worrying, or pointing out a problem, however mild. Getting the word order backwards (e.g. saying 一点儿贵 instead of 有点儿贵, or 有点儿快一点儿 instead of 快一点儿) is one of the most common beginner errors in Mandarin. This page gives you the exact word-order formulas, the connotation rules, and a list of frequent mistakes so you can use both correctly from day one.

tables.caption_tr: Core comparison: 一点儿[yìdiǎnr] vs 有点儿[yǒudiǎnr]
rows: BEFORE the adjective (rarely before a verb)
Softening requests, comparative degree, small quantity of a noun
Complaining mildly, expressing a minor problem or discomfort
Yes: 一点儿[yìdiǎnr] + N (e.g. 一点儿水 'a little water')
No — 有点儿 cannot directly precede a bare noun
Often used with or implying a comparison ('a bit more/less than before')
No comparison needed — describes the current state alone
点儿[diǎnr] (e.g. 来点儿茶 'bring some tea')
有点[yǒudiǎn] (儿 often dropped in speech)

tables.caption_tr: Structural formulas with examples
rows: Adj + 一点儿[yìdiǎnr] (often with 比[bǐ])
这个比那个便宜一点儿[Zhège bǐ nàge piányi yìdiǎnr]
This one is a little cheaper than that one.
请你说慢一点儿[Qǐng nǐ shuō màn yìdiǎnr]
我要一点儿水[Wǒ yào yìdiǎnr shuǐ]
我有点儿想家[Wǒ yǒudiǎnr xiǎngjiā]
一点儿[yìdiǎnr] + 也/都 + 不/没 + Adj/V
我一点儿也不累[Wǒ yìdiǎnr yě bú lèi]

tables.caption_tr: Connotation check: which adjectives sound natural with 有点儿[yǒudiǎnr]
rows: 贵[guì], 累[lèi], 冷[lěng], 难[nán], 胖[pàng], 疼[téng]
Yes — very common (有点儿贵 'a bit expensive')
Yes, especially in comparisons (贵一点儿 'a bit more expensive')
好[hǎo], 漂亮[piàoliang], 聪明[cōngming], 便宜[piányi]
Unusual — sounds sarcastic or implies a hidden problem
Yes, very natural (便宜一点儿 'a bit cheaper')
大[dà], 小[xiǎo], 高[gāo], 长[cháng]
Possible if framed as a problem (有点儿大 'a bit too big')
Yes, natural in comparisons (大一点儿 'a bit bigger')
footnotes_tr: Rule of thumb: 有点儿 + Adj almost always means 'this is a slight problem.' If the adjective is normally 'good news,' 有点儿 flips it into something unwanted (有点儿聪明 can sound like 'suspiciously/annoyingly clever').

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes to avoid
rows: 一点儿[yìdiǎnr] must come AFTER the adjective/complement, never before it.
一点儿 needs a comparison anchor (比...); for a standalone complaint about the current state, use 有点儿.
Before a bare noun expressing a small quantity, only 一点儿 is possible — 有点儿 cannot modify a noun directly.
这个蛋糕好吃一点儿。/ 这个蛋糕很好吃。
有点儿 sounds odd or sarcastic with strongly positive adjectives like 好吃[hǎochī]; use 一点儿 for comparison or 很 for a plain positive statement.
我有点儿不高兴。 / 我快乐一点儿了。
Never combine both markers on the same adjective — choose one pattern, not both.

tables.caption_tr: Special fixed patterns worth memorizing
rows: 他一点儿也不笨。[Tā yìdiǎnr yě bú bèn.] — He's not stupid at all.
这一点儿都不难。[Zhè yìdiǎnr dōu bù nán.] — This isn't difficult at all.
来点儿茶。[Lái diǎnr chá.] — Bring some tea.
a friendly request for slightly more/less
快一点儿吧![Kuài yìdiǎnr ba!] — Hurry up a bit!
有(一)点儿 + Adj (spoken, 儿 dropped)
天有点冷。[Tiān yǒudiǎn lěng.] — It's a bit cold.

examples.target: 这道题有点儿难。

examples.translation_tr: This problem is a bit difficult (and that's not great).

examples.target: 我今天有点儿不舒服。

examples.target: 这件衣服太贵了,便宜一点儿吧。

yuelaiyue.intro_tr: 越来越[yuèláiyuè] literally means "the more it comes, the more it..." and is used to express that a situation, quality, or state is progressively increasing or changing over time — equivalent to English "more and more..." or "increasingly...". It is one of the most common adverbial patterns in Mandarin and is placed directly before an adjective or a verb phrase that describes a state. Unlike a normal adjective sentence, 很[hěn] is NOT used with 越来越[yuèláiyuè], and the sentence very often ends with the particle 了[le] to show that the change is ongoing up to now. This pattern is different from 越...越...[yuè...yuè...], which compares two variables changing together (e.g., "the more you study, the more you know"), while 越来越[yuèláiyuè] describes a single thing changing over time on its own.

tables.caption_tr: Basic structure of 越来越[yuèláiyuè]
rows: 天气越来越冷了。[Tiānqì yuèláiyuè lěng le.]
The weather is getting colder and colder.
我越来越喜欢这里。[Wǒ yuèláiyuè xǐhuan zhèlǐ.]
I like it here more and more.
Subject + V + 得[de] + 越来越[yuèláiyuè] + Adj
他说得越来越流利。[Tā shuō de yuèláiyuè liúlì.]
He speaks more and more fluently.
越来越多[yuèláiyuè duō]的[de] + Noun + V
越来越多的人喜欢旅游。[Yuèláiyuè duō de rén xǐhuan lǚyóu.]
More and more people like traveling.

tables.caption_tr: 越来越[yuèláiyuè] vs. similar patterns — common confusion points
rows: 他越来越胖了。[Tā yuèláiyuè pàng le.]
One subject, changing over time; no second clause needed.
他越吃越胖。[Tā yuè chī yuè pàng.]
Links two actions/qualities that change together (cause & effect).
Static comparison between two points, not a continuous process.
S + 越来越[yuèláiyuè] + Adj + 了[le]
他越来越忙了。[Tā yuèláiyuè máng le.]
了[le] emphasizes the change has been happening and continues now.

tables.caption_tr: Grammar rules and restrictions
rows: 越来越[yuèláiyuè] already carries the intensifying meaning; 很[hěn] is redundant/wrong here.
Sentence-final 了[le] is common but optional
他越来越高了。[Tā yuèláiyuè gāo le.]
了[le] stresses that the change is continuing up to the present moment.
Can be followed by a noun with 越来越多的[yuèláiyuè duō de] + N
越来越多的问题[yuèláiyuè duō de wèntí]
多[duō] + 的[de] is required to modify a noun directly.
Cannot take a direct object after the adjective/verb
他越来越喜欢音乐。[Tā yuèláiyuè xǐhuan yīnyuè.]
Works fine with psychological verbs like 喜欢[xǐhuan], 讨厌[tǎoyàn], 了解[liǎojiě] that can take objects.
越来越[yuèláiyuè] needs a gradable state (adjective or state-verb), not an identity statement with 是[shì].

tables.caption_tr: Common collocations with 越来越[yuèláiyuè]
rows: fewer and fewer / less and less

yue-yue.intro_tr: 越...越... [yuè...yuè...] is a correlative structure meaning "the more..., the more...", linking two conditions that increase or change together. The first 越 introduces the cause/condition, and the second 越 introduces the resulting effect, both attaching directly to verbs or adjectives (never nouns). The subject of the sentence can be shared by both clauses, or each clause can have its own separate subject. This pattern is distinct from 越来越 [yuèláiyuè], which tracks a single subject's change over time rather than correlating two variables. 越...越... is extremely common in spoken Chinese and appears in many fixed expressions like 越快越好 [yuè kuài yuè hǎo] "the faster the better".

tables.caption_tr: Basic Formation Patterns: What Can Follow 越
rows: Tiānqì yuè rè, rén yuè lǎn.
The hotter the weather, the lazier people get.
The more I think about it, the angrier I get.
Dōngxi yuè guì, tā yuè xiǎng mǎi.
The more expensive the item, the more he wants to buy it.
footnotes_tr: 越 must attach directly to a verb or adjective; it cannot attach directly to a bare noun.
Adverbs of degree like 很/非常 cannot appear between 越 and the verb/adjective.

tables.caption_tr: Same-Subject vs Different-Subject Patterns
rows: The more she sings, the better it sounds.
Subj1 + 越 + Pred1，Subj2 + 越 + Pred2
你越不让他去，他越想去。
Nǐ yuè bú ràng tā qù, tā yuè xiǎng qù.
The more you forbid him to go, the more he wants to go.
越 + Clause1（no subj before 1st 越 if implied）
The later it gets, the colder it is.
Subj + 越 + V + 越 + 想/要 + V
Tā yuè chī yuè xiǎng chī.
The more he eats, the more he wants to eat.
footnotes_tr: When both clauses share one subject, the subject usually appears once at the very beginning of the sentence.
When subjects differ, each subject is placed right before its own 越.

tables.caption_tr: 越...越... vs 越来越 (yuèláiyuè): Key Differences
rows: 雨越下越大。 [Yǔ yuè xià yuè dà.]
天气越来越冷了。 [Tiānqì yuèláiyuè lěng le.]
The harder it rains, the heavier it gets.
The weather is getting colder and colder.
Very commonly added at the end
No, both 越 clauses are required
N/A — 来 is fixed, only the adjective/verb changes

tables.caption_tr: Common Fixed Expressions with 越...越...
rows: The more people, the livelier it is
The busier one gets, the more chaotic things become
The more one talks about it, the angrier one gets
One gets more youthful with age (said as a compliment)
footnotes_tr: Many of these short two-clause phrases function as standalone idiomatic sayings, not requiring a full sentence context.

tables.caption_tr: Word Order Rules and Common Errors
rows: Subject goes before the first 越 (shared subject)
The subject must precede 越, never come between 越 and the verb.
No degree adverbs between 越 and V/Adj
越 attaches directly to the verb/adjective with nothing in between.
Final 了 goes at the very end, not after each clause
天气越来越冷，我越穿越多了。
天气越来越冷了，我越穿越多。
If 了 is used, it typically closes the whole sentence rather than each clause separately.
Negation attaches after 越, not before
不 sits between 越 and the verb it negates, just like any other verb/adjective would.
Both 越 clauses must be structurally parallel
Dropping the second 越 breaks the correlative structure; both halves are required.

you-you.intro_tr: 又...又... [yòu...yòu...] is a paired-adverb pattern meaning "both...and..." — it links two adjectives, two verbs, or two "是[shì]" phrases that describe the SAME subject at the SAME time. Unlike English "both", 又...又... doesn't need a word for "and": you simply put 又 before each item, as in 又大又贵[yòu dà yòu guì] "both big and expensive". This is one of the most common ways beginners describe two qualities or two simultaneous actions of one person or thing. A key rule for zero-level learners: the two items paired together are almost always both positive (nice things) or both negative (bad things) — mixing a compliment with a complaint sounds odd unless you intend a deliberate contrast (for that, other structures like 虽然...但是... are better). No 很[hěn], 太[tài], or other degree adverbs are needed before the adjectives, because 又...又... itself already carries emphasis.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure: Subject + 又[yòu] + A + 又[yòu] + B
rows: Subject + 又 + Adj₁ + 又 + Adj₂
Zhège fángjiān yòu dà yòu liàng.
This room is both big and bright.
Subject + 又 + V₁ + 又 + V₂
Subject + 又是 + N₁ + 又是 + N₂
Tā yòu shì xuésheng yòu shì lǎoshī.
He is both a student and a teacher.
Subject + 又不 + A₁ + 又不 + A₂ (negative form)
这个菜又不辣又不咸,没味道。
Zhège cài yòu bú là yòu bù xián, méi wèidao.
This dish is neither spicy nor salty — it has no flavor.

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Paired Adjectives (Common Combinations)
又...又... vs. Similar 'Two-Item' Structures — How to Tell Them Apart
rows: States two simultaneous qualities/actions of ONE subject; everyday, spoken; both items usually same polarity
她又漂亮又聪明。 Tā yòu piàoliang yòu cōngming. — She's pretty and smart.
Same meaning as 又...又... but more formal/written; often used with longer or more abstract adjectives
这个方案既经济又实用。 Zhège fāng'àn jì jīngjì yòu shíyòng. — This plan is both economical and practical.
Two actions happening AT THE SAME MOMENT, subject actively doing both (dynamic, in-progress); NOT for adjectives
他一边吃饭一边看电视。 Tā yìbiān chīfàn yìbiān kàn diànshì. — He eats while watching TV.
One thing increases AS another increases (correlated change), not simple coexistence
天气越来越冷。 Tiānqì yuè lái yuè lěng. — The weather is getting colder and colder.
Adds a SECOND, often STRONGER point; the two clauses can have different subjects/verbs, not just paired adjectives
他不但聪明,而且很努力。 Tā búdàn cōngming, érqiě hěn nǔlì. — He's not only smart, but also very hardworking.

tables.caption_tr: Key Rules and Common Mistakes
rows: The two qualities are normally both positive or both negative; mixing a good trait with a bad one sounds strange without a contrastive marker
✅ 又便宜又好吃 (both good) ❌ 又便宜又难吃 sounds odd — say 虽然便宜,但是很难吃 instead
Don't add 很[hěn] or 非常[fēicháng] before the adjectives inside the pattern — 又...又... already supplies emphasis
✅ 又大又贵 ❌ 又很大又很贵
Works with adjectives, verbs, or 是-phrases
Not limited to adjectives — verbs (又哭又笑) and nouns with 是 (又是...又是...) are equally common
又是经理又是老板 — both a manager and a boss
The two items are often similar in length (both 1-character or both 2-character words) for a smoother rhythm, though this is a style preference, not a strict grammar rule
又高又帅 (1+1) rather than mixing very uneven lengths
Means 'neither...nor...'; both items are negated with 不[bù] (or 没[méi] for past/completed situations)
他又不高又不帅。 Tā yòu bù gāo yòu bú shuài. — He's neither tall nor handsome.
Do not confuse with repetitive 又 (adverb meaning 'again')
又 alone before a single verb (without a second 又) usually means 'again' for a past repeated action — that is a different, unrelated usage covered under 再 vs 又
他又来了。 Tā yòu lái le. — He came again. (single 又, not the 又...又... pattern)

zhiyao-jiu.intro_tr: 只要...就... (zhǐyào...jiù...) means "as long as... then..." and it introduces a SUFFICIENT condition: whatever follows 只要 is enough on its own to guarantee the result that follows 就, even though other conditions might also lead to the same result. This is different from 只有...才..., which marks a NECESSARY (exclusive) condition — meaning that is the ONLY way to get the result. 只要 opens the condition clause and can appear before or after its own subject, while 就 is an adverb that must always come right after the subject of the second clause, directly before the verb. This pattern is extremely common in promises, encouragement, rules, and reassurances, e.g. "as long as you try, you'll succeed."

tables.caption_tr: Core formula: how 只要 and 就 connect the two clauses
rows: States the minimal condition that is ENOUGH to trigger the result
States the guaranteed outcome; 就 always sits right before the verb, after the subject

tables.caption_tr: Word order depending on whether the subject is the same in both clauses
rows: Same subject — subject before 只要
Subject + 只要[zhǐyào] + Condition, 就[jiù] + Result
Nǐ zhǐyào nǔlì, jiù néng chénggōng.
As long as you work hard, you can succeed.
Same subject — 只要 before subject
只要[zhǐyào] + Subject + Condition, 就[jiù] + Result
Zhǐyào nǐ nǔlì, jiù néng chénggōng.
As long as you work hard, you can succeed.
只要[zhǐyào] + Subject1 + Condition, Subject2 + 就[jiù] + Result
Zhǐyào tiānqì hǎo, wǒmen jiù qù.
As long as the weather's good, we'll go.

tables.caption_tr: Negative forms
rows: 只要[zhǐyào] + 不[bù]/没[méi] + V..., 就[jiù] + Result
Zhǐyào bú xiàyǔ, wǒmen jiù qù.
As long as it doesn't rain, we'll go.
只要[zhǐyào] + Condition, 就[jiù] + 不[bù]/没[méi] + V...
只要你不说，我就不知道。
Zhǐyào nǐ bù shuō, wǒ jiù bù zhīdào.
As long as you don't say it, I won't know.

tables.caption_tr: 只要...就... vs. similar conditional patterns
rows: Sufficient — this condition alone is enough; other paths may also work
As long as you work hard, you can succeed.
Necessary — this is the ONLY way; nothing else works
Only by working hard can you succeed (nothing else will do).
General — no claim about sufficiency or necessity
If it rains, we won't go.

tables.caption_tr: Common modal/adverb collocations after 就 in the result clause
rows: then can / will be able to
只要努力，就能成功。 (Zhǐyào nǔlì, jiù néng chénggōng.)
只要坚持，就会有进步。 (Zhǐyào jiānchí, jiù huì yǒu jìnbù.)
只要你愿意，就可以来。 (Zhǐyào nǐ yuànyì, jiù kěyǐ lái.)
只要努力，就一定能成功。 (Zhǐyào nǔlì, jiù yídìng néng chénggōng.)
只要你在，就没问题。 (Zhǐyào nǐ zài, jiù méi wèntí.)

tables.caption_tr: Common beginner mistakes
rows: 才[cái] marks a NECESSARY condition and clashes with 只要, which marks a SUFFICIENT one — mixing the two patterns is a logical/grammatical error
只要努力，就能成功。 (Zhǐyào nǔlì, jiù néng chénggōng.)
就[jiù] cannot be dropped — it is the required link that signals 'then, as a result' in the second clause
只要努力，就能成功。 (Zhǐyào nǔlì, jiù néng chénggōng.)
就[jiù] must come AFTER the subject of its own clause, never before it
只要天气好，我们就去。 (Zhǐyào tiānqì hǎo, wǒmen jiù qù.)

zhiyou-cai.title_tr: 只有[zhǐyǒu]...才[cái]... ("Only if... then..." — Necessary Condition)
zhiyou-cai.intro_tr: 只有[zhǐyǒu]...才[cái]... is used to state a NECESSARY condition — the ONE AND ONLY circumstance under which the result can happen. 只有[zhǐyǒu] introduces the required condition ("only [this]"), and 才[cái] introduces the result, meaning "only then / only in that case." Unlike a general "if...then..." statement, this pattern implies that without the stated condition, the result is impossible — there is no other way to achieve it. 才[cái] must always sit directly in front of the verb of the result clause, and it can never be replaced by 就[jiù] in this pattern. Because it expresses an exclusive requirement, 只有[zhǐyǒu]...才[cái]... often sounds stronger and more emphatic than 如果[rúguǒ]...就[jiù]... (a plain hypothetical) or 只要[zhǐyào]...就[jiù]... (a minimum/sufficient condition).

tables.caption_tr: Core Formula of 只有[zhǐyǒu]...才[cái]...
rows: introduces the ONE and ONLY acceptable condition
states the result that becomes possible ONLY under that condition
condition clause, then result clause joined by comma
只有[zhǐyǒu] 努力[nǔlì]，才[cái] 能[néng] 成功[chénggōng]。
Only by working hard can [you] succeed.

tables.caption_tr: 只有[zhǐyǒu]...才[cái]... vs. Other Conditional Patterns
rows: necessary / exclusive condition — no other way exists
只有[zhǐyǒu] 你[nǐ] 帮[bāng] 我[wǒ]，我[wǒ] 才[cái] 能[néng] 做[zuò] 完[wán]。 (Only if you help me can I finish.)
sufficient / minimum condition — one way among possibly many others
只要[zhǐyào] 你[nǐ] 帮[bāng] 我[wǒ]，我[wǒ] 就[jiù] 能[néng] 做[zuò] 完[wán]。 (As long as you help me, I can finish — other help would also work.)
如果[rúguǒ] 下[xià] 雨[yǔ]，我[wǒ] 就[jiù] 不[bù] 去[qù]。 (If it rains, I won't go.)
exception — the ONLY exception that changes the outcome
除非[chúfēi] 你[nǐ] 来[lái]，我[wǒ] 才[cái] 去[qù]。 (Unless you come, I won't go — i.e., I'll go only if you come.)

tables.caption_tr: Subject Placement Rules
rows: Subject + 只有[zhǐyǒu] + condition，才[cái] + result (subject stated once, before 只有[zhǐyǒu])
你[nǐ] 只有[zhǐyǒu] 努力[nǔlì] 学习[xuéxí]，才[cái] 能[néng] 考[kǎo] 上[shàng] 大学[dàxué]。 (You will get into university only if you study hard.)
只有[zhǐyǒu] + Subject A + condition，Subject B + 才[cái] + result
只有[zhǐyǒu] 老师[lǎoshī] 帮[bāng] 忙[máng]，学生[xuésheng] 才[cái] 能[néng] 懂[dǒng]。 (Only if the teacher helps can the students understand.)
只有[zhǐyǒu] 努力[nǔlì]，才[cái] 能[néng] 成功[chénggōng]。 (Only by working hard can one succeed.)

tables.caption_tr: Common Collocations After 才[cái]
rows: only then can / only then is able to
...才[cái] 能[néng] 进[jìn] 去[qù] (only then can [one] go in)
only then may / is allowed to
...才[cái] 可以[kěyǐ] 出[chū] 去[qù] (only then may [one] go out)
...才[cái] 会[huì] 明白[míngbai] (only then will [one] understand)
...才[cái] 是[shì] 真[zhēn] 朋友[péngyou] (only then is [someone] a true friend)
only then will it work / do
...才[cái] 行[xíng] (only then will it be OK)

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes to Avoid
rows: Using 就[jiù] instead of 才[cái] after 只有[zhǐyǒu]
只有[zhǐyǒu] pairs exclusively with 才[cái]; 就[jiù] belongs to sufficient-condition patterns like 只要[zhǐyào] or 如果[rúguǒ]
✗ 只有[zhǐyǒu] 努力[nǔlì]，就[jiù] 能[néng] 成功[chénggōng]。 → ✓ 只有[zhǐyǒu] 努力[nǔlì]，才[cái] 能[néng] 成功[chénggōng]。
Placing 才[cái] before the subject of the result clause
才[cái] must come directly before the verb, i.e. AFTER the subject, never before it
✗ 只有[zhǐyǒu] 你[nǐ] 来[lái]，才[cái] 我[wǒ] 会[huì] 去[qù]。 → ✓ 只有[zhǐyǒu] 你[nǐ] 来[lái]，我[wǒ] 才[cái] 会[huì] 去[qù]。
Treating 只有[zhǐyǒu]...才[cái]... and 只要[zhǐyào]...就[jiù]... as interchangeable
只有[zhǐyǒu] expresses an exclusive/necessary condition (no other way); 只要[zhǐyào] expresses a minimum/sufficient condition (any one of several ways is enough)
choose 只有[zhǐyǒu]...才[cái]... only when the condition is truly the ONLY possible way
Dropping 才[cái] in the result clause
Without 才[cái] the 'only then' logical link is lost and the sentence sounds unfinished or like a plain statement
always keep 才[cái] directly before the verb of the result clause

examples.target: 只有[zhǐyǒu] 努力[nǔlì] 学习[xuéxí]，才[cái] 能[néng] 考[kǎo] 上[shàng] 好[hǎo] 大学[dàxué]。
examples.reading: Zhǐyǒu nǔlì xuéxí, cái néng kǎoshàng hǎo dàxué.

examples.target: 只有[zhǐyǒu] 你[nǐ] 同意[tóngyì]，我们[wǒmen] 才[cái] 能[néng] 开始[kāishǐ]。
examples.reading: Zhǐyǒu nǐ tóngyì, wǒmen cái néng kāishǐ.
examples.translation_tr: Only if you agree can we start.

examples.target: 只有[zhǐyǒu] 多[duō] 练习[liànxí]，你[nǐ] 的[de] 汉语[Hànyǔ] 才[cái] 会[huì] 进步[jìnbù]。

examples.target: 只有[zhǐyǒu] 有[yǒu] 护照[hùzhào]，才[cái] 可以[kěyǐ] 出[chū] 国[guó]。

examples.target: 我[wǒ] 只有[zhǐyǒu] 吃[chī] 药[yào]，病[bìng] 才[cái] 会[huì] 好[hǎo]。
examples.reading: Wǒ zhǐyǒu chī yào, bìng cái huì hǎo.
examples.translation_tr: I will only get better if I take the medicine.

examples.target: 只有[zhǐyǒu] 大家[dàjiā] 一起[yìqǐ] 努力[nǔlì]，我们[wǒmen] 才[cái] 能[néng] 成功[chénggōng]。
examples.reading: Zhǐyǒu dàjiā yìqǐ nǔlì, wǒmen cái néng chénggōng.

ruguo-jiu.intro_tr: 如果[rúguǒ]...就[jiù]... is the most common and neutral way to express "if... then..." in Mandarin. 如果[rúguǒ] introduces a hypothetical or possible condition in the first clause, and 就[jiù] introduces the result that follows in the second clause. This pattern is used constantly in everyday speech, so mastering its word order and common variations (如果...的话, 要是...就...) is essential for basic conversation. Unlike English "if", 如果[rúguǒ] can freely move before or after the subject of its own clause, but 就[jiù] has a fixed position: it must always come right after the subject of the second clause, never before it.

tables.caption_tr: Core structure of 如果[rúguǒ]...就[jiù]...
rows: Introduces the hypothetical or possible condition
如果[rúguǒ]明天[míngtiān]下雨[xiàyǔ] — if it rains tomorrow
States the result that follows from the condition
就[jiù]不[bù]去[qù]公园[gōngyuán]了[le] — then (we) won't go to the park
如果[rúguǒ] can appear before OR after this subject
如果[rúguǒ]你[nǐ]忙[máng] / 你[nǐ]如果[rúguǒ]忙[máng] — both correct
就[jiù] must always come AFTER this subject, never before it
你[nǐ]就[jiù]别[bié]去[qù]了[le] (correct) — NOT 就[jiù]你[nǐ]别[bié]去[qù]了[le]

tables.caption_tr: Common variations of the 如果[rúguǒ]...就[jiù]... pattern
rows: Standard, neutral, works in speech and writing
如果[rúguǒ]你[nǐ]累[lèi]了[le]，就[jiù]休息[xiūxi]一下[yíxià]吧[ba]。— If you're tired, rest a bit.
Adds 的话[dehuà] after the condition; very common in spoken Chinese, slightly casual
如果[rúguǒ]你[nǐ]不[bù]喜欢[xǐhuan]的话[dehuà]，就[jiù]别[bié]吃[chī]了[le]。— If you don't like it, then don't eat it.
Colloquial synonym of 如果[rúguǒ], mostly spoken
要是[yàoshi]明天[míngtiān]天气[tiānqì]好[hǎo]，我们[wǒmen]就[jiù]去[qù]爬山[páshān]。— If the weather's good tomorrow, we'll go hiking.
In casual speech, 如果[rúguǒ] can be dropped when context makes the condition clear; 就[jiù] always stays
你[nǐ]不[bù]去[qù]，我[wǒ]就[jiù]去[qù]。— (If) you don't go, then I will.
那么[nàme] adds emphasis/formality before 就[jiù]; more written style
如果[rúguǒ]你[nǐ]不[bù]同意[tóngyì]，那么[nàme]就[jiù]算了[suànle]。— If you don't agree, then never mind.

tables.caption_tr: Word order and subject placement rules
rows: 如果[rúguǒ] may precede or follow the subject of Clause A
如果[rúguǒ]我[wǒ]有[yǒu]钱[qián]... / 我[wǒ]如果[rúguǒ]有[yǒu]钱[qián]...
就[jiù] must follow the subject of Clause B
When both clauses share the same subject, it is often dropped in Clause B
如果[rúguǒ]他[tā]忙[máng]，就[jiù]不[bù]来[lái]了[le]。(subject 他[tā] omitted before 就[jiù])
如果[rúguǒ]他[tā]忙[máng]，他[tā]就[jiù]不[bù]来[lái]了[le]。(also correct, just more explicit)
就[jiù] can never start the sentence or stand for a new, unmentioned subject
就[jiù]先[xiān]走[zǒu]吧[ba]，你[nǐ]忙[máng]。 (✗ wrong order)

tables.caption_tr: 如果[rúguǒ]...就[jiù]... compared to similar conditional patterns
rows: Neutral, default choice for any hypothetical condition
Emphasizes a minimum sufficient condition, not just any condition
The condition is already known/true, not hypothetical
Concessive: the result holds true regardless of the condition
More formal/literary register, common in writing rather than speech

tables.caption_tr: Frequent mistakes made by beginners
rows: 就[jiù] must come AFTER the subject, never before it
Missing 就[jiù] in Clause B weakens the if-then link; 就[jiù] is required for a natural sentence
了[le] is not needed for a hypothetical future event after 如果[rúguǒ]
Mixing the conditional marker 如果[rúguǒ] with the causal marker 所以[suǒyǐ] — they belong to different patterns
如果[rúguǒ]我[wǒ]忙[máng]，就[jiù]不[bù]去[qù]。 (or: 因为[yīnwèi]我[wǒ]忙[máng]，所以[suǒyǐ]不[bù]去[qù]。)

examples.target: 如果明天不下雨，我们就去公园。
examples.reading: Rúguǒ míngtiān bú xiàyǔ, wǒmen jiù qù gōngyuán.
examples.translation_tr: If it doesn't rain tomorrow, we'll go to the park.

examples.target: 如果你有问题，就给我打电话。
examples.reading: Rúguǒ nǐ yǒu wèntí, jiù gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà.
examples.translation_tr: If you have a question, call me.

examples.target: 你如果喜欢这件衣服，就买吧。
examples.reading: Nǐ rúguǒ xǐhuan zhè jiàn yīfu, jiù mǎi ba.
examples.translation_tr: If you like this piece of clothing, then buy it.

examples.target: 如果我是你，我就不会那样做。
examples.reading: Rúguǒ wǒ shì nǐ, wǒ jiù bú huì nàyàng zuò.
examples.translation_tr: If I were you, I wouldn't do it that way.

examples.target: 如果你不想去的话，就别去了。
examples.reading: Rúguǒ nǐ bù xiǎng qù de huà, jiù bié qù le.
examples.translation_tr: If you don't want to go, then don't go.

examples.target: 要是明天天气好，我们就去爬山。
examples.reading: Yàoshi míngtiān tiānqì hǎo, wǒmen jiù qù páshān.
examples.translation_tr: If the weather is good tomorrow, we'll go hiking.

examples.target: 如果他不来，那么我们就开始吧。
examples.reading: Rúguǒ tā bù lái, nàme wǒmen jiù kāishǐ ba.
examples.translation_tr: If he doesn't come, then let's start.

examples.target: 你不说，我就不知道。

examples.translation_tr: If you don't tell (me), I won't know.

chule-yiwai.intro_tr: 除了[chúle]...以外[yǐwài] is one of the most useful HSK3 structures because it can express TWO opposite ideas depending on which adverb follows it in the second clause: "except for" (exclusive, paired with 都[dōu]/全[quán]) or "besides / in addition to" (additive, paired with 还[hái]/也[yě]). The literal meaning of 除了 is "remove/take away" and 以外 means "outside of," so the phrase literally means "outside of what has been removed." Both 除了 and 以外 can be dropped in casual speech as long as the meaning stays clear from context. This structure is essential for describing exceptions, exclusive members of a group, or extra items added to a list.

tables.caption_tr: Core structure
rows: literally 'remove'; can be dropped in casual speech
the item being excepted or added
can be a noun, a verb phrase, or a full clause
optional; often dropped, especially with short A
the main statement about the rest of the group
usually contains 都[dōu], 全[quán], 还[hái], or 也[yě]

tables.caption_tr: Two meanings depending on the follow-up adverb in clause B
rows: EXCLUSIVE — 'except for A, all of B...' (A is NOT included in B)
除了小猫[chúle xiǎomāo]，别的动物我都喜欢[biéde dòngwù wǒ dōu xǐhuan]。
Except for cats, I like every other animal.
ADDITIVE — 'besides A, B is also true' (A IS included, plus more)
除了英语[chúle Yīngyǔ]，我还会说日语[wǒ hái huì shuō Rìyǔ]。
Besides English, I can also speak Japanese.
'there is nothing/no one other than A' (A is the only one)
除了他，没有别的人知道[méiyǒu biéde rén zhīdào]。
Other than him, no one else knows.

tables.caption_tr: Structural variations and where 除了 can appear
rows: 除了下雨以外[chúle xiàyǔ yǐwài]，比赛照常进行[bǐsài zhàocháng jìnxíng]。
most formal / clearest form, common in writing
除了下雨[chúle xiàyǔ]，比赛照常进行[bǐsài zhàocháng jìnxíng]。
very common in speech, meaning unchanged
除了 placed after the subject
这个班除了小明以外[zhège bān chúle Xiǎomíng yǐwài]，都是女生[dōu shì nǚshēng]。
subject can come before 除了 when A is not the subject
除了他没来以外[chúle tā méi lái yǐwài]，别人都到了[biérén dōu dào le]。
除了 can introduce an entire clause, not just a noun
之外[zhīwài] instead of 以外
除了工作之外[chúle gōngzuò zhīwài]，他没有别的爱好[tā méiyǒu biéde àihào]。
之外[zhīwài] is a more literary/formal synonym of 以外[yǐwài]

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes and confusions for beginners
rows: Using 都[dōu] when you actually mean 'besides / also'
都 signals EXCLUSION, not addition — reverses your intended meaning
use 还[hái] or 也[yě] instead: 除了咖啡以外，我还喜欢喝茶[chúle kāfēi yǐwài, wǒ hái xǐhuan hē chá]
Forgetting the adverb (都/还/也) in clause B
without an adverb, the sentence is ambiguous or sounds incomplete
除了A以外 almost always needs 都/全/还/也 in B
Confusing 除了...以外 with 除非[chúfēi]...(才/否则)
除了 = 'except/besides' (a fact); 除非 = 'unless' (a necessary condition)
除非你请假[chúfēi nǐ qǐngjià]，否则不能不上课[fǒuzé bùnéng bú shàngkè] — a different structure
Placing 以外 right after 除了 with nothing in between
以外 must attach to the excepted item, not stand alone right after 除了
除了他以外[chúle tā yǐwài], not 除了以外他[chúle yǐwài tā]

examples.target: 除了苹果以外，我什么水果都喜欢。
examples.reading: Chúle píngguǒ yǐwài, wǒ shénme shuǐguǒ dōu xǐhuan.
examples.translation_tr: Except for apples, I like every fruit. (exclusive meaning + 都)

examples.reading: Chúle Yīngyǔ yǐwài, tā hái huì shuō Fǎyǔ.

examples.target: 除了他以外，大家都来了。
examples.reading: Chúle tā yǐwài, dàjiā dōu lái le.
examples.translation_tr: Except for him, everyone came.

examples.target: 除了周末，我每天都上班。

examples.translation_tr: Except for weekends, I go to work every day. (以外 dropped)

examples.target: 除了打篮球以外，他也喜欢踢足球。
examples.reading: Chúle dǎ lánqiú yǐwài, tā yě xǐhuan tī zúqiú.
examples.translation_tr: Besides playing basketball, he also likes playing soccer.

examples.target: 这个班除了小明以外，都是女生。
examples.reading: Zhège bān chúle Xiǎomíng yǐwài, dōu shì nǚshēng.
examples.translation_tr: Except for Xiaoming, everyone in this class is a girl. (除了 placed after the subject)

examples.target: 除了这本书，我还买了两支笔。
examples.reading: Chúle zhè běn shū, wǒ hái mǎile liǎng zhī bǐ.
examples.translation_tr: Besides this book, I also bought two pens.

examples.target: 除了下雨，什么都不能让他不出门。
examples.reading: Chúle xiàyǔ, shénme dōu bùnéng ràng tā bù chūmén.
examples.translation_tr: Except for rain, nothing can stop him from going out.

weile-purpose.title_tr: 为了 (wèile): "In order to, for the purpose of"
weile-purpose.intro_tr: 为了[wèile] means "in order to" or "for the purpose of" and introduces the GOAL that motivates an action — it always looks forward to something you want to achieve, not backward to a reason something already happened. The pattern is 为了 + Goal, Subject + Verb Phrase(Action), and the 为了 clause is most commonly placed at the very beginning of the sentence, before the subject. Because 为了 already signals purpose on its own, you should never add 所以[suǒyǐ] after it — that word belongs only to the 因为...所以... (cause-and-effect) pattern. Beginners frequently confuse 为了 with 因为[yīnwèi] ("because"): remember that 为了 answers "what for?" while 因为 answers "why did this happen?". This entry lays out the core sentence pattern, what kinds of phrases can follow 为了, how it differs from similar connectors, and the most common mistakes zero-level learners make.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Sentence Pattern with 为了[wèile]
rows: 为了 + Goal, Subject + Verb Phrase (most common — sentence-initial)
为了学习中文，我每天看书。
Wèile xuéxí Zhōngwén, wǒ měitiān kànshū.
In order to study Chinese, I read books every day.
Subject + 为了 + Goal + Verb Phrase (also correct, slightly more formal)
我为了学习中文，每天看书。
Wǒ wèile xuéxí Zhōngwén, měitiān kànshū.
I, in order to study Chinese, read books every day.
footnotes_tr: The goal clause (为了...) is the reason FOR the action; the second clause is the action itself taken to reach that goal.
No comma is required after 为了's clause in short sentences, but it is common and helps readability in longer ones.

tables.caption_tr: What Can Follow 为了
rows: in order to learn Chinese well
Causative goal (making someone else do/feel something)
为了 + 让/使 + Person + Adj/Verb
in order to make (my) parents happy
为了 + 不 + Verb / 为了避免 + Noun
in order not to be late

tables.caption_tr: 为了 vs Similar Connectors
rows: in order to / for the purpose of
states a GOAL you are working toward (forward-looking)
为了健康，他每天运动。[Wèile jiànkāng, tā měitiān yùndòng.] — For the sake of health, he exercises every day.
states a CAUSE for something that already happened (backward-looking)
因为 clause first, 所以 clause second
因为下雨，所以比赛取消了。[Yīnwèi xiàyǔ, suǒyǐ bǐsài qǔxiāo le.] — Because it rained, the match was cancelled.
states purpose; introduces the SECOND clause, after the main action
placed at the start of the second clause
他提前出发，以便赶上火车。[Tā tíqián chūfā, yǐbiàn gǎnshàng huǒchē.] — He left early so that he could catch the train.
so as not to, in order to avoid
states a negative purpose (avoidance); second clause
placed at the start of the second clause
早点儿出发，以免迟到。[Zǎodiǎnr chūfā, yǐmiǎn chídào.] — Leave a bit earlier so as not to be late.
simple preposition meaning 'for the benefit of'; not a full purpose clause
我为你高兴。[Wǒ wèi nǐ gāoxìng.] — I'm happy for you.
footnotes_tr: 为了 and 为 are related but not interchangeable: 为了 introduces a full goal clause with its own action, while 为 simply marks a beneficiary or target.

tables.caption_tr: Common Errors with 为了
rows: ❌ 为了他生病了，没来上课。[wèile tā shēngbìng le, méi lái shàngkè]
✅ 因为他生病了，所以没来上课。[yīnwèi tā shēngbìng le, suǒyǐ méi lái shàngkè]
为了 states a goal you are pursuing, not an existing reason for a past event. Use 因为...所以... for causes.
❌ 为了减肥，所以她每天跑步。[wèile jiǎnféi, suǒyǐ tā měitiān pǎobù]
✅ 为了减肥，她每天跑步。[wèile jiǎnféi, tā měitiān pǎobù]
为了's clause already signals purpose; do not add 所以 afterward the way you would with 因为...所以...
Leaving the goal clause without a main action
✅ 为了找到更好的工作，他努力学习。[wèile zhǎodào gèng hǎo de gōngzuò, tā nǔlì xuéxí]
A 为了 clause must always be followed by a main clause describing the action taken to reach that goal.
Using 为了 to explain the cause of a state/event
❌ 为了下雨，比赛取消了。[wèile xiàyǔ, bǐsài qǔxiāo le]
✅ 因为下雨，比赛取消了。[yīnwèi xiàyǔ, bǐsài qǔxiāo le]
Rain causing a cancellation is a REASON, not a GOAL someone is pursuing — use 因为 instead.

xian-ranhou-zai.title_tr: 先...然后...再... (first..., then..., after that...)
xian-ranhou-zai.intro_tr: 先...然后...再... is one of the most common ways in Chinese to describe a sequence of actions, equivalent to English "first..., then..., after that...". 先[xiān] marks the action that happens first, 然后[ránhòu] introduces a later step, and 再[zài] here means "then/next" (not "again") and can replace 然后 or follow it for a smoother link between two steps. The entire sequence normally shares a single subject, stated only once before 先, while each connector (先/然后/再) attaches directly in front of its own verb. This pattern shows up constantly in daily routines, travel plans, instructions, and recipes.

tables.caption_tr: Core Connectors in a Sequence
rows: Marks the first action in the sequence
Right before the first verb/verb phrase
Right before the second (or a later) verb phrase
Marks an action that follows another, "then/next" (NOT "again" here)
Right before the following verb phrase
Marks an action immediately following, "next, right after"
Right before the following verb phrase
Right before the last verb phrase

tables.caption_tr: Common Sentence Patterns for Sequencing Actions
rows: Two steps; casual, very common in spoken Chinese
Two steps; neutral, slightly more narrative than 再
Two steps; 然后 and 再 combined for a smoother transition (extremely common)
Three steps; 最后 emphasizes the final result
Four+ steps; used for detailed narration such as instructions or recipes

tables.caption_tr: Word Order and Subject Placement Rules
rows: Same subject for the whole sequence → state it once, before 先
我先洗澡，然后再睡觉。[Wǒ xiān xǐzǎo, ránhòu zài shuìjiào.]
The subject 我 is NOT repeated before 然后 or 再
Different subjects → each clause needs its own subject
你先说，我再说。[Nǐ xiān shuō, wǒ zài shuō.]
Each clause has its own subject placed before its own connector
Connectors attach directly before the verb, not before the subject
我们先坐火车，再坐飞机。[Wǒmen xiān zuò huǒchē, zài zuò fēijī.]
Correct order: subject once, then connector+verb repeated for each step

tables.caption_tr: 先...然后...再... vs. Similar Words — Common Points of Confusion
rows: Same character, different meaning depending on context; in a 先...再... sequence it means "then/next", not "repeat an action"
先吃饭，再睡觉。[Xiān chīfàn, zài shuìjiào.] = First eat, then sleep (NOT "eat again")
然后 cannot open the very first clause
然后 always introduces a LATER step; it cannot substitute for 先 to mark the first action
❌ 然后吃饭，先睡觉 — wrong logical order
又 is not used for future planned sequences
又[yòu] marks a repeated action that has already happened; use 再 for a future or planned next step
先复习，再考试。[Xiān fùxí, zài kǎoshì.] (not 又考试)
就[jiù] can also link two actions, but usually stresses immediacy ("as soon as..."); 然后 is a neutral step-by-step connector
一下课，我们就去吃饭。 (immediate) vs. 我们先下课，然后去吃饭。 (sequenced steps)

jiu-vs-cai.title_tr: 就 (jiù) vs 才 (cái): Emphasizing "Early" vs "Late"
jiu-vs-cai.intro_tr: 就[jiù] and 才[cái] are both time-related adverbs placed directly before the verb, and both can attach to the same clock time or age — but they express opposite speaker attitudes. 就[jiù] signals that something happens sooner, faster, or more easily than expected ("already, right away"), while 才[cái] signals that something happens later, slower, or with more difficulty than expected ("only then, finally"). This is a subjective judgment, not an objective measurement: "他八点就到了" and "他八点才到" both describe an 8 o'clock arrival, but the first sounds impressed/early and the second sounds like a complaint about lateness. Beyond simple time, both words also lock into fixed two-part patterns (一...就..., 只有...才...) where the other adverb cannot be substituted. A small but important detail is sentence-final 了[le]: it usually appears with 就[jiù] sentences but is usually dropped with 才[cái] sentences.

tables.caption_tr: Core Semantic Contrast
rows: "That's early, quite normal, or even impressive"
"Finally! That took long enough / unfortunately late"
"as much/many as" — surprisingly large or fast
Usually absent — do NOT add 了[le] after 才[cái] clauses

tables.caption_tr: Same Clock Time, Opposite Meaning
rows: 他八点就到了。[tā bā diǎn jiù dào le.] — He arrived by 8 already!
他八点才到。[tā bā diǎn cái dào.] — He didn't arrive until 8.
他六岁就上学了。[tā liù suì jiù shàngxué le.] — He started school as early as 6.
他六岁才上学。[tā liù suì cái shàngxué.] — He didn't start school until 6.
他十分钟就写完作业了。[tā shí fēnzhōng jiù xiěwán zuòyè le.] — He finished homework in just 10 minutes.
他写了两个小时才写完作业。[tā xiěle liǎng ge xiǎoshí cái xiěwán zuòyè.] — It took him two hours to finish homework.

tables.caption_tr: Fixed Two-Part Patterns (cannot swap 就[jiù] and 才[cái])
rows: 一下课就走。[yī xiàkè jiù zǒu.] — He leaves the moment class ends.
只要你努力，就会成功。[zhǐyào nǐ nǔlì, jiù huì chénggōng.]
就是下雨，我也要去。[jiùshì xiàyǔ, wǒ yě yào qù.]
只有努力，才能成功。[zhǐyǒu nǔlì, cái néng chénggōng.]
除非你道歉，我才原谅你。[chúfēi nǐ dàoqiàn, wǒ cái yuánliàng nǐ.]
因为堵车，他才迟到。[yīnwèi dǔchē, tā cái chídào.]

tables.caption_tr: Quantity Emphasis: 就[jiù] ("as much/many as") vs 才[cái] ("only/merely")
rows: 就[jiù] states it matter-of-factly, often neutral or with a hint of "that's all, and that's fine".
He's only written two pages (so far).
才[cái] frames it as less than expected — implies "not enough yet".
他一晚上就写了二十页。
tā yì wǎnshang jiù xiěle èrshí yè.
He wrote twenty pages in just one night.
就[jiù] emphasizes a surprisingly large amount achieved quickly.
他写了三天才写完二十页。
tā xiěle sān tiān cái xiěwán èrshí yè.
It took him three days to finish just twenty pages.
才[cái] emphasizes it took too long for too little output.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: ✅ 他八点才来。[tā bā diǎn cái lái.]
才[cái] clauses almost never take sentence-final 了[le]; adding it sounds unnatural.
❌ 只有努力学习，就能考上大学。
✅ 只有努力学习，才能考上大学。[zhǐyǒu nǔlì xuéxí, cái néng kǎoshàng dàxué.]
只有...才... is a fixed pairing; 就[jiù] cannot replace 才[cái] in this pattern.
✅ 一下课，他就跑出去了。[yī xiàkè, tā jiù pǎo chūqù le.]
一...就... is a fixed pairing; 才[cái] cannot replace 就[jiù] here.
✅ 我五岁就会游泳了。 OR 我十岁才学会游泳。
就[jiù] and 才[cái] cannot both modify the same verb in one clause — choose one based on the intended nuance.
❌ Using 就[jiù] when the speaker actually wants to complain about slowness
✅ Use 才[cái] to signal frustration or lateness
才[cái] carries the "finally / not enough / too late" nuance that 就[jiù] does not.

duo-questions.title_tr: 多 (duō) + Adjective Questions (多长, 多高, 多远)
duo-questions.intro_tr: 多 (duō) combines with a small, fixed set of monosyllabic adjectives to ask questions about degree or measurement — age, height, length, distance, weight, duration, and similar dimensions. The basic pattern is Subject + 多[duō] + Adjective, and when a precise numeric measurement is expected, an optional 有[yǒu] can appear before 多: Subject + 有[yǒu] + 多[duō] + Adjective. A key rule that trips up English speakers: only the "positive" member of an antonym pair (大[dà] "big," not 小[xiǎo] "small"; 高[gāo] "tall," not 矮[ǎi] "short") is used as the neutral question word — this does not mean you expect a big answer, it is simply the fixed, unmarked way to ask. Answers generally mirror the question's structure: Subject + (有[yǒu]) + Number + Measure Word + Adjective.

tables.caption_tr: Common 多[duō] + Adjective Question Words
rows: How old are you? / How big is it?
How fast is the car going?

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Structure Patterns
rows: Place A + 离[lí] + Place B + 有[yǒu] + 多[duō] + 远[yuǎn]?
你家离[lí]学校有[yǒu]多远[duō yuǎn]?
How far is your home from school?
这条河有[yǒu]五十米[wǔshí mǐ]长[cháng]。

tables.caption_tr: Antonym Pairs: Which Form Is the Neutral Question Word?
rows: 多大[duō dà] is the standard neutral question; 多小[duō xiǎo] is very rare and implies you expect a small answer
多高[duō gāo] is neutral; 多矮[duō ǎi] is not used as a question word
多长[duō cháng] is neutral; 多短[duō duǎn] is unusual
多远[duō yuǎn] is neutral; 多近[duō jìn] is not standard
多重[duō zhòng] is neutral; 多轻[duō qīng] is rare
多宽[duō kuān] is neutral; 多窄[duō zhǎi] is rare
多深[duō shēn] is neutral; 多浅[duō qiǎn] is rare
多厚[duō hòu] is neutral; 多薄[duō báo] is rare
多快[duō kuài] is neutral; 多慢[duō màn] is rare

tables.caption_tr: Answer Patterns with Measure Words
Politeness Variants for Asking Age
rows: 你多大了[nǐ duō dà le]?
你几岁了[nǐ jǐ suì le]?
几[jǐ] used because a small number is expected
您多大年纪了[nín duō dà niánjì le]?
polite/respectful, uses 您[nín] and 年纪[niánjì]

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: 小[xiǎo] is not the neutral form for age
Always use 大[dà], not 小[xiǎo], for a neutral age question
你几多大[nǐ jǐ duō dà]?
mixing 几[jǐ] and 多[duō] together
Don't combine 几[jǐ] with 多[duō] + Adjective
桌子多长有[zhuōzi duō cháng yǒu]?
桌子有多长[zhuōzi yǒu duō cháng]?
有[yǒu] goes before 多[duō] + Adj, never after
多[duō] cannot stand alone without an adjective
这个多大[zhège duō dà]?/多重[duō zhòng]?
多[duō] must always be paired with a specific adjective

rang-jiao-causative.title_tr: 让 / 叫 (ràng/jiào): the causative "to make/let someone do"
rang-jiao-causative.intro_tr: 让[ràng] and 叫[jiào] are the two everyday "causative" verbs in Chinese — they turn a sentence into "Subject makes/lets/tells Someone do Something." Structurally both work the same way: Subject + 让/叫 + Person + Verb Phrase, with no 了[le] or 的[de] attached to 让/叫 itself. The two words overlap heavily but differ slightly in flavor: 让[ràng] is softer and covers "let, allow, have someone do" as well as emotional causation ("this makes me feel..."), while 叫[jiào] leans toward "tell/order someone to" and sounds a bit more like a direct instruction, especially in spoken Mandarin. Both can also appear in passive-style sentences (叫/让 + Agent + V), which overlaps with 被[bèi] but is more colloquial. Negation and modals (不, 没, 别) attach before 让/叫, not before the second verb.

tables.caption_tr: Core sentence pattern
rows: 打扫房间[dǎsǎo fángjiān] 'clean the room'
妈妈让我打扫房间。[Māma ràng wǒ dǎsǎo fángjiān.] 'Mom has me clean the room.'

tables.caption_tr: 让 vs 叫: shades of meaning and register
rows: let, allow; have someone do; cause a feeling (this makes me ...)
Neutral, works in both speech and writing
让我想想。[Ràng wǒ xiǎngxiang.] 'Let me think.'
tell/order to; summon; also literally 'to call/be named'
妈妈叫我回家。[Māma jiào wǒ huí jiā.] 'Mom told me to come home.'
Both can mean 'tell someone to do something' and both can form passive-like sentences
老师让/叫我们安静。[Lǎoshī ràng/jiào wǒmen ānjìng.] 'The teacher tells us to be quiet.'
Emotional causation (让 X 感觉/生气/高兴...) is far more common than 叫 in this use
这件事让我很生气。[Zhè jiàn shì ràng wǒ hěn shēngqì.] 'This matter makes me very angry.'

tables.caption_tr: Negation and modal placement
rows: 爸爸不让我开车。[Bàba bú ràng wǒ kāichē.] 'Dad doesn't let me drive.'
别让他等太久。[Bié ràng tā děng tài jiǔ.] 'Don't make him wait too long.'
didn't let / didn't tell (past, specific event)
老师没叫我回答问题。[Lǎoshī méi jiào wǒ huídá wèntí.] 'The teacher didn't call on me to answer.'
should not let (softer than 别 in writing)
请不要让孩子玩手机太久。[Qǐng búyào ràng háizi wán shǒujī tài jiǔ.] 'Please don't let children play on their phone too long.'

tables.caption_tr: 让/叫 vs other causative & passive-flavored verbs
rows: 让我进去。[Ràng wǒ jìnqù.] 'Let me in.'
tell/order to; also passive-like agent marker
他叫我别说话。[Tā jiào wǒ bié shuōhuà.] 'He told me not to talk.'
cause (a state/result); no direct 'person object' feel, more literary
这个消息使大家很惊讶。[Zhège xiāoxi shǐ dàjiā hěn jīngyà.] 'This news made everyone very surprised.'
这幅画令人赞叹。[Zhè fú huà lìng rén zàntàn.] 'This painting is admirable (causes people to admire it).'
politely ask/invite someone to do something
请大家安静。[Qǐng dàjiā ānjìng.] 'Please everyone be quiet.'
true passive marker (X is acted upon by Y)
他被老师叫去了。[Tā bèi lǎoshī jiào qùle.] 'He was called away by the teacher.'

tables.caption_tr: Common set patterns with 让
rows: 这首歌让我觉得很放松。[Zhè shǒu gē ràng wǒ juéde hěn fàngsōng.] 'This song makes me feel relaxed.'
let X go first / do first
让他先走吧。[Ràng tā xiān zǒu ba.] 'Let him go first.'
让我看看。[Ràng wǒ kànkan.] 'Let me have a look.'
X was made to / ended up doing (completed causation)
他的话让我笑了。[Tā de huà ràng wǒ xiàole.] 'His words made me laugh.'
