examples.reading: Nǐ de huà ràng wǒ hěn shīwàng.
examples.translation_tr: Your words made me very disappointed.

examples.target: 我们让他先说,他不肯。
examples.reading: Wǒmen ràng tā xiān shuō, tā bù kěn.
examples.translation_tr: We let him speak first, but he refused.

yinggai-dei-modals.title_tr: 应该 / 得 (děi) / 必须: Modals of Necessity and Obligation
yinggai-dei-modals.intro_tr: Chinese has three core ways to express obligation or necessity, each carrying a different strength and register. 应该[yīnggāi] expresses what SHOULD happen — a moral, logical, or advisory obligation, close to English "should/ought to". 得[děi] is the colloquial, spoken-only "have to/must", used for subjective necessity forced by circumstances, and it shares its hanzi with two other readings (dé, de) that mean completely different things. 必须[bìxū] is the strongest and most formal "must", typically used for rules, laws, and requirements that leave no choice. All three behave irregularly in the negative — you almost never just add 不[bù] directly in front of them the way you would with an ordinary verb — so mastering the correct negation pattern for each is the single most important skill in this lesson.

tables.caption_tr: The Three Core Necessity Modals at a Glance
rows: Neutral — used in both speech and writing
Moral, logical, or advice-based obligation; what is reasonable or expected
Colloquial — spoken language only, avoid in formal writing
Subjective necessity driven by circumstances; personal urgency, felt pressure
Formal — common in both speech and writing, especially rules/notices
Objective, mandatory requirement; no choice, often externally imposed (law, rule, order)
The formal written twin of 应该[yīnggāi]; interchangeable with it in official contexts

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Patterns: Positive, Negative, and Question Forms
rows:
Subj + 应该[yīnggāi] + V(O)
e.g. 你应该休息[nǐ yīnggāi xiūxi] "You should rest"

Subj + 不应该[bù yīnggāi] + V(O)
e.g. 你不应该生气[nǐ bù yīnggāi shēngqì] "You shouldn't be angry"

Subj + 应不应该[yīng bu yīnggāi] + V(O)? / ...应该...吗[ma]?
e.g. 我应该去吗[wǒ yīnggāi qù ma]? "Should I go?"

Subj + 得[děi] + V(O)
e.g. 我得走了[wǒ děi zǒu le] "I have to go"

⚠ NOT 不得[bù děi]; use 不用[bú yòng] / 不必[bú bì] + V(O)
e.g. 你不用来[nǐ bú yòng lái] "You don't have to come"

是不是得[shì bu shì děi]...? (得 itself is rarely repeated as V-not-V)
e.g. 我是不是得交钱[wǒ shì bu shì děi jiāo qián]? "Do I have to pay?"

Subj + 必须[bìxū] + V(O)
e.g. 你必须遵守规则[nǐ bìxū zūnshǒu guīzé] "You must follow the rules"

⚠ NOT 不必须[bù bìxū]; use 不必[bú bì] + V(O)
e.g. 你不必担心[nǐ bú bì dānxīn] "You don't have to worry"

是不是必须[shì bu shì bìxū]...? / 必须...吗[ma]?
e.g. 我们必须交作业吗[wǒmen bìxū jiāo zuòyè ma]? "Must we hand in the homework?"

tables.caption_tr: The Negation Trap: How to Correctly Say 'Don't Have To' / 'Shouldn't'
rows: 不得[bù děi] used to mean "don't have to" — this is a common learner error
不用[bú yòng] / 不必[bú bì]
不必须[bù bìxū] — ungrammatical, never used
footnotes_tr: Note: 不得[bùdé] does exist as a separate, formal fixed expression meaning "must not / not allowed to" (e.g. 不得吸烟[bùdé xīyān] "smoking not allowed"), but it is NOT used in everyday speech as the casual negative of 得[děi] "have to". Confusing these two is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

tables.caption_tr: One Character, Three Readings: 得 (dé / děi / de)
rows: 他得了第一名[tā déle dì yī míng] — "He got first place"
Modal verb: "must / have to" (topic of this lesson)
我得走了[wǒ děi zǒu le] — "I must go now"
Structural particle introducing a degree/result complement after a verb
他说得很好[tā shuō de hěn hǎo] — "He speaks very well"
footnotes_tr: Position tells you the reading: right after a verb + describing HOW something is done = de (particle); directly before a verb expressing obligation = děi (modal); used alone as a full verb meaning "obtain" = dé.

tables.caption_tr: Related Necessity / Obligation Words at a Glance
column_headers: How It Differs from 应该 / 得 / 必须
rows: Formal written twin of 应该[yīnggāi]; interchangeable with it in most formal or official contexts
Weaker and broader than 必须[bìxū]; can also express simple future or desire, not only obligation
Focuses on a need or requirement (often for things/conditions), not a direct command to act; e.g. 需要帮助[xūyào bāngzhù] "need help"
"have no choice but to / be forced to"
Emphasizes reluctant compulsion due to circumstances; stronger emotional coloring than 得[děi]
Implies "no better option remained"; describes the resulting action, not a general rule or obligation
Emphatic double-negative construction; more dramatic and forceful than 必须[bìxū]

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Corrections
rows: 我不得去。[Wǒ bù děi qù.] (intending "I don't have to go")
不得[bùdé] actually means "must not / forbidden to" — the opposite of the intended meaning
我不用去。[Wǒ bú yòng qù.] / 我不必去。[Wǒ bú bì qù.] — "I don't have to go"
你不必须来。[Nǐ bù bìxū lái.]
必须[bìxū] cannot take 不[bù] directly in front of it; this combination is ungrammatical
你不必来。[Nǐ bú bì lái.] — "You don't have to come"
乘客应该系安全带。[Chéngkè yīnggāi jì ānquándài.] used on an official safety notice
应该[yīnggāi] is too soft/advisory for legal or mandatory rule contexts
乘客必须系安全带。[Chéngkè bìxū jì ānquándài.] — "Passengers must fasten seatbelts"
Reading 得 the same way in every sentence
得 has three different pronunciations/tones depending on grammatical role, and mixing them up changes the meaning entirely
Check position: before a verb = děi (modal, this lesson); after a verb = de (particle); alone as a verb = dé ("to obtain")

examples.target: 你应该多喝水。
examples.reading: Nǐ yīnggāi duō hē shuǐ.
examples.translation_tr: You should drink more water.

examples.target: 我得走了，不然会迟到。
examples.reading: Wǒ děi zǒu le, bùrán huì chídào.
examples.translation_tr: I have to go now, or I'll be late.

examples.target: 学生必须按时交作业。
examples.reading: Xuésheng bìxū ànshí jiāo zuòyè.
examples.translation_tr: Students must submit homework on time.

examples.target: 你不应该那样说话。
examples.reading: Nǐ bù yīnggāi nàyàng shuōhuà.
examples.translation_tr: You shouldn't talk like that.

examples.target: 明天是周末，你不用早起。
examples.reading: Míngtiān shì zhōumò, nǐ bú yòng zǎo qǐ.
examples.translation_tr: Tomorrow is the weekend, so you don't have to get up early.
examples.note_tr: 不用[bú yòng] is the everyday way to negate 得[děi] — never say 不得[bù děi] here.

examples.target: 这里禁止吸烟，你不得抽烟。
examples.reading: Zhèlǐ jìnzhǐ xīyān, nǐ bùdé chōuyān.
examples.translation_tr: Smoking is prohibited here; you must not smoke.
examples.note_tr: Here 不得[bùdé] means formal 'not allowed to' — a different word from negating 得[děi] 'have to'.

examples.target: 谢谢你的帮助！——这是我应该的。
examples.reading: Xièxie nǐ de bāngzhù! — Zhè shì wǒ yīnggāi de.
examples.translation_tr: Thank you for your help! — It's the least I could do.

examples.target: 我们得努力学习，才能通过考试。
examples.reading: Wǒmen děi nǔlì xuéxí, cái néng tōngguò kǎoshì.
examples.translation_tr: We have to study hard in order to pass the exam.

xiang-resemble.intro_tr: 像 [xiàng] is a verb meaning "to resemble, to look like, to be similar to." Unlike English "like," 像 is a full verb that can stand alone directly between two things being compared (A 像 B), with no extra linking word required. It is extremely common in the pattern 像...一样 [xiàng...yíyàng] ("just like..."), which is used to compare a shared quality (an adjective or a verb) between two things. This page covers 像 as a stand-alone resemblance verb, the 像...一样/似的 comparison structures, negation and question forms, and how 像 differs from close cousins like 好像 [hǎoxiàng] ("seem"), 跟...一样 [gēn...yíyàng] ("be the same as"), and 看起来 [kànqǐlai] ("look [visually]").

tables.caption_tr: Core Functions of 像 [xiàng]
rows: 他像他爸爸。[Tā xiàng tā bàba.]
她像花一样美。[Tā xiàng huā yíyàng měi.]
She is as beautiful as a flower.
天冷得像冬天似的。[Tiān lěng de xiàng dōngtiān shìde.]
It's as cold as if it were winter.
这不像你说的那样。[Zhè bú xiàng nǐ shuō de nàyàng.]
This isn't like what you said.
A + 像不像 [xiàng bu xiàng] + B
这像不像苹果?[Zhè xiàng bu xiàng píngguǒ?]
Does this look like an apple or not?
footnotes_tr: 像 can also introduce examples in formal writing, similar to 比如 [bǐrú] ('for example'), though this usage is less common at HSK3 level.

tables.caption_tr: 像 [xiàng] ...一样 [yíyàng] Sentence Templates
rows: 这个孩子像妈妈。[Zhège háizi xiàng māma.]
This child looks like his mother.
A + 像 + B + 一样 + Adj/Verb
他跑得像兔子一样快。[Tā pǎo de xiàng tùzi yíyàng kuài.]
He runs as fast as a rabbit.
A + 有/是 + 像 + B + 一样 + 的 + Noun
她有一双像星星一样的眼睛。[Tā yǒu yì shuāng xiàng xīngxīng yíyàng de yǎnjing.]
A + V + 得 + 像 + B + 一样
他忙得像陀螺一样。[Tā máng de xiàng tuóluó yíyàng.]
He's as busy as a spinning top.
A + 不像 + B + (那么/这么) + Adj
今天不像昨天那么热。[Jīntiān bú xiàng zuótiān nàme rè.]
Today isn't as hot as yesterday.

tables.caption_tr: 像 [xiàng] vs. Similar 'Like / Seem' Expressions
rows: Main verb, can take an object directly
他长得像妈妈。[Tā zhǎng de xiàng māma.]
Sentence adverb, precedes the whole clause
他好像不在家。[Tā hǎoxiàng bú zài jiā.]
Comparison structure with no resemblance nuance
我跟他一样高。[Wǒ gēn tā yíyàng gāo.]
Sentence adverb based on visual judgment
这道菜看起来很好吃。[Zhè dào cài kànqǐlai hěn hǎochī.]
他似乎很累。[Tā sìhū hěn lèi.]
footnotes_tr: 像 focuses on actual resemblance between two things; 好像/似乎/看起来 focus on the speaker's impression or uncertainty about a single situation.

tables.caption_tr: Common Collocations and Fixed Expressions with 像 [xiàng]
rows: 做得不像样。[Zuò de bú xiàngyàng.] - It wasn't done properly.
他好像生气了似的。[Tā hǎoxiàng shēngqì le shìde.] - He acts as if he's angry.
她像天使一样善良。[Tā xiàng tiānshǐ yíyàng shànliáng.] - She's as kind as an angel.
生活就像一场旅行。[Shēnghuó jiù xiàng yì chǎng lǚxíng.] - Life is just like a journey.
像他这样的人不多。[Xiàng tā zhèyàng de rén bù duō.] - There aren't many people like him.

tables.caption_tr: Common Learner Mistakes with 像 [xiàng]
rows: *他是像他爸爸。[Tā shì xiàng tā bàba.]
像 is already a full verb meaning 'to resemble'; adding 是 before it is redundant and ungrammatical.
他像他爸爸。[Tā xiàng tā bàba.] - He looks like his father.
*她像花很美。[Tā xiàng huā hěn měi.]
When comparing a shared quality, the linking word 一样 [yíyàng] must appear between the compared noun and the adjective.
她像花一样美。[Tā xiàng huā yíyàng měi.] - She's as beautiful as a flower.
*他很像他哥哥高。[Tā hěn xiàng tā gēge gāo.]
Don't insert 很 before 像 when using the full 像...一样+Adj comparison pattern; 一样 already carries the comparative meaning.
他像他哥哥一样高。[Tā xiàng tā gēge yíyàng gāo.] - He is as tall as his brother.
*这不好像你说的那样。[Zhè bù hǎoxiàng nǐ shuō de nàyàng.]
不像 (negating resemblance) and 好像 (expressing uncertainty) serve different functions and cannot be combined this way.
这不像你说的那样。[Zhè bú xiàng nǐ shuō de nàyàng.] - This isn't like what you said.
*他跑得很像风。[Tā pǎo de hěn xiàng fēng.]
To express 'as fast as X', use 像 + X + 一样 + Adjective after 得, not 很 + 像 + X alone.
他跑得像风一样快。[Tā pǎo de xiàng fēng yíyàng kuài.] - He runs as fast as the wind.

examples.target: 她长得像她妈妈。
examples.reading: Tā zhǎng de xiàng tā māma.
examples.translation_tr: She looks like her mother (in appearance).
examples.note_tr: 长得像 [zhǎng de xiàng] is the standard fixed phrase for saying someone physically resembles another person.

examples.target: 这朵云像一只小狗。
examples.reading: Zhè duǒ yún xiàng yì zhī xiǎogǒu.
examples.translation_tr: This cloud looks like a little dog.
examples.note_tr: Simple A + 像 + B pattern — no 一样 [yíyàng] is needed when you're just naming what something looks like.

examples.target: 他跑得像风一样快。
examples.reading: Tā pǎo de xiàng fēng yíyàng kuài.
examples.translation_tr: He runs as fast as the wind.
examples.note_tr: Degree complement 得 [de] + 像...一样 [xiàng...yíyàng] + Adjective is one of the most common HSK3 comparison patterns.

examples.target: 你不像你哥哥那么高。
examples.reading: Nǐ bú xiàng nǐ gēge nàme gāo.
examples.translation_tr: You aren't as tall as your brother.
examples.note_tr: Negative comparison pattern: 不像 [bú xiàng] ... 那么/这么 [nàme/zhème] + Adjective.

examples.target: 这个问题像上次那个一样难。
examples.reading: Zhège wèntí xiàng shàng cì nàge yíyàng nán.
examples.translation_tr: This problem is just as difficult as the last one.

examples.target: 那座山像不像一头大象?
examples.reading: Nà zuò shān xiàng bu xiàng yì tóu dàxiàng?
examples.translation_tr: Does that mountain look like an elephant or not?
examples.note_tr: V-not-V question form: 像不像 [xiàng bu xiàng] is the natural way to ask 'does it resemble...?'

examples.target: 他说话的样子很像他爸爸。
examples.reading: Tā shuōhuà de yàngzi hěn xiàng tā bàba.
examples.translation_tr: The way he talks is a lot like his father.
examples.note_tr: 很 [hěn] + 像 [xiàng] (without 一样) simply intensifies the resemblance itself; this is different from the 很 + 像...一样 + Adj mistake.

examples.target: 这件事像是真的。
examples.reading: Zhè jiàn shì xiàng shì zhēn de.
examples.translation_tr: This matter seems to be true.
examples.note_tr: 像是 [xiàng shì] + Noun/Clause = 'seems to be...', a common pattern that blends 像 with 是.

double-object-verbs.title_tr: Double-Object Verbs (给, 教, 送, 问)
double-object-verbs.intro_tr: Double-object verbs in Chinese can be followed directly by two objects in a row: first the person (indirect object) who receives the action, then the thing (direct object) that is given, taught, asked about, and so on. The basic word order is Subject + Verb + Person + Thing — unlike English, no preposition such as "to" or "for" is placed between the verb and the person. Common double-object verbs include 给[gěi] (give), 教[jiāo] (teach), 送[sòng] (give as a gift), 问[wèn] (ask), 告诉[gàosù] (tell), 借[jiè] (lend/borrow), 还[huán] (return), and 找[zhǎo] (give change). Not every transitive verb behaves this way — verbs like 买[mǎi] (buy) or 做[zuò] (make) normally need the coverb 给[gěi] to introduce the beneficiary instead of taking two objects directly. Keeping the person (O1) immediately after the verb and before the thing (O2) is the single most important rule to master here.

tables.caption_tr: Core Sentence Pattern: Subject + Verb + Person (O1) + Thing (O2)
rows: the person affected by the action

tables.caption_tr: Common Double-Object Verbs
rows: 我给你钱。[Wǒ gěi nǐ qián.] — I give you money.
他教我们英语。[Tā jiāo wǒmen Yīngyǔ.] — He teaches us English.
to give (as a gift) / to see off
我送她花。[Wǒ sòng tā huā.] — I give her flowers.
我问老师一个问题。[Wǒ wèn lǎoshī yí gè wèntí.] — I ask the teacher a question.
他告诉我一个秘密。[Tā gàosù wǒ yí gè mìmì.] — He tells me a secret.
我借他一百块。[Wǒ jiè tā yìbǎi kuài.] — I lend him 100 yuan.
我还你书。[Wǒ huán nǐ shū.] — I return the book to you.
服务员找我十块。[Fúwùyuán zhǎo wǒ shí kuài.] — The waiter gives me ten yuan in change.
我寄他一封信。[Wǒ jì tā yì fēng xìn.] — I mail him a letter.

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Forms: Affirmative, Negative, Question, and Aspect
rows: Wǒ gěi nǐ yì běn shū.
Are you giving me the book?
Nǐ gěi bu gěi wǒ shū?
Are you giving me the book or not?
Wǒ gěi le tā yìbǎi kuài.
I want to teach you Chinese.

tables.caption_tr: Double-Object Structure vs the 给-Prepositional Alternative
rows: 我送你一本书。[Wǒ sòng nǐ yì běn shū.]
Most natural and most common in everyday speech.
我送一本书给你。[Wǒ sòng yì běn shū gěi nǐ.]
Also correct; shifts slight emphasis onto the thing being given.
我给你买了一本书。[Wǒ gěi nǐ mǎi le yì běn shū.]
Required for verbs like 买[mǎi] (buy) or 做[zuò] (make), which cannot take two bare objects.

tables.caption_tr: Common Word-Order Mistakes
rows: The person (O1) must come immediately after the verb, before the thing (O2), not after it.
我给你买了一本书。 / 我买了一本书给你。
买[mǎi] is not a double-object verb; it needs 给[gěi] to introduce the beneficiary.
Fixed order is Verb + Person + Thing, never Verb + Thing + Person.
The person asked must precede the question itself.

examples.target: 我给你一本书。
examples.reading: Wǒ gěi nǐ yì běn shū.
examples.translation_tr: I'll give you a book.

examples.target: 老师教我们汉语。
examples.reading: Lǎoshī jiāo wǒmen Hànyǔ.
examples.translation_tr: The teacher teaches us Chinese.

examples.target: 我想送她一个生日礼物。
examples.reading: Wǒ xiǎng sòng tā yí gè shēngrì lǐwù.
examples.translation_tr: I want to give her a birthday present.

examples.target: 他问我一个很难的问题。
examples.reading: Tā wèn wǒ yí gè hěn nán de wèntí.
examples.translation_tr: He asked me a very difficult question.

examples.target: 你可以告诉我你的电话号码吗?
examples.reading: Nǐ kěyǐ gàosù wǒ nǐ de diànhuà hàomǎ ma?
examples.translation_tr: Can you tell me your phone number?

examples.target: 服务员找了我十块钱。
examples.reading: Fúwùyuán zhǎo le wǒ shí kuài qián.
examples.translation_tr: The waiter gave me ten yuan in change.

examples.target: 我借了他五十块钱。
examples.reading: Wǒ jiè le tā wǔshí kuài qián.
examples.translation_tr: I lent him fifty yuan.

examples.target: 我送一本书给你。
examples.reading: Wǒ sòng yì běn shū gěi nǐ.
examples.translation_tr: I'm giving a book to you.
examples.note_tr: Alternative word order using 给[gěi] to reintroduce the receiver after the thing — emphasizes the object being given, but the basic double-object order above is more common in speech.

approximate-numbers.title_tr: Approximate Numbers (几, 多, 左右, 大概)
approximate-numbers.intro_tr: Chinese has four common tools for turning an exact number into a rough one. 几[jǐ] goes before a measure word to mean "a few/several" (usually under ten), or slots into compound numbers like 十几[shíjǐ] and 几十[jǐshí] to show that one digit is unknown. 多[duō] attaches directly to a number to mean "more than that, and a bit extra" — whether it sits before or after the measure word depends on whether the base number is a round one (ends in 0) or not. 左右[zuǒyòu] is tacked onto the very end of a complete number phrase to mean "around, give or take." 大概[dàgài] is a full adverb placed before the predicate, expressing the speaker's own subjective guess, and it can even be combined with the other markers for extra vagueness. Mastering the exact word order of each is the key skill here, since small placement changes shift the meaning.

tables.caption_tr: Overview: Four Ways to Say "Approximately"
rows: Before a measure word (几+MW+N) or inside a compound number (十几, 几十, 几百)
Right after the number OR right after the measure word (depends on number type)
Fixed phrase, attaches at the end
After the complete Number + Measure Word (+ Noun) phrase
Before the verb / predicate, usually near the start of the estimate
footnotes_tr: These four markers can be combined (e.g. 大概 + Number + 左右) but stacking more than two at once sounds redundant.

tables.caption_tr: 几[jǐ] — "A Few" and Unknown-Digit Patterns
rows: 十几个人[shí jǐ ge rén]
"several tens of yuan / dozens of yuan"
一百 + 几十 + MW + N
一百几十块钱[yìbǎi jǐshí kuài qián]
几 + 千 / 万 + MW + N
footnotes_tr: Don't confuse this with the question word 几[jǐ] meaning "how many?" (你几岁了?[Nǐ jǐ suì le?] — usually asked to children, implying an answer under 10). This table covers the non-question, "some/several" usage.

tables.caption_tr: 多[duō] — "More Than" Placement Rules
rows: 十多个人[shí duō ge rén]
二十多本书[èrshí duō běn shū]
一百多块钱[yìbǎi duō kuài qián]
十五个多小时[shíwǔ ge duō xiǎoshí]
三十五块多钱[sānshí wǔ kuài duō qián]
footnotes_tr: With money the two orders create a real meaning contrast: 十块多钱[shí kuài duō qián] = "just over 10 yuan" (10.x yuan), while 十多块钱[shí duō kuài qián] = "more than 10, up to 20 yuan" (11–19 yuan). Same words, different order, different meaning!

tables.caption_tr: 左右[zuǒyòu] — "Around / Approximately" After a Number Phrase
rows: 一个星期左右[yí ge xīngqī zuǒyòu]
二十个人左右[èrshí ge rén zuǒyòu]
一百块钱左右[yìbǎi kuài qián zuǒyòu]
footnotes_tr: 左右 always sits at the very end of the number phrase. It normally isn't combined with 几[jǐ], since 几 is already vague on its own.

tables.caption_tr: 大概[dàgài] — Adverb of Estimation
rows: 他大概是老师。[Tā dàgài shì lǎoshī.]
Subject + 大概 + 有/是 + Number + MW
班里大概有二十个学生。[Bān lǐ dàgài yǒu èrshí ge xuésheng.]
大概明天会下雨。[Dàgài míngtiān huì xiàyǔ.]
Combined with 左右 for extra vagueness
大概 + Number + MW + 左右
大概三十个左右。[Dàgài sānshí ge zuǒyòu.]
footnotes_tr: 大概 expresses the speaker's own subjective guess and works even without any number in the sentence, unlike 几, 多, and 左右, which all require an attached number.

tables.caption_tr: 几 vs 多 vs 左右 vs 大概 at a Glance
rows: A number (before or after the MW)
End of the full number phrase
Small quantity, or one unknown digit
"Around X", could be a bit more or less
No — it IS the indefinite part
No — works with or without a number

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with Approximate Numbers
rows: 多 is duplicated / wrongly placed twice
Choose one: 十多块钱[shí duō kuài qián] (11–19 yuan) or 十块多钱[shí kuài duō qián] (10.x yuan)
几 already means "approximate"; adding 左右 is redundant and mis-ordered
Just say 几个人[jǐ ge rén]
左右 was placed before the measure word 岁
他三十岁左右。[Tā sānshí suì zuǒyòu.] — 左右 must come after 岁
Stacking three approximators (大概 + 几 + 左右) at once is overloaded and unnatural
Pick one or two: 大概几十个人来了[dàgài jǐshí ge rén lái le] or 几十个人左右来了[jǐshí ge rén zuǒyòu lái le]

examples.target: 教室里有几个学生。
examples.reading: Jiàoshì lǐ yǒu jǐ ge xuésheng.
examples.translation_tr: There are a few students in the classroom.
examples.note_tr: 几[jǐ] + measure word 个[gè] here means 'a few/several', not a question.

examples.target: 我买了十多本书。
examples.reading: Wǒ mǎi le shí duō běn shū.
examples.translation_tr: I bought more than ten books.
examples.note_tr: 十 is a whole number (ends in 0), so 多[duō] goes right after it, before the measure word 本[běn].

examples.target: 他今年三十岁左右。
examples.reading: Tā jīnnián sānshí suì zuǒyòu.
examples.translation_tr: This year he is around thirty years old.
examples.note_tr: 左右[zuǒyòu] attaches to the very end of the full number phrase 三十岁.

examples.target: 这个班大概有二十个学生。
examples.reading: Zhège bān dàgài yǒu èrshí ge xuésheng.
examples.translation_tr: This class probably has about twenty students.
examples.note_tr: 大概[dàgài] is an adverb placed before 有[yǒu], expressing the speaker's own guess.

examples.target: 我们等了三十多分钟。
examples.reading: Wǒmen děng le sānshí duō fēnzhōng.
examples.translation_tr: We waited for more than thirty minutes.
examples.note_tr: 三十 ends in 0, so 多 sits right after the number: 三十多分钟.

examples.target: 那本词典大概一百块钱左右。
examples.reading: Nà běn cídiǎn dàgài yìbǎi kuài qián zuǒyòu.
examples.translation_tr: That dictionary is probably around a hundred yuan.
examples.note_tr: 大概 and 左右 stack together here for a doubly-vague, casual estimate.

examples.target: 教室里坐着十几个人。
examples.reading: Jiàoshì lǐ zuòzhe shí jǐ ge rén.
examples.translation_tr: There are ten-something (11–19) people sitting in the classroom.
examples.note_tr: 十几[shí jǐ] means an unknown ones-digit between 11 and 19.

examples.target: 他有几十本汉语书。
examples.reading: Tā yǒu jǐshí běn Hànyǔ shū.
examples.translation_tr: He has dozens of Chinese books.
examples.note_tr: 几十[jǐshí] means an unknown tens-digit, i.e. anywhere from about 20 to 90-something.

ba-construction-full.title_tr: 把 (bǎ) Construction Full Coverage (Mandatory Complement Rule)
ba-construction-full.intro_tr: The 把 (bǎ) construction moves a specific, definite object in front of the verb to show that it is being handled, moved, or changed in some deliberate way. The single most important rule that trips up English-speaking learners is this: the verb in a 把-sentence can NEVER stand alone. Chinese grammar requires something extra after the verb — an aspect particle, a resultative complement, a directional complement, a quantity phrase, or a reduplicated verb — to show the result, direction, duration, or degree of the action. This required extra element is called a complement (补语[bǔyǔ]), and a sentence like 我把书看。[Wǒ bǎ shū kàn.] is simply ungrammatical without one. This page catalogs every type of complement that can legally complete a 把-sentence, along with negation rules and which verbs are even eligible to appear in this pattern.

tables.caption_tr: Types of Complements That Can Legally Follow the Verb in a 把-Sentence
rows: 我把书看了。[Wǒ bǎ shū kàn le.]
I read the book (I did the reading).
我把衣服洗干净了。[Wǒ bǎ yīfu xǐ gānjìng le.]
Directional complement (来/去/上/下/进/出 etc.)
请把书拿过来。[Qǐng bǎ shū ná guòlai.]
把 + Obj + V + 在/到/给/成 + …
我把书放在桌子上了。[Wǒ bǎ shū fàng zài zhuōzi shang le.]
I put the book on the table.
把 + Obj + V + 了 + Time/Measure
他把这首歌唱了三遍。[Tā bǎ zhè shǒu gē chàng le sān biàn.]
He sang this song three times.
你把房间打扫打扫。[Nǐ bǎ fángjiān dǎsǎo dǎsǎo.]
Tidy up the room a bit.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistake: Bare Verb vs. Correct Complement
rows: 我把书看。[Wǒ bǎ shū kàn.]
我把书看完了。[Wǒ bǎ shū kàn wán le.]
Bare verb 看 has nothing after it; add resultative 完 + 了 to show the book was finished.
他把门开。[Tā bǎ mén kāi.]
他把门开了。[Tā bǎ mén kāi le.]
Add aspect particle 了 to mark that the opening actually happened.
请把窗户关。[Qǐng bǎ chuānghu guān.]
请把窗户关上。[Qǐng bǎ chuānghu guān shang.]
Add directional/resultative 上 to show the window ends up shut.
我把钱花。[Wǒ bǎ qián huā.]
我把钱花完了。[Wǒ bǎ qián huā wán le.]
Add 完了 to show the money is entirely used up.

tables.caption_tr: Negation, Prohibition, and Modal Placement in 把-Sentences
rows: 没(有) + 把 + Obj + V + Complement
我没把作业写完。[Wǒ méi bǎ zuòyè xiě wán.]
Most common way to negate a 把-sentence; means the action did not reach completion.
我不把这件事告诉他。[Wǒ bù bǎ zhè jiàn shì gàosu tā.]
Used for a deliberate refusal, not for describing an unfinished past event.
别/不要 + 把 + Obj + V + Complement
别把杯子打破了！[Bié bǎ bēizi dǎ pò le!]
Warns someone not to let something happen to the object.
Modal verbs (要, 想, 应该, 可以, 得)
你应该把房间收拾好。[Nǐ yīnggāi bǎ fángjiān shōushi hǎo.]
Modals always sit before 把, never between 把 and the verb.
Adverbs (已经, 都, 先, 刚)
我已经把电影看完了。[Wǒ yǐjīng bǎ diànyǐng kàn wán le.]
Time/scope adverbs also come before 把, not before the bare verb.

tables.caption_tr: Which Verbs Are Eligible to Appear in a 把-Sentence
rows: Disposal/transitive action verbs (放, 拿, 写, 吃, 关, 打开, 洗)
把书放好[bǎ shū fàng hǎo], 把饭吃了[bǎ fàn chī le]
These verbs actively change, move, or affect the object — exactly what 把 is designed to express.
Stative/perception verbs (是, 有, 在, 喜欢, 知道, 觉得, 看见, 听见)
These verbs describe states or perceptions rather than an action performed on the object.
Plain motion verbs without a complement (来, 去, 回)
Motion verbs need a further complement or simply don't take a 把-object in this bare form.
Emotion/cognition verbs (爱, 恨, 希望, 认为)
Emotions and opinions are not 'disposed of'; use plain SVO instead: 我爱她。[Wǒ ài tā.]
Any eligible verb once a valid complement is added
把门关上[bǎ mén guān shang], 把书看完[bǎ shū kàn wán]
Adding a resultative/directional/aspect complement turns the action into a completed disposal, satisfying the 把 requirement.

tables.caption_tr: 把-Sentence vs. Plain SVO: When Each Is Required
rows: Object is specific/definite and undergoes a change or is disposed of
我把苹果吃了。[Wǒ bǎ píngguǒ chī le.] (a particular apple)
Object is indefinite/generic, no specific result emphasized
我吃苹果。[Wǒ chī píngguǒ.] (apples in general)
Speaker wants to emphasize the result or destination of the object
把车开到公司。[Bǎ chē kāi dào gōngsī.]
Simple habitual or generic action, no disposal/result meaning
我每天开车上班。[Wǒ měitiān kāichē shàngbān.]
Verb has no complement available at all
No — would be ungrammatical with 把
我看书。[Wǒ kàn shū.] (NOT ✗我把书看。)

examples.target: 我把书看完了。
examples.reading: Wǒ bǎ shū kàn wán le.
examples.translation_tr: I finished reading the book.
examples.note_tr: Resultative complement 完 + aspect particle 了 — the verb 看 alone would be ungrammatical here.

examples.target: 请把门关上。
examples.reading: Qǐng bǎ mén guān shang.
examples.translation_tr: Please close the door.
examples.note_tr: Directional complement 上 shows the door reaches a closed state.

examples.target: 她把衣服洗干净了。
examples.reading: Tā bǎ yīfu xǐ gānjìng le.
examples.translation_tr: She washed the clothes clean.
examples.note_tr: Resultative complement 干净 describes the outcome of the washing.

examples.target: 你把这封信送到他家。
examples.reading: Nǐ bǎ zhè fēng xìn sòng dào tā jiā.
examples.translation_tr: Deliver this letter to his house.
examples.note_tr: Complement 到 + place tells you where the object ends up.

examples.target: 我没把作业写完。
examples.reading: Wǒ méi bǎ zuòyè xiě wán.
examples.translation_tr: I didn't finish writing the homework.
examples.note_tr: Negation word 没 goes before 把, never between 把 and the verb.

examples.target: 别把手机忘在家里！
examples.reading: Bié bǎ shǒujī wàng zài jiā li!
examples.translation_tr: Don't forget the phone at home!
examples.note_tr: Prohibition 别 before 把; complement 在 + place shows where the phone would be left.

examples.target: 他把这个故事讲了两遍。
examples.reading: Tā bǎ zhège gùshi jiǎng le liǎng biàn.
examples.translation_tr: He told this story twice.
examples.note_tr: A quantity/frequency phrase (两遍) can serve as the required complement.

examples.target: 我把钥匙放好了。
examples.reading: Wǒ bǎ yàoshi fàng hǎo le.
examples.translation_tr: I put the keys away properly.
examples.note_tr: Resultative complement 好 shows the keys are now properly placed.

bei-passive-full.title_tr: Full-Scope Passive Voice (被 / 叫 / 让)
bei-passive-full.intro_tr: Chinese marks the passive voice with one of three coverbs — 被[bèi], 叫[jiào], or 让[ràng] — placed between the subject (the thing/person affected) and the agent that performs the action. Unlike English, a bare passive verb is almost never grammatical: the verb must be followed by some other element (了, a resultative/directional complement, a quantity phrase, etc.) that shows a completed or specific result. 被[bèi] is the most versatile and can drop the agent (被打破了), while 叫[jiào] and 让[ràng] are colloquial and normally REQUIRE the agent to be stated. Chinese passive sentences overwhelmingly describe something adverse, unexpected, or undesirable happening to the subject — using it for neutral, everyday actions (the way English uses passive constantly) usually sounds unnatural or wrong.

tables.caption_tr: The Three Passive Markers Compared
rows: Neutral — used in both writing and speech
Optional (被 alone, or 被 + agent)
The default, most common and most flexible passive marker
杯子被打破了。 [Bēizi bèi dǎpò le.] — The cup got broken.
Casual, everyday spoken narration, often about mishaps
钱被/叫他花光了。 [...jiào tā huā guāng le.] — The money was all spent by him.
Interchangeable with 叫 in speech; slightly more common overall
他让雨淋湿了。 [Tā ràng yǔ lín shī le.] — He got soaked by the rain.

tables.caption_tr: Full Sentence Structure (Slot by Slot)
rows: The person or thing that RECEIVES the action
被 / 叫 / 让 — placed right after the subject
Optional after 被; MANDATORY after 叫/让; if unknown/unimportant with 被, just omit it
他 [tā] 'him' (may be omitted only with 被)
A bare, single verb alone is normally ungrammatical here
了, resultative complement (破/坏/湿...), directional complement (上去/出来...), quantity/duration phrase, etc.

tables.caption_tr: Negation, Adverbs, and Modals: Where Do They Go?
rows: BEFORE 被/叫/让, never before the verb
杯子没被打破。 [Bēizi méi bèi dǎpò.]
这种事不会被忘记。 [Zhè zhǒng shì bú huì bèi wàngjì.]
This kind of thing won't be forgotten.
他常常被老师批评。 [Tā chángcháng bèi lǎoshī pīpíng.]
He is often criticized by the teacher.
这个秘密可能会被发现。 [Zhège mìmì kěnéng huì bèi fāxiàn.]

tables.caption_tr: With vs. Without a Stated Agent
rows: Yes — very common, especially in writing
No — agent is mandatory; must say 叫(小偷)偷了 or switch to 被
No — agent is mandatory; must say 让(雨)淋湿了 or switch to 被

tables.caption_tr: The Reinforcing 给 [gěi] Pattern (Colloquial Emphasis)
rows: 杯子被他给打破了。 [Bēizi bèi tā gěi dǎpò le.]
给 [gěi] adds emphasis before the verb; purely colloquial, optional, does not change the meaning
衣服叫雨给淋湿了。 [Yīfu jiào yǔ gěi lín shī le.]
Same emphatic function; very common in spoken Mandarin
Rare/awkward without an agent — 给 reinforcement is normally used together with a stated agent

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: Bare verb with no complement — sounds incomplete, like a rule/label rather than an event
杯子被打破了。 — add a resultative complement + 了
钱包叫偷了。 [Qiánbāo jiào tōu le.]
叫 used without stating the agent — not allowed
钱包叫小偷偷了。 — state the agent, or switch to 被: 钱包被偷了。
我被生成一份报告。 (translating English 'I was asked to generate...')
Passive used for a neutral/routine task with no adversity — unnatural in Chinese
Use active voice instead: 我要写一份报告。 / Use 让/叫 causative if someone assigned it: 老板让我写一份报告。
没 placed after the verb instead of before 被
杯子没被他打破。 — negation always goes right before 被/叫/让
他被老师表扬了一下，很高兴。
Not actually wrong grammatically, but note: passive here is neutral/positive — acceptable, though 被 is still statistically more common with negative events
(No correction needed — shown for contrast: 被 CAN carry positive meaning, just less typically)

examples.target: 杯子被他打破了。
examples.reading: Bēizi bèi tā dǎpò le.
examples.translation_tr: The cup was broken by him. (被 + agent + verb + resultative complement 破 + 了)

examples.target: 我的钱包叫小偷偷走了。
examples.reading: Wǒ de qiánbāo jiào xiǎotōu tōu zǒu le.
examples.translation_tr: My wallet was stolen by a thief. (叫 always needs the agent 小偷 stated)

examples.target: 他让老板骂了一顿。
examples.reading: Tā ràng lǎobǎn mà le yí dùn.
examples.translation_tr: He got scolded by his boss. (让 + agent + verb + quantity complement 一顿)

examples.target: 这本书还没被借走。
examples.reading: Zhè běn shū hái méi bèi jiè zǒu.
examples.translation_tr: This book hasn't been borrowed yet. (negation 没 goes BEFORE 被, not before the verb)

examples.target: 衣服被雨淋湿了。
examples.reading: Yīfu bèi yǔ lín shī le.
examples.translation_tr: The clothes got soaked by the rain. (被 + agent 雨 + verb + resultative complement 湿)

examples.target: 那个秘密已经被大家知道了。
examples.reading: Nàge mìmì yǐjīng bèi dàjiā zhīdao le.
examples.translation_tr: That secret is already known by everyone. (adverb 已经 placed before 被)

examples.target: 小心，别叫车撞了！
examples.reading: Xiǎoxīn, bié jiào chē zhuàng le!
examples.translation_tr: Be careful, don't get hit by a car! (叫 in a warning/imperative, colloquial register)

examples.target: 作业被老师收上去了。
examples.reading: Zuòyè bèi lǎoshī shōu shàngqù le.
examples.translation_tr: The homework was collected by the teacher. (被 + agent + verb + directional complement 上去)

potential-complements.title_tr: Potential Complements (听得懂 / 听不懂): Expressing 'Can/Cannot Achieve the Result'
potential-complements.intro_tr: Potential complements (可能补语[kěnéng bǔyǔ]) tell you whether the result or direction of an action can actually be achieved — not whether it is allowed. They are built by inserting 得[de] ('can') or 不[bù] ('cannot') between a verb and its resultative or directional complement, e.g. 听[tīng] + 懂[dǒng] → 听得懂[tīng de dǒng] 'can understand by listening' vs 听不懂[tīng bu dǒng] 'can't understand by listening'. Unlike 能[néng] or 可以[kěyǐ], which express permission or general capability, potential complements zero in on whether a specific outcome is physically or mentally attainable in that situation. Any object goes after the whole verb-complement unit, and yes/no questions are most naturally formed with the affirmative-negative pattern 'V得C V不C?'. A handful of potential complements — 得了[deliǎo], 得起[deqǐ], 得住[dezhù], 得下[dexià] — are fixed idiomatic units worth memorizing as whole chunks rather than building from scratch.

tables.caption_tr: Formation from Resultative Verb Complements: Verb + 得/不 + Complement
rows: can / cannot finish reading or watching
can / cannot get hold of (by buying)

tables.caption_tr: Formation from Directional Complements: Verb + 得/不 + Directional Word
Common Fixed/Idiomatic Potential Complements
rows: V得了/不了[de liǎo / bu liǎo]
physically/practically able or unable to complete V
吃不了[chī bu liǎo] — can't eat that much
V得起/不起[de qǐ / bu qǐ]
买不起[mǎi bu qǐ] — can't afford to buy
V得动/不动[de dòng / bu dòng]
have/lack the physical strength to do V
搬不动[bān bu dòng] — too heavy to move
V得下/不下[de xià / bu xià]
there is/isn't enough space or room
坐不下[zuò bu xià] — no room to sit
V得住/不住[de zhù / bu zhù]
can/cannot hold, retain, or keep steady
记不住[jì bu zhù] — can't remember/retain
V得上/不上[de shàng / bu shàng]
can/cannot reach a standard or catch up in time
赶不上[gǎn bu shàng] — can't catch up / make it in time

tables.caption_tr: Forming Questions with Potential Complements
rows: 你听得懂吗?[Nǐ tīng de dǒng ma?]
你听得懂听不懂中文?[Nǐ tīng de dǒng tīng bu dǒng Zhōngwén?]
Can you understand Chinese or not?
这个字,你看得懂看不懂?[Zhège zì, nǐ kàn de dǒng kàn bu dǒng?]
This character — can you understand it or not?

tables.caption_tr: Potential Complement vs. 能[néng] / 可以[kěyǐ]: Key Differences
rows: whether a specific RESULT can be physically/mentally achieved
general permission, rule, or overall capability
obstacles like size, distance, noise, quantity, skill
social rules, official permission, general skill
这个字太小,我看不见。[Zhège zì tài xiǎo, wǒ kàn bu jiàn.] — too small to see
这里不能抽烟。[Zhèlǐ bù néng chōuyān.] — not allowed here
often interchangeable for physical/mental ability: 我看得见 ≈ 我能看见
能 + V(+Complement) can restate the same idea more formally
built into the structure: 得 → 不 (e.g. 得懂 → 不懂)
negation goes before the modal: 不能, 不可以

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Points to Watch
rows: Confusing this 得[de] with the manner-complement 得[de]
Both look identical, but here 得[de] simply marks 'can'; it is not measuring HOW an action is done
他跑得快[tā pǎo de kuài] (manner: runs fast) vs 他跑得了/跑不了[tā pǎo de liǎo / pǎo bu liǎo] (potential: can/cannot escape by running)
Adding 不能 in front of an already-negative form
Don't stack 不能 with a negative potential complement — it's redundant/wrong
✗ 我不能看不懂 → ✓ 我看不懂[wǒ kàn bu dǒng] (I can't understand)
The object goes AFTER the full verb+得/不+complement unit, never between the verb and 得/不
✗ 我听中文得懂 → ✓ 我听得懂中文[wǒ tīng de dǒng Zhōngwén]
The potential-complement 了 is pronounced liǎo, meaning 'able to'; it is unrelated to the aspect particle 了(le)
吃得了[chī de liǎo] (can eat it all) vs 吃了[chī le] (ate / have eaten)
Assuming every verb has a potential form
Potential complements only attach to verbs that naturally take a resultative or directional complement
学得会[xué de huì] ✓ (learnable) — but not every verb pairs freely with every complement

examples.target: 我听得懂中文。
examples.reading: Wǒ tīng de dǒng Zhōngwén.
examples.translation_tr: I can understand Chinese (when I listen to it).

examples.target: 你听得懂我说的话吗?
examples.reading: Nǐ tīng de dǒng wǒ shuō de huà ma?
examples.translation_tr: Can you understand what I'm saying?

examples.target: 这么多菜,我们吃得完吗?
examples.reading: Zhème duō cài, wǒmen chī de wán ma?
examples.translation_tr: With so much food, can we finish it all?

examples.target: 太贵了,我买不起。
examples.reading: Tài guì le, wǒ mǎi bu qǐ.
examples.translation_tr: It's too expensive, I can't afford it.
examples.note_tr: 起[qǐ] here is a fixed potential complement meaning 'afford'.

examples.target: 教室里人太多,我进不去。
examples.reading: Jiàoshì lǐ rén tài duō, wǒ jìn bu qù.
examples.translation_tr: There are too many people in the classroom, I can't get in.

examples.target: 黑板上的字,你看得见看不见?
examples.reading: Hēibǎn shang de zì, nǐ kàn de jiàn kàn bu jiàn?
examples.translation_tr: The characters on the blackboard — can you see them or not?
examples.note_tr: Object 黑板上的字 is topicalized before the subject; question uses the affirmative-negative (V得C V不C) pattern.

examples.target: 这个箱子太重,我搬不动。
examples.reading: Zhège xiāngzi tài zhòng, wǒ bān bu dòng.
examples.translation_tr: This box is too heavy, I don't have the strength to move it.

examples.target: 今天的作业,你做得完做不完?
examples.reading: Jīntiān de zuòyè, nǐ zuò de wán zuò bu wán?
examples.translation_tr: Today's homework — will you be able to finish it or not?

separable-verbs.title_tr: Separable Verbs 离合词[líhécí] (见面, 帮忙, 睡觉)
separable-verbs.intro_tr: 离合词[líhécí] ("separate-together words") are verbs that look like a single two-character word but are secretly built from a Verb + Object pair fused together, for example 见面[jiànmiàn] (see + face = "to meet") or 帮忙[bāngmáng] (help + busyness = "to help"). Unlike ordinary two-character verbs, a 离合词 can be pulled apart so that grammar markers like 了[le], 过[guo], durations, frequencies, or a possessive 的[de] phrase slot in between the two halves. Because the second half is technically a noun-like object, you can never attach another object directly after the whole compound (✗ 见面他); instead you must use 跟[gēn] + person + verb, or insert the person with 的 in the middle. This page gives you the full insertion map, the reduplication pattern, and a list of the most common 离合词 you'll meet at HSK4.

tables.caption_tr: Common Separable Verbs (离合词) and Their Hidden Components
Insertion Rules — What Can Go Between the Verb Part and the Object Part
rows: directly after the verb part, before the object part
睡了八个小时觉[shuì le bā ge xiǎoshí jiào]
见过两次面[jiànguo liǎng cì miàn]
between the two parts, replaces a missing object
生我的气[shēng wǒ de qì]
give a big favor / great help
帮一个忙[bāng yí ge máng]

tables.caption_tr: Reduplication and 'Do It a Little' Patterns
rows: only 帮 repeats, 忙 stays single
take a nap / get some sleep
uses 一 + object instead of reduplication
uses 个 as a light measure word filler

tables.caption_tr: Negation and Question Forms with Separable Verbs
rows: 他还没结婚。[Tā hái méi jiéhūn.]
我今天不游泳。[Wǒ jīntiān bù yóuyǒng.]
你帮不帮忙?[Nǐ bāng bu bāngmáng?]
Are you going to help or not?
你们见过面吗?[Nǐmen jiànguo miàn ma?]
compound split + 多长时间/多久
How long have you known each other?

tables.caption_tr: Adding a Person or Object — Common Mistakes vs Correct Forms
rows: ✓ 我跟他见面。[Wǒ gēn tā jiànmiàn.]
✓ 我帮你的忙。[Wǒ bāng nǐ de máng.] / 我帮你。[Wǒ bāng nǐ.]
✓ 他跟她结婚。[Tā gēn tā jiéhūn.]
✓ 我生他的气。[Wǒ shēng tā de qì.]
✓ 我们见过三次面。[Wǒmen jiànguo sān cì miàn.]
footnotes_tr: The object part of a 离合词 already fills the 'object slot' of the verb, so a second direct object cannot follow it — the extra person/thing must be introduced earlier with 跟[gēn] or inserted in the middle with 的[de].

examples.target: 我们见过面。
examples.reading: Wǒmen jiànguo miàn.
examples.translation_tr: We've met before. (过 is inserted between 见 and 面, not attached to the end of the whole word)

examples.target: 你能帮我一个忙吗?
examples.reading: Nǐ néng bāng wǒ yí ge máng ma?
examples.translation_tr: Can you do me a favor? (an object 我 and measure word 一个 are inserted between 帮 and 忙)

examples.target: 昨天晚上我睡了八个小时觉。
examples.reading: Zuótiān wǎnshang wǒ shuì le bā ge xiǎoshí jiào.
examples.translation_tr: Last night I slept for eight hours. (the duration '8 hours' sits between 睡 and 觉)

examples.target: 他跟一个中国女孩结婚了。
examples.reading: Tā gēn yí ge Zhōngguó nǚhái jiéhūn le.
examples.translation_tr: He married a Chinese girl. (you cannot say 结婚她; the person must appear with 跟 before the verb)

examples.target: 你别生我的气了。
examples.reading: Nǐ bié shēng wǒ de qì le.
examples.translation_tr: Don't be angry with me anymore. (的 + person is inserted between 生 and 气 to show who the anger is directed at)

examples.target: 我明天要请假。
examples.reading: Wǒ míngtiān yào qǐngjià.
examples.translation_tr: I need to ask for leave tomorrow.

examples.target: 我们见见面吧。
examples.reading: Wǒmen jiànjiànmiàn ba.
examples.translation_tr: Let's meet up for a bit. (only the verb part 见 reduplicates, the object 面 stays single)

examples.target: 他今年夏天毕业。
examples.reading: Tā jīnnián xiàtiān bìyè.
examples.translation_tr: He graduates this summer.

qilai-extended.title_tr: 起来[qǐlai] Extended Uses (看起来, 想起来)
qilai-extended.intro_tr: 起来[qǐlai] literally means "to rise up" or "to get up," but far beyond that literal, physical use, it very commonly attaches to verbs and adjectives in an abstract, metaphorical way. In this extended use it does NOT mean physical upward motion at all — instead it signals that an action or state has just begun and is continuing (哭起来[kū qǐlai] "burst into crying"), or it frames a comment about how something appears/feels/sounds/turns out when you actually do or consider it (看起来[kàn qǐlai] "it looks like...", 说起来[shuō qǐlai] "speaking of it..."). A handful of Verb+起来 combinations have also become fixed, idiomatic expressions (想起来[xiǎng qǐlai] "to recall", 算起来[suàn qǐlai] "all things considered") that every learner simply needs to memorize as vocabulary chunks. This page collects all three extended functions, the object-insertion rule (起 + Object + 来), and the potential-complement forms (想得起来 / 想不起来) in one place.

tables.caption_tr: The three extended (non-literal) functions of 起来[qǐlai]
rows: an action or state begins and keeps going
笑起来[xiào qǐlai] — 'burst into laughter (and keep laughing)'
'when you V it, it turns out to be...' — used to comment on how something looks, sounds, feels, tastes, or works
这件衣服穿起来很舒服[zhè jiàn yīfu chuān qǐlai hěn shūfu] — 'this clothing is comfortable to wear'
meanings that must be learned as whole chunks: recall, seem, add up, combine, hide, lock up...

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed Verb+起来[qǐlai] combinations to memorize
rows: it looks like / it seems that (visual impression)
speaking of it; to tell the truth; in theory
counting it up; all things considered
combined together; put together as one

tables.caption_tr: Object-insertion rule: 起...来[qǐ...lái] splits apart when the verb has an object
rows: burst into crying (no split — no object)
burst into laughter (no split — no object)
footnotes_tr: Rule: if the verb takes a direct object, insert the object between 起 and 来 → V + 起 + Object + 来. If there is no object, keep 起来 together right after the verb.

tables.caption_tr: The evaluative/experiential frame: Topic + V起来 + Adjective
rows: 这本书读起来很有意思。
This book is interesting to read.
footnotes_tr: The item being commented on is pulled to the front as the topic; 起来 signals 'when [topic] is [verbed]'. Very common with 穿 (wear), 听 (listen), 看 (look), 吃 (eat), 用 (use), 做 (do).

tables.caption_tr: Potential complement forms: 得/不 inserted for 'can/cannot'
rows: can / cannot stand up (physically able to)
purely evaluative 'looks like' does not take potential form
footnotes_tr: Only combinations that describe a genuine physical or mental ability normally take the 得/不 potential insertion; purely evaluative idioms like 看起来 and 说起来 do not.

tables.caption_tr: Common mix-ups: extended 起来[qǐlai] vs similar expressions
rows: 'it looks like...' based on visual/general impression
'it appears to be...' — near-synonym of 看起来
largely interchangeable with 看起来 in most contexts
'it seems as if...' — can be used without any visual basis
broader than 看起来; can precede a whole clause
'to suddenly recall' — an active mental event of remembering
implies the memory was momentarily lost, then returned
'to remember, to still have in memory' — a continuous state
does NOT imply the memory was ever lost; not interchangeable with 想起来

examples.target: 天气突然冷起来了。
examples.reading: Tiānqì tūrán lěng qǐlai le.
examples.translation_tr: The weather suddenly started turning cold (and is staying cold).

examples.target: 孩子们看见妈妈,高兴地笑起来。
examples.reading: Háizimen kànjiàn māma, gāoxìng de xiào qǐlai.
examples.translation_tr: When the children saw their mother, they burst out laughing with joy.

examples.target: 外面下起雨来了。
examples.reading: Wàimiàn xià qǐ yǔ lái le.
examples.translation_tr: It has started raining outside. (note how 起...来 splits around the object 雨)

examples.target: 这个问题听起来很简单,其实很难。
examples.reading: Zhège wèntí tīng qǐlai hěn jiǎndān, qíshí hěn nán.
examples.translation_tr: This problem sounds simple, but it's actually very hard.

examples.target: 我突然想起来他的名字了。
examples.reading: Wǒ tūrán xiǎng qǐlai tā de míngzi le.
examples.translation_tr: I suddenly remembered his name.

examples.target: 对不起,我想不起来你的名字了。
examples.reading: Duìbuqǐ, wǒ xiǎng bu qǐlai nǐ de míngzi le.
examples.translation_tr: Sorry, I can't recall your name. (potential negative form)

examples.target: 这件衣服穿起来很舒服。
examples.reading: Zhè jiàn yīfu chuān qǐlai hěn shūfu.
examples.translation_tr: This piece of clothing is comfortable to wear (when you actually wear it).

examples.target: 说起来容易,做起来难。
examples.reading: Shuō qǐlai róngyì, zuò qǐlai nán.
examples.translation_tr: It's easier said than done.

xiaqu-continue.title_tr: 下去 (xiàqu): Directional Complement for 'Continuing' an Action (说下去)
xiaqu-continue.intro_tr: 下去[xiàqu] is a directional complement that, when attached to a verb, no longer means physical "to go down" — instead it marks that an ongoing action continues from the present moment into the future ("to keep on doing", "to carry on"). The classic example is 说下去[shuōxiàqu], "to keep talking/continue speaking." Because 下去 signals continuation *from now on*, it pairs naturally with encouragements, requests to keep going, and statements of endurance or fatigue. A key structural rule: 下去 attaches directly to the bare verb with no object in between — if the verb needs an object, that object must be moved to the front of the sentence as the topic. 下去 also has a potential-complement pair, V不下去[V bu xiàqù] ("can't continue") and V得下去[V de xiàqù] ("can manage to continue"), which are extremely common in daily speech to express that something has become too hard, boring, or exhausting to carry on with.

tables.caption_tr: Core Pattern: V + 下去[xiàqu] and Its Forms
rows: 别/不要 + V + 下去 + 了
can't keep talking (words fail, too hard/awkward)
Nǐ hái shuō de xiàqù ma?

tables.caption_tr: Common Verb + 下去[xiàqu] Collocations
rows: keep walking (also figurative: keep going in life)

tables.caption_tr: 下去[xiàqu] vs. 下来[xiàlai] vs. 继续[jìxù]: Three Ways to Say 'Continue'
rows: complement attached after a verb; action already in progress will keep going forward
from the PAST up to NOW
complement attached after a verb; action has continued up to the present, often implying settling/stabilizing
This custom has been preserved (up to now).
stands alone as a full verb before another verb; no directional nuance

tables.caption_tr: Object Placement Rule with 下去[xiàqu]
rows: No object may sit between V and 下去
Object moved to front (topic) + V + 下去
Zhè běn shū, nǐ kàn xiàqu.
Object can also simply be dropped if understood from context
把 is generally NOT used with 下去 continuative complement
Zhè fèn gōngzuò, wǒ zuò xiàqu.
footnotes_tr: In the potential forms (V不下去 / V得下去), 去 keeps a light, often neutral tone in casual speech, written as xiàqu; in the plain complement without 得/不 it is commonly read with a fuller tone as xiàqù, especially in careful or emphatic speech. Both are widely accepted.

examples.target: 请你说下去。
examples.reading: Qǐng nǐ shuō xiàqu.
examples.translation_tr: Please keep talking (continue what you were saying).

examples.target: 老师,我可以说下去吗?
examples.reading: Lǎoshī, wǒ kěyǐ shuō xiàqu ma?
examples.translation_tr: Teacher, may I continue speaking?

examples.target: 这件事,我们必须做下去。
examples.reading: Zhè jiàn shì, wǒmen bìxū zuò xiàqu.
examples.translation_tr: We must keep doing this (matter), no matter what.
examples.note_tr: The object 这件事 is topicalized at the front of the sentence because an object cannot sit between the verb and 下去.

examples.target: 别说下去了,我不想听了。
examples.reading: Bié shuō xiàqu le, wǒ bù xiǎng tīng le.
examples.translation_tr: Stop talking (don't continue), I don't want to listen anymore.
examples.note_tr: 别/不要 + V + 下去 + 了 is the standard pattern for telling someone to stop an ongoing action.

examples.target: 太累了,我实在走不下去了。
examples.reading: Tài lèi le, wǒ shízài zǒu bu xiàqù le.
examples.translation_tr: I'm too tired, I really can't keep walking.
examples.note_tr: Potential complement form V+不下去 = physically/mentally unable to continue the action.

examples.target: 只要你努力,就能坚持下去。
examples.reading: Zhǐyào nǐ nǔlì, jiù néng jiānchí xiàqu.
examples.translation_tr: As long as you work hard, you'll be able to keep persisting.

examples.target: 这个故事太无聊了,我看不下去了。
examples.reading: Zhège gùshi tài wúliáo le, wǒ kàn bu xiàqù le.
examples.translation_tr: This story is too boring — I can't bring myself to keep reading it.

examples.target: 虽然很难,但是我们要坚持学下去。
examples.reading: Suīrán hěn nán, dànshì wǒmen yào jiānchí xué xiàqu.
examples.translation_tr: Although it's hard, we must persist and keep studying.

budebu.title_tr: 不得不 (bùdébù): "Have No Choice But To"
budebu.intro_tr: 不得不 [bùdébù] is a fixed adverbial phrase meaning "have no choice but to," "cannot avoid," or "be forced to" do something. It is built from two negatives (不...不) sandwiching the modal 得 [dé] ("must"), so literally it reads as "not not-have-to," which grammatically cancels out into a strong, emphatic obligation. It always sits directly in front of a verb, in the pattern Subject + 不得不 + Verb (+ Object), and it signals that the action happened reluctantly, because of outside pressure or circumstances beyond the speaker's control — never a free personal choice. Because the obligation comes from the situation itself, 不得不 sentences are frequently introduced by a cause clause with 因为/由于 ("because") or a purpose clause with 为了 ("in order to"). Compare it carefully with 只好 [zhǐhǎo] (settling, with resignation, for the only option left) and 必须 [bìxū] (a neutral, objective rule) to catch the subtle difference in tone.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: The Double-Negative Structure of 不得不
rows: fixed adverbial phrase meaning 'have no choice but to'
footnotes_tr: The two negatives cancel each other out, producing an emphatic forced obligation — similar to English 'cannot help but' or 'can't not do it.'
得 here is pronounced dé (2nd tone) — not de (neutral tone, structural particle) and not děi (3rd tone, colloquial 'must').

tables.caption_tr: Basic Sentence Pattern: Subject + 不得不 + Verb (+ Object)
rows: 我不得不接受这个结果。
I have no choice but to accept this result.

tables.caption_tr: 不得不 vs. Similar Necessity Expressions
rows: forced by external circumstances; often reluctant
他不得不辞职。[Tā bùdébù cízhí.] 'He had no choice but to resign.'
the only remaining option after other paths failed; resigned tone
没有车,我只好走路。[Méiyǒu chē, wǒ zhǐhǎo zǒulù.] 'There was no car, so I had to walk.'
objective, neutral rule or requirement, no reluctance implied
你必须按时完成。[Nǐ bìxū ànshí wánchéng.] 'You must finish on time.'
moral or logical expectation, not a forced necessity
你应该道歉。[Nǐ yīnggāi dàoqiàn.] 'You should apologize.'
near-synonym of 不得不, slightly more literary/emphatic
我不能不说这件事。[Wǒ bùnéngbù shuō zhè jiàn shì.] 'I cannot but mention this matter.'
footnotes_tr: 只好 often implies the speaker tried other options first and settled for this one; 不得不 emphasizes that the pressure came from the situation itself, sometimes with no prior attempts.

tables.caption_tr: Frequent Verbs Paired with 不得不
rows: 不得不承认 [bùdébù chéngrèn] 'have to admit'
不得不接受 [bùdébù jiēshòu] 'have to accept'
不得不放弃 [bùdébù fàngqì] 'have to give up'
不得不离开 [bùdébù líkāi] 'have to leave'
不得不取消 [bùdébù qǔxiāo] 'have to cancel'
不得不佩服 [bùdébù pèifú] 'can't help but admire'

tables.caption_tr: Word Order Rules: Position of 不得不 Relative to Other Elements
rows: Time expressions go before 不得不
他昨天不得不加班。[Tā zuótiān bùdébù jiābān.]
Cannot be modified by degree adverbs like 很/非常
不得不 is a fixed adverbial phrase, not a gradable adjective — never add a degree adverb in front of it.
Often preceded by a cause clause with 因为/由于
因为..., Subject + 不得不 + Verb
因为病了,他不得不请假。[Yīnwèi bìng le, tā bùdébù qǐngjià.]
'Because he was sick, he had to take leave.'
Can combine with adverbs like 已经/终于 for added nuance
已经/终于 + 不得不 + Verb
他终于不得不低头。[Tā zhōngyú bùdébù dītóu.]
'He finally had no choice but to give in.'

examples.target: 我不得不承认他是对的。
examples.reading: Wǒ bùdébù chéngrèn tā shì duì de.
examples.translation_tr: I have no choice but to admit he's right.
examples.note_tr: 承认 is one of the most common verbs paired with 不得不 for reluctant admissions.

examples.target: 因为下雨,我们不得不取消了比赛。
examples.reading: Yīnwèi xiàyǔ, wǒmen bùdébù qǔxiāo le bǐsài.
examples.translation_tr: Because it rained, we had no choice but to cancel the match.
examples.note_tr: A 因为 cause-clause commonly precedes 不得不 to explain the external reason for the forced action.

examples.target: 为了赶飞机,他不得不提前出发。
examples.reading: Wèile gǎn fēijī, tā bùdébù tíqián chūfā.
examples.translation_tr: In order to catch the flight, he had to leave earlier than planned.

examples.target: 公司资金短缺,老板不得不裁员。
examples.reading: Gōngsī zījīn duǎnquē, lǎobǎn bùdébù cáiyuán.
examples.translation_tr: The company's funds ran short, so the boss had no choice but to lay off staff.

examples.target: 面对这种情况,我们不得不重新考虑计划。
examples.reading: Miànduì zhè zhǒng qíngkuàng, wǒmen bùdébù chóngxīn kǎolǜ jìhuà.
examples.translation_tr: Facing this situation, we have to reconsider the plan.

examples.target: 他病得很重,不得不住院。
examples.reading: Tā bìng de hěn zhòng, bùdébù zhùyuàn.
examples.translation_tr: He was so seriously ill that he had to be hospitalized.

examples.target: 你不得不佩服她的勇气。
examples.reading: Nǐ bùdébù pèifú tā de yǒngqì.
examples.translation_tr: You can't help but admire her courage.
examples.note_tr: With verbs like 佩服 (admire), 不得不 shifts from 'forced obligation' to a subjective 'cannot help but' feeling — the constraint is emotional, not circumstantial.

examples.target: 时间不够了,我们不得不加快速度。
examples.reading: Shíjiān bú gòu le, wǒmen bùdébù jiākuài sùdù.
examples.translation_tr: Time is running short — we have to speed up.

budan-erqie.title_tr: 不但...而且... (not only... but also...)
budan-erqie.intro_tr: 不但[búdàn]...而且[érqiě]... is the standard Chinese "not only... but also..." construction, used to add a second, often more emphatic, piece of information to a first one. The two clauses can share the same subject or have different subjects, and this changes where 不但[búdàn] is placed in the sentence. 而且[érqiě] is frequently paired or replaced with 也[yě], 还[hái], 并且[bìngqiě], or even 甚至[shènzhì] for extra emphasis. A negative variant, 不但不[búdàn bù]/没[méi]...反而[fǎn'ér]..., means "not only not... but on the contrary...". This pattern is extremely common in both spoken and written Chinese and appears constantly from HSK4 onward.

tables.caption_tr: Core structure: same subject vs. different subjects
rows: Subject + 不但[búdàn] + VP1，而且[érqiě] + VP2 (subject stated only once, BEFORE 不但)
他不但会说汉语，而且会说日语。 [Tā búdàn huì shuō Hànyǔ, érqiě huì shuō Rìyǔ.]
He can not only speak Chinese, but also Japanese.
不但[búdàn] + Subject1 + VP1，而且[érqiě] + Subject2 + VP2 (subject comes AFTER 不但 in both clauses)
不但他去，而且我也去。 [Búdàn tā qù, érqiě wǒ yě qù.]
Not only is he going, but I'm going too.
Subject + 不但[búdàn] + Adj/VP1，而且[érqiě] + Adj/VP2
这本书不但便宜，而且好看。 [Zhè běn shū búdàn piányi, érqiě hǎokàn.]
This book is not only cheap, but also good.

tables.caption_tr: Word order rule: where does 不但[búdàn] go relative to the subject?
rows: Same subject → subject BEFORE 不但
Because both clauses talk about the same person/thing, the subject is stated once, at the very front of the sentence: 她不但漂亮，而且聪明。
Different subjects → subject AFTER 不但
不但 must directly introduce the first clause, so the first subject follows it: 不但天气冷，而且风也很大。
Never split 不但 from its own clause
不但 always sits at the boundary of the FIRST clause, right before what is being added to — never inside the second clause.

tables.caption_tr: Words that can pair with 不但[búdàn] instead of / together with 而且[érqiě]
rows: Neutral 'and also, moreover' — the default pairing
不但便宜，而且质量好。 [búdàn piányi, érqiě zhìliàng hǎo] — not only cheap, but also good quality
Simple 'also, too' — lighter, very common in speech
不但我去，他也去。 [búdàn wǒ qù, tā yě qù]
'Also, in addition' — adds a further point, common in speech
他不但会开车，还会修车。 [Tā búdàn huì kāichē, hái huì xiūchē.]
More formal/written 'and furthermore', often for actions/plans
公司不但赚钱，并且扩大了规模。 [Gōngsī búdàn zhuànqián, bìngqiě kuòdàle guīmó.]
'Even' — escalates to an extreme example, strong emphasis
他不但会说英语，甚至能说一点儿法语。 [Tā búdàn huì shuō Yīngyǔ, shènzhì néng shuō yìdiǎnr Fǎyǔ.]

tables.caption_tr: Negative form: 不但不[búdàn bù] / 不但没[búdàn méi]...反而[fǎn'ér]/还[hái]...
rows: 不但不[búdàn bù] + V，反而[fǎn'ér] + V2
Not only did X not happen, the opposite happened (present/habitual, negating a verb/adjective)
他不但不累，反而更有精神了。 [Tā búdàn bú lèi, fǎn'ér gèng yǒu jīngshen le.] — He isn't tired at all — on the contrary, he's more energetic.
不但没[búdàn méi] + V，反而[fǎn'ér] + V2
Same meaning but negating a completed action (with 没 instead of 不)
他不但没生气，反而笑了。 [Tā búdàn méi shēngqì, fǎn'ér xiào le.] — He wasn't angry at all — instead he laughed.
Milder version of 反而, 'not only not... but still...'
这样做不但不能解决问题，还会带来麻烦。 [Zhèyàng zuò búdàn bù néng jiějué wèntí, hái huì dàilái máfan.]

tables.caption_tr: Synonyms of 不但[búdàn]: register and usage differences
rows: Safe default choice in speech and writing; used throughout this guide.
Very common in essays, news, textbooks; pairs equally well with 而且/也/还.
Slightly more colloquial, also 'not only... alone'
Often pairs with 也/还 rather than 而且; feels a bit more conversational.
Common in casual speech, especially in northern Mandarin; pairs with 还/也.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes
rows: 不但 placed after the subject's adjective/verb instead of before it
不但他去，而且他也很高兴。
Second clause repeats the same subject with 也 when clauses should logically add a NEW point, not just restate — while grammatically possible, check that clause 2 truly adds new information
不但他去，而且他非常兴奋。 (adds a genuinely new point)
他不但很累而且没有睡好觉，但是他还是来了。
Mixing 不但...而且 with 但是 in the same sentence without a clear reason — 但是 introduces contrast, don't force it after an additive structure unless truly contrastive
他不但很累，而且没有睡好觉。他还是来了。 (split into two sentences, or use 尽管...但是 for real contrast)
不但我们班第一，而且他们班第一。
而且 alone doesn't fit for comparing two DIFFERENT winners — this needs a different connector, not an additive one
我们班第一，他们班也不错。 (不但...而且 is for adding related facts, not contrasting separate results)

jinguan-danshi.intro_tr: 尽管[jǐnguǎn]...但是[dànshì]... means "even though / despite the fact that... still...". It introduces a concession clause with 尽管 (stating a real, acknowledged fact) and then a contrasting result clause marked with 但是 or another connector like 可是[kěshì], 却[què], 还是[háishi], or 仍然[réngrán]. Unlike a single-word "although", Chinese requires BOTH halves of the pair to appear — the second clause always needs its own contrast word. 尽管 is close in meaning to 虽然[suīrán] but tends to sound a little more formal/emphatic and can also be used with exaggerated or hypothetical situations. Be careful: 尽管 has a completely different, unrelated meaning as a single-clause adverb ("feel free to, go ahead and..."), e.g. 你尽管问[nǐ jǐnguǎn wèn] "Feel free to ask".

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure of 尽管...但是...
rows: States the real fact/situation being conceded
但是/可是/却/还是/仍然 + Subject + Predicate
States the unexpected or contrasting result

tables.caption_tr: Connectors That Can Pair With 尽管 in the Second Clause
rows: Literary/emphatic, often placed right before the verb
Sharper sense of "yet, on the contrary"

tables.caption_tr: Where Does the Subject Go?
rows: 尽管 + Subject + ..., 但是/却 + (subject dropped) + ...
尽管他很忙,但是每天都锻炼身体。 Jǐnguǎn tā hěn máng, dànshì měitiān dōu duànliàn shēntǐ.
Even though he's busy, he exercises every day.
尽管 + Subject A + ..., 但是/却 + Subject B + ...
尽管天气不好,但是我们还是出发了。 Jǐnguǎn tiānqì bù hǎo, dànshì wǒmen háishi chūfā le.
Even though the weather is bad, we still set off.
Subject before 尽管 (same subject, less common)
他尽管很忙,但是每天都锻炼身体。 Tā jǐnguǎn hěn máng, dànshì měitiān dōu duànliàn shēntǐ.
He, even though busy, exercises every day.

tables.caption_tr: 尽管 vs 虽然: Key Differences
rows: Neutral, the most common everyday choice
Can concede real facts OR exaggerated/hypothetical extremes
Almost always used with real, factual situations
Second meaning as a standalone word
Also an adverb meaning "feel free to, go ahead and..." (你尽管说 nǐ jǐnguǎn shuō)
Often paired with 却/还是/仍然/可是
Most often paired with 但是/可是

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: 尽管 alone does not create the "but/still" meaning; the second clause needs its own contrast word
✗ 尽管很难,他做出来了。 → ✓ 尽管很难,但是他做出来了。 Jǐnguǎn hěn nán, dànshì tā zuò chūlái le.
Confusing concession 尽管 with adverb 尽管 ("feel free to")
Same characters, but the adverb use is a single clause with no 但是 and means permission, not contrast
你尽管问。 Nǐ jǐnguǎn wèn. = "Feel free to ask." (not a concession sentence)
尽管 signals concession/contrast, never reason or cause
For "because... so..." use 因为[yīnwèi]...所以[suǒyǐ]... instead
Placing 却 at the start of the second clause
却 is an adverb and must go directly before the verb/predicate, after the subject
✗ 却他很忙 → ✓ 他却很忙 tā què hěn máng

buguan-dou.intro_tr: 不管...都... [bùguǎn...dōu...] is a conjunction pair meaning "no matter (what/who/how)..., the result is always the same." The clause after 不管 [bùguǎn] must express "any possibility," so it needs a question word (谁, 什么, 哪儿, 怎么...), an either/or choice with 还是, a verb-not-verb pattern (去不去), or 多 + adjective (多难, 多贵). The second clause always keeps the adverb 都 [dōu] right before the main verb to show the outcome never changes. 不管 is the everyday spoken counterpart of the more formal 无论 [wúlùn] — the two share the same grammar rules but differ in tone. This is one of the first "all-inclusive condition" patterns beginners meet, and it is very frequent in daily conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Core structure: three ways to fill the 不管 clause
rows: 不管 [bùguǎn] + 谁/什么/哪儿/怎么... + 都 [dōu] + V
不管你说什么，我都不生气。[Bùguǎn nǐ shuō shénme, wǒ dōu bù shēngqì.]
No matter what you say, I won't get angry.
不管 [bùguǎn] + A 还是 [háishi] B + 都 [dōu] + V
不管你来还是不来，聚会都会开始。[Bùguǎn nǐ lái háishi bù lái, jùhuì dōu huì kāishǐ.]
Whether you come or not, the party will start.
不管 [bùguǎn] + V不V / Adj不Adj + 都 [dōu] + V
不管累不累，他都不休息。[Bùguǎn lèi bu lèi, tā dōu bù xiūxi.]
Whether he's tired or not, he doesn't rest.
不管 [bùguǎn] + 多 [duō] + Adj + 都 [dōu] + V
不管多晚，妈妈都等我回家。[Bùguǎn duō wǎn, māma dōu děng wǒ huí jiā.]
No matter how late it is, mom waits for me to come home.

tables.caption_tr: Common question words / phrases used after 不管
rows: 不管谁问，我都不说。[Bùguǎn shéi wèn, wǒ dōu bù shuō.]
不管什么问题，他都能回答。[Bùguǎn shénme wèntí, tā dōu néng huídá.]
不管在哪儿，我都会想你。[Bùguǎn zài nǎr, wǒ dōu huì xiǎng nǐ.]
不管你怎么解释，他都不听。[Bùguǎn nǐ zěnme jiěshì, tā dōu bù tīng.]
不管什么时候找我，我都在。[Bùguǎn shénme shíhou zhǎo wǒ, wǒ dōu zài.]
不管多少人来，饭都够吃。[Bùguǎn duōshao rén lái, fàn dōu gòu chī.]
不管几点开始，我都会准时到。[Bùguǎn jǐ diǎn kāishǐ, wǒ dōu huì zhǔnshí dào.]
不管多贵，他都要买那台电脑。[Bùguǎn duō guì, tā dōu yào mǎi nà tái diànnǎo.]

tables.caption_tr: 不管 [bùguǎn] vs 无论 [wúlùn]: register comparison
rows: same (needs Q-word / 还是 / V不V / 多+Adj)
common, e.g. 无论如何 [wúlùn rúhé] 'in any case'

tables.caption_tr: 不管...都... vs similar 'condition/result' patterns
rows: no matter which option — result unchanged
needs Q-word / 还是 / V不V / 多+Adj (exhaustive options)
不管冷不冷，他都游泳。[Bùguǎn lěng bu lěng, tā dōu yóuyǒng.]
无论多冷，他都游泳。[Wúlùn duō lěng, tā dōu yóuyǒng.]
no exhaustive-option word needed, just one scenario
即使天很冷，他也游泳。[Jíshǐ tiān hěn lěng, tā yě yóuyǒng.]
as long as (one condition is sufficient)
只要不下雨，他就去游泳。[Zhǐyào bú xiàyǔ, tā jiù qù yóuyǒng.]
condition is a known fact, not hypothetical
既然你来了，就留下吃饭吧。[Jìrán nǐ láile, jiù liúxià chīfàn ba.]

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes with 不管...都...
rows: 不管 clause is a plain statement, not an 'any possibility' phrase
不管你喜不喜欢，我都做。[Bùguǎn nǐ xǐhuan bu xǐhuan, wǒ dōu zuò.]
不管天气怎么样，我们要去爬山。
missing 都 [dōu] in the result clause
不管天气怎么样，我们都要去爬山。[Bùguǎn tiānqì zěnmeyàng, wǒmen dōu yào qù páshān.]
不管你信不信，但是我都要说。
但是 [dànshì] is redundant — 都 already carries the contrastive sense
不管你信不信，我都要说。[Bùguǎn nǐ xìn bu xìn, wǒ dōu yào shuō.]
不管他会不会来，可能都要等他。
mixing an uncertain modal (可能) with the definite 都 weakens the 'always true' meaning
不管他来不来，我们都要等他。[Bùguǎn tā lái bu lái, wǒmen dōu yào děng tā.]
footnotes_tr: 不管 cannot be followed by a simple yes/no statement — it always needs an element covering 'every possibility' (question word, 还是 choice, V不V, or 多+Adj).
In casual speech 都 is occasionally replaced by 也 [yě], especially in single-option emphatic sentences, but 都 is the default and safest choice for learners.

wulun-dou.intro_tr: 无论[wúlùn]...都[dōu]... is a formal, written-style construction meaning "no matter (what/who/where/how)..., the result is always the same." The clause introduced by 无论 must contain an open-ended element rather than a single fixed fact: a question word (什么, 谁, 哪儿, 怎么...), an "A 还是 B" choice, or a V-不-V / Adj-不-Adj pair. The second clause is completed with 都[dōu] (sometimes 也[yě] or 总[zǒng]) to state that the outcome holds true across every possible case. 无论 is the literary counterpart of the more casual 不管[bùguǎn] — the grammar is identical, but 无论 belongs in essays, news, speeches, and formal writing rather than everyday chat. Because zero-level learners often haven't seen 不管 yet, think of 无论...都... simply as "whatever/whoever/however..., always..."

tables.caption_tr: Core Structure of 无论[wúlùn]...都[dōu]...
rows: 无论[wúlùn] + Question Word (什么/谁/哪儿/怎么/几/多少/多么) + clause, 都[dōu]/也[yě] + VP
无论[wúlùn]谁[shéi]来[lái]，我[wǒ]都[dōu]欢迎[huānyíng]。 — No matter who comes, I welcome them.
无论[wúlùn] + A 还是[háishi] B + clause, 都[dōu]/也[yě] + VP
无论[wúlùn]晴天[qíngtiān]还是[háishi]雨天[yǔtiān]，他[tā]都[dōu]去[qù]上班[shàngbān]。 — Whether it's sunny or rainy, he goes to work.
无论[wúlùn] + V/Adj + 不 + V/Adj + clause, 都[dōu]/也[yě] + VP
无论[wúlùn]你[nǐ]信[xìn]不[bù]信[xìn]，事实[shìshí]都[dōu]是[shì]这样[zhèyàng]。 — Whether you believe it or not, that's the fact.

tables.caption_tr: Question Words Commonly Paired with 无论[wúlùn]
rows: 无论[wúlùn]发生[fāshēng]什么[shénme]事[shì]，我们[wǒmen]都[dōu]要[yào]冷静[lěngjìng]。 — No matter what happens, we must stay calm.
无论[wúlùn]谁[shéi]反对[fǎnduì]，他[tā]都[dōu]坚持[jiānchí]自己[zìjǐ]的[de]想法[xiǎngfǎ]。 — No matter who objects, he sticks to his own idea.
无论[wúlùn]你[nǐ]在[zài]哪儿[nǎr]，都[dōu]可以[kěyǐ]给[gěi]我[wǒ]打电话[dǎ diànhuà]。 — Wherever you are, you can call me.
无论[wúlùn]怎么[zěnme]劝[quàn]，他[tā]都[dōu]不[bù]听[tīng]。 — No matter how we persuade him, he won't listen.
无论[wúlùn]花[huā]多少[duōshao]钱[qián]，他[tā]都[dōu]要[yào]买[mǎi]那[nà]幅[fú]画[huà]。 — No matter how much it costs, he wants to buy that painting.
无论[wúlùn]多[duō]难[nán]，我们[wǒmen]都[dōu]要[yào]坚持[jiānchí]下去[xiàqu]。 — No matter how hard it is, we must keep going.
无论[wúlùn]什么时候[shénme shíhou]找[zhǎo]我[wǒ]，我[wǒ]都[dōu]会[huì]帮[bāng]你[nǐ]。 — Whenever you look for me, I'll help you.
无论[wúlùn]结果[jiéguǒ]如何[rúhé]，我们[wǒmen]都[dōu]接受[jiēshòu]。 — Whatever the result is, we accept it.

tables.caption_tr: 无论[wúlùn] vs. 不管[bùguǎn]: Formal vs. Colloquial
rows: Essays, news reports, speeches, formal writing
Needs question word / A还是B / V不V + 都/也
Yes in most sentences; sounds more literary/serious

tables.caption_tr: Second-Clause Adverb Choice: 都[dōu] vs 也[yě] vs 总[zǒng]
rows: Most common choice; plainly states 'in every case'
无论[wúlùn]什么[shénme]天气[tiānqì]，他[tā]都[dōu]出门[chūmén]跑步[pǎobù]。 — No matter the weather, he goes out to run.
Slightly softer; often used with an extreme/single case to mean 'even'
无论[wúlùn]多么[duōme]困难[kùnnan]，他[tā]也[yě]不[bù]放弃[fàngqì]。 — However difficult it is, he still won't give up.
无论[wúlùn]发生[fāshēng]什么[shénme]事[shì]，她[tā]总[zǒng]保持[bǎochí]冷静[lěngjìng]。 — Whatever happens, she always stays calm.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with 无论[wúlùn]...都[dōu]...
rows: The 无论 clause needs an open-ended element (question word/choice/V不V), not a plain fixed statement like 很忙
无论[wúlùn]他[tā]多[duō]忙[máng]，都[dōu]要[yào]锻炼[duànliàn]。 (add 多 to open the condition)
下雨 alone names one single fixed condition, not a full range of possibilities
无论[wúlùn]下不下雨[xià bu xiàyǔ]，我[wǒ]都[dōu]出门[chūmén]。 (use V-不-V)
Dropping 都/也 in the second clause
无论 needs a matching 都/也 (or 总) to complete the 'regardless of everything' meaning
无论[wúlùn]谁[shéi]问[wèn]，我[wǒ]都[dōu]不[bù]说[shuō]。 (not 无论谁问，我不说。)
footnotes_tr: Remember: no question word, no A-还是-B, and no V-不-V inside the 无论 clause almost always signals an error.

jishi-ye.intro_tr: 即使...也... [jíshǐ...yě...] means "even if... (the result is) still..." It links a hypothetical, extreme, or unlikely condition (Clause 1, with 即使) to a result that stays unchanged no matter what happens (Clause 2, with 也 or 还是). Unlike 虽然...但是... [suīrán...dànshì...], which reports a fact that has already happened or is true, 即使 is typically used for something that has NOT happened yet, is uncertain, or is presented as an extreme/unlikely case just to make a point. This pattern appears constantly in both spoken and written Chinese, and it has several close cousins — 即便, 就算, 哪怕 — that share the same "even if... still..." meaning but differ slightly in formality. Because 即使 is a zero-level-friendly but very productive pattern, mastering its word order and its difference from 虽然/如果/不管 will immediately make your sentences sound more natural.

tables.caption_tr: Core Structure of 即使...也...
rows: Introduces an extreme, hypothetical, or unlikely situation — it may or may not actually be true
States that the result does NOT change no matter what happens in Clause 1
footnotes_tr: If the subject is the same in both clauses, it is usually stated only once — either right before 即使 or right after it — and can be omitted before 也 in Clause 2.
也[yě] is by far the most common partner for 即使; 还是[háishi] adds a slightly stronger 'despite everything' nuance.

tables.caption_tr: 即使...也... vs. Similar Conjunctions
rows: Hypothetical / extreme / not-yet-real (or real, but framed as an extreme case)
Real fact, often more formal or emphatic than 虽然
Simple condition — the result actually depends on Clause 1
ALL possible conditions, not just one single hypothetical one

tables.caption_tr: Colloquial and Literary Variants of 即使
rows: Neutral — safe in speech and writing
The default, most widely used form; good for zero-level learners to start with
Nearly interchangeable with 即使 in most sentences
Very common in casual conversation; feels lighter than 即使
Often paired with a small/extreme example, e.g. 哪怕一分钟也... ('even if it's just one minute')

tables.caption_tr: Word Order Rules
rows: 即使 may come before or after the subject; 也 sits directly before the verb in Clause 2, and the subject can be dropped there if it's already clear
(我)即使很累,也要完成作业。 / 即使我很累,也要完成作业。 — 'Even if I'm tired, I still have to finish the homework.'
Each clause keeps its own subject; 即使 opens Clause 1, and 也 sits right before the subject or verb of Clause 2
即使老板生气,我们也不怕。 — 'Even if the boss gets angry, we're still not afraid.'
即使-clause placed after the result (for emphasis)
In speech, the 即使 clause can follow the main clause to add emphasis after the fact
我们也要去,即使下雨。 — 'We're still going, even if it rains.'

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: 就[jiù] signals a plain cause-and-result link, not a 'no matter what' concession — it clashes with the meaning of 即使
即使他昨天没来,我们也开会了。
即使 is for hypothetical/extreme conditions, not events that have already definitely happened; a completed real fact should use 虽然...但是... instead
虽然他昨天没来,我们还是开了会。
Clause 2 is missing 也/还是, so the 'no matter what, the result stays the same' meaning is lost
即使很难,我们也要试试。

examples.target: 即使下雨,我们也要去爬山。

examples.note_tr: 哪怕[nǎpà] is the more colloquial, emphatic cousin of 即使, often used with a small/extreme example like '一分钟' to stress how little it takes.

jiran-jiu.intro_tr: 既然[jìrán]...就[jiù]... is a two-clause connector meaning "since (as we both already know/accept)... then...". It is used when the speaker treats the premise in the first clause as an established, already-known fact — not new information — and then draws a conclusion, gives advice, or announces a decision in the second clause. This makes it different from 因为...所以..., which introduces a reason the listener may not yet know. 既然 opens the first clause (it can stand before or after the subject), and 就 sits right before the verb in the second clause to link the conclusion to the accepted premise. The pattern is extremely common in everyday advice-giving ("since you're already here, might as well...") as well as in more formal reasoning.

tables.caption_tr: Core Structure of 既然[jìrán]...就[jiù]...
rows: States the reason both speaker and listener already accept as true
States the logical conclusion, decision, advice, or suggestion that follows
既然[jìrán] can appear before OR after the subject of clause A
既然你不想去 [Jìrán nǐ bù xiǎng qù] = 你既然不想去 [Nǐ jìrán bù xiǎng qù] — both correct
Always directly before the verb (after the subject) in clause B
我们就开始吧 [wǒmen jiù kāishǐ ba], not 就我们开始吧

tables.caption_tr: 既然[jìrán]...就[jiù]... vs 因为[yīnwèi]...所以[suǒyǐ]...
rows: A fact already known/obvious to both speaker and listener
New information being introduced as the cause
Giving advice, making a decision, drawing a conclusion from a shared fact
No — the premise must already be true/established, not a guess
No — also states a real cause, not a hypothetical
既然你已经决定了，就去做吧。[Jìrán nǐ yǐjīng juédìng le, jiù qù zuò ba.]
因为下雨了，所以我们没去。[Yīnwèi xià yǔ le, suǒyǐ wǒmen méi qù.]

tables.caption_tr: Adverb Choices for the Second Clause
rows: Neutral and by far the most common choice
既然你来了，就坐下吧。[Jìrán nǐ lái le, jiù zuò xià ba.] — Since you've come, sit down.
Softer tone: 'then... as well / might as well'
既然大家都同意，我也没意见了。[Jìrán dàjiā dōu tóngyì, wǒ yě méi yìjiàn le.] — Since everyone agrees, I have no objections either.
'Still...', often in rhetorical questions expressing surprise/reproach
既然知道错了，还不改正？[Jìrán zhīdào cuò le, hái bù gǎizhèng?] — Since you know it's wrong, why still not fix it?
既然如此，那么我们就开始吧。[Jìrán rúcǐ, nàme wǒmen jiù kāishǐ ba.] — Since that's how it is, then let's begin.

tables.caption_tr: Common Fixed Collocations with 既然[jìrán]
rows: since that's the case / given this being so

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes to Avoid
rows: 既然你累了，就休息吧。[Jìrán nǐ lèi le, jiù xiūxi ba.]
就[jiù] is required to link the conclusion back to the premise; without it the sentence feels incomplete or unnatural
Using 既然[jìrán] for an unconfirmed/hypothetical reason
既然明天可能下雨，就带伞吧。
如果明天下雨，就带伞吧。[Rúguǒ míngtiān xià yǔ, jiù dài sǎn ba.]
既然[jìrán] requires a fact already established as true; use 如果[rúguǒ] for hypothetical or uncertain conditions
Detaching 既然[jìrán] from its clause with a comma
你既然累了，就休息吧。 / 既然你累了，就休息吧。
既然[jìrán] must sit directly before or right after the subject with no pause in between, forming one continuous clause
Confusing 既然 with 既...又...
既聪明又努力 [jì cōngmíng yòu nǔlì]
既然[jìrán]...就[jiù]... is a reason-conclusion pair; 既[jì]...又[yòu]... is a separate 'both...and...' pattern — do not mix them

examples.target: 既然你已经知道错了，就应该道歉。

examples.translation_tr: Since you don't like this job, then switch to another one.

examples.target: 既然大家都到了，我们就开始吧。
examples.reading: Jìrán dàjiā dōu dào le, wǒmen jiù kāishǐ ba.
examples.translation_tr: Since everyone has arrived, let's get started.

examples.target: 既然你说得对，我就听你的。
examples.reading: Jìrán nǐ shuō de duì, wǒ jiù tīng nǐ de.
examples.translation_tr: Since what you're saying is correct, I'll go along with you.

examples.target: 既然如此，那我们就不勉强了。
examples.reading: Jìrán rúcǐ, nà wǒmen jiù bù miǎnqiǎng le.
examples.translation_tr: Since that's the case, then we won't force the matter.

examples.target: 你既然已经来了，就多待一会儿吧。
examples.reading: Nǐ jìrán yǐjīng lái le, jiù duō dāi yíhuìr ba.
examples.translation_tr: Since you've already come, stay a little longer.
