you-shoudao-zaodao.title_tr: Formal Passive Constructions (由, 受到, 遭到)
you-shoudao-zaodao.intro_tr: In formal writing, news reports, and official documents, Chinese has three additional ways—besides 被[bèi]—to express that a subject undergoes an action or to identify who is responsible for it: 由[yóu], 受到[shòudào], and 遭到[zāodào]. 由[yóu] is not really a 'suffering' passive at all; it introduces the agent or cause of an action ('by X', 'done by X') and is common in patterns like 由...组成[yóu...zǔchéng] ('composed of') or 由...负责[yóu...fùzé] ('in charge of'). 受到[shòudào] literally means 'to receive' and is followed by an abstract noun describing treatment or effect—it can be neutral, positive, or negative. 遭到[zāodào] literally means 'to encounter/suffer' and is followed by an abstract noun, but it is used exclusively for unfortunate, negative events. All three are more literary and formal than 被[bèi], and mixing them up is a very common intermediate-to-advanced learner mistake.

tables.caption_tr: Overview: the three formal agent/passive markers
rows: 'by, done by' — introduces the agent or cause responsible for an action
Neutral, formal; not a true 'suffering' passive — just marks the doer
这个项目由[yóu]他负责。= This project is handled by him.
Subject + 受到[shòudào] + Abstract Noun (+的[de] + Agent)
Formal; neutral to positive, occasionally negative
他受到[shòudào]了老师的表扬。= He was praised by the teacher.
Subject + 遭到[zāodào] + Abstract Noun (+的[de] + Agent)
提议遭到[zāodào]了反对。= The proposal was opposed.

tables.caption_tr: 由[yóu] usage patterns in detail
rows: 早饭由[yóu]我来做。[Zǎofàn yóu wǒ lái zuò.]
I'll be the one to make breakfast.
这个团队由[yóu]十个人组成[zǔchéng]。[Zhège tuánduì yóu shí gè rén zǔchéng.]
This team is made up of ten people.
Introduces the cause of a result
事故由[yóu]疲劳驾驶引起[yǐnqǐ]。[Shìgù yóu píláo jiàshǐ yǐnqǐ.]
The accident was caused by fatigued driving.
这件事由[yóu]校长决定[juédìng]。[Zhè jiàn shì yóu xiàozhǎng juédìng.]
This matter will be decided by the principal.
'from A to B' (spatial/temporal — unrelated to passive meaning)
由[yóu]此到那儿很远。[Yóu cǐ dào nàr hěn yuǎn.]
It's far from here to there.

tables.caption_tr: 受到[shòudào] + common collocations (neutral to positive)
rows: 这部电影受到[shòudào]了观众的欢迎[huānyíng]。= This film was well received by the audience.
他的决定受到[shòudào]了父母的影响[yǐngxiǎng]。= His decision was influenced by his parents.
她受到[shòudào]了老板的表扬[biǎoyáng]。= She was praised by her boss.
这种做法受到[shòudào]了批评[pīpíng]。= This practice was criticized.
老人应该受到[shòudào]尊重[zūnzhòng]。= The elderly should be respected.

环境受到[shòudào]了严重威胁[wēixié]。= The environment is seriously threatened.

那个国家遭到[zāodào]了攻击[gōngjī]。= That country was attacked.
他的说法遭到[zāodào]了质疑[zhìyí]。= His claim was called into question.

rows: Yes — 被 can drop the agent
Yes, marked with 的[de] before the agent
Yes, marked with 的[de] before the agent
Everyday passive sentences of any tone
Reporting how something was received or affected

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes and usage notes
rows: 由[yóu] cannot express a direct negative action done TO a person the way 被[bèi] can — 由 only marks agency/responsibility, not being harmed.
✓ 他被[bèi]老师批评了。 (He was scolded by the teacher.)
✗ 受到 / 遭到 + bare verb
受到[shòudào] and 遭到[zāodào] must be followed by an abstract NOUN (often the nominal use of a 2-character verb like 批评[pīpíng], 反对[fǎnduì]), not an ordinary action verb.
✓ 受到[shòudào]批评[pīpíng] / 遭到[zāodào]反对[fǎnduì] (noun objects)
遭到[zāodào] is reserved for negative/unfortunate outcomes; using it with a positive noun like 表扬[biǎoyáng] (praise) is a contradiction.
✓ 他受到[shòudào]了表扬[biǎoyáng]。 (He was praised.)
受到[shòudào] and 遭到[zāodào] take abstract nouns as objects, never concrete physical objects.
✓ 他的表现受到[shòudào]了大家的关注[guānzhù]。 (His performance received everyone's attention.)
受到[shòudào] and 遭到[zāodào] very commonly take 了[le] right after them when reporting a completed event.
受到[shòudào]了影响[yǐngxiǎng] / 遭到[zāodào]了破坏[pòhuài]

degree-complements-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Degree Complements (得很, 极了, 死了)
degree-complements-advanced.intro_tr: Advanced degree complements are set patterns that attach directly after an adjective (or certain emotion verbs) to push its meaning to an extreme, replacing the plain intensifier 很 [hěn] with something much stronger. The main patterns are 得很 [de hěn] "really/very indeed," 极了 [jí le] "extremely," 死了 [sǐ le] "to death, unbearably," along with the equally common 得要命 [de yàomìng] and 得不得了 [de bùdéliǎo]. None of these can be negated with 不 [bù] — they only intensify, they never reverse meaning — and most of them (极了, 死了, 坏了) require a mandatory sentence-final 了 [le] that is simply part of the fixed pattern, not the aspect particle. These forms are heavily colloquial, frequently emotional or exaggerated in tone, and are extremely common in everyday spoken Chinese, so mastering their word order and restrictions is essential for natural-sounding speech.

tables.caption_tr: Degree Complement Patterns — Overview

漂亮极了 [piàoliang jí le] — extremely beautiful
累死了 [lèi sǐ le] — dead tired
疼得要命 [téng de yàomìng] — hurts like crazy
高兴得不得了 [gāoxìng de bùdéliǎo] — extremely happy
气坏了 [qì huài le] — furious / broke with anger

Yes — 了 is fixed and mandatory

Strongly exaggerated/hyperbolic; very common in spoken complaints and exclamations
Complaint tone; literally 'to the point of taking a life'
No extra 了 needed (不得了 itself is final)
Can express either positive or negative extremes; slightly less exaggerated than 死了
Emotion verbs/adjectives only (气, 乐, 笑, 急, 吓)
Very limited vocabulary set; means the emotion 'broke' the person

tables.caption_tr: Nuance Comparison: Intensity & Emotional Tone

Often negative/complaint, but also used for strong positive exclamations

Neutral — can be positive or negative
Slightly more measured than 死了/要命, still colloquial

yiwei-vs-renwei.title_tr: 以为[yǐwéi] vs 认为[rènwéi]: "Thought (mistakenly)" vs "Think/Believe"
yiwei-vs-renwei.intro_tr: 以为[yǐwéi] and 认为[rènwéi] both translate as "to think" in English, but they are NOT interchangeable. 认为[rènwéi] is a neutral verb for stating an opinion or belief — like English "I think/believe that..." — and carries no hint about whether the belief is right or wrong. 以为[yǐwéi], by contrast, almost always signals that the speaker's assumption turned out to be mistaken or different from reality — much closer to English "I thought... (but I was wrong)". Because of this built-in "wrong guess" flavor, 以为[yǐwéi] is very often followed by a contrasting clause with 但是[dànshì], 可是[kěshì], 其实[qíshí], or 结果[jiéguǒ]. Confusing the two is one of the most common intermediate-learner mistakes: using 以为[yǐwéi] to state a serious formal opinion accidentally implies "and I was wrong about it."

tables.caption_tr: Core meaning and implication
rows: Strongly implies the belief was WRONG or turned out different from reality
Neutral — states an opinion with no judgment on correctness
Neutral, personal, casual feeling — even less formal than 认为[rènwéi]
Neutral, but stronger conviction/faith than 认为[rènwéi]

tables.caption_tr: Sentence patterns
rows: Subject + 以为[yǐwéi] + Clause (+ 其实/可是/结果 + reality)

Wǒ rènwéi tā shì duì de.

Subject + 认为[rènwéi] + Clause + 是不对/不合适的

Wǒ rènwéi zhèyàng zuò shì bú duì de.

nanguai-guaibude.intro_tr: 难怪[nánguài] and 怪不得[guàibude] both translate as "no wonder..." or "so that explains it..." — they signal that the speaker has just realized the reason behind something they noticed, and that the reason makes the situation understandable rather than blameworthy. Literally, both words break down as "hard/cannot + blame," reflecting the core idea: once you know the cause, you can no longer find fault with the result. They are near-synonyms and often interchangeable, but 怪不得 is more colloquial and spoken, while 难怪 leans slightly more literary/neutral and is common in both speech and writing. A key extra fact: 怪不得 can ALSO function as an ordinary verb phrase meaning "cannot blame [someone]" — a separate, literal use unrelated to the "no wonder" adverb function. These expressions are frequently paired with 原来[yuánlái] ("so it turns out that..."), which introduces the newly discovered reason.

tables.caption_tr: 难怪 vs. 怪不得: core comparison
rows: hard to blame / strange that... not
sentence adverb 'no wonder' AND a literal verb phrase 'cannot blame [X]'
neutral, common in both speech and writing
more colloquial, very common in spoken Chinese
usually at the start of the clause, right before the subject
same — start of clause, before the subject
yes, with 怪不得 in almost all contexts
yes, with 难怪 in almost all contexts

tables.caption_tr: Sentence patterns with 难怪 / 怪不得
rows: 难怪/怪不得 + S + Predicate (reason given after, with 原来)
难怪他今天很累,原来他没睡觉。[Nánguài tā jīntiān hěn lèi, yuánlái tā méi shuìjiào.]
No wonder he's tired today — it turns out he didn't sleep.
原来..., 难怪/怪不得... (reason first, then result)
原来你是老师,难怪你懂这么多。[Yuánlái nǐ shì lǎoshī, nánguài nǐ dǒng zhème duō.]
So you're a teacher — no wonder you know so much.
难怪/怪不得 + noun phrase (no verb, short reaction)
难怪呢!/怪不得呢![Nánguài ne! / Guàibude ne!]
难怪/怪不得 + S + 会/这么/那么 + Adj/V
怪不得她会哭。[Guàibude tā huì kū.]
No wonder she's crying / would cry.
不能怪 + Person / 怪不得 + Person (literal 'cannot blame')
不能怪他,怪不得他,是天气不好。[Bù néng guài tā, guài bu dé tā, shì tiānqì bù hǎo.]
Can't blame him — it's the bad weather's fault.

tables.caption_tr: 难怪/怪不得 as adverb vs. 怪不得 as literal verb phrase
rows: Adverb 'no wonder' (难怪 or 怪不得)
难怪你迟到,原来路上堵车了。[Nánguài nǐ chídào, yuánlái lùshang dǔchē le.] — No wonder you're late, there was traffic.
Verb phrase 'cannot blame' (only 怪不得, written as 怪 + 不得)
这事怪不得他。[Zhè shì guài bu dé tā.] — This matter cannot be blamed on him.
Negative version of the verb phrase
不能怪 + Person (equivalent, more common in speech)
不能怪你。[Bù néng guài nǐ.] — Can't blame you.
难怪 does NOT have this literal verb use
难怪他 ✗ is NOT grammatical as 'cannot blame him' — only 怪不得/不能怪 work here.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes
rows: 难怪 only works as the adverb 'no wonder'; it has no literal verb-phrase reading
Use 怪不得他 or 不能怪他 instead.
Placing 难怪/怪不得 after the reason clause without 原来
Without 原来 the causal link can sound abrupt or unclear in longer explanations
Prefer 原来..., 难怪/怪不得... or add 原来 in the reason clause for clarity.
Using 难怪/怪不得 for a reason the speaker already knew in advance
Both words specifically mark a *newly realized* reason, not previously known information
Use 因为...所以... instead if the reason was already known, not just discovered.
Confusing 怪 (to blame, verb) with 怪 (strange, adjective)
怪 alone can mean 'strange' (这个人很怪) or 'to blame' (别怪我) depending on context
Check whether 怪 is followed by 不得/a person (blame) or stands as a predicate adjective (strange).

examples.target: 难怪你今天这么高兴,原来你考试得了第一名。
examples.reading: Nánguài nǐ jīntiān zhème gāoxìng, yuánlái nǐ kǎoshì dé le dì yī míng.
examples.translation_tr: No wonder you're so happy today — it turns out you got first place in the exam.
examples.note_tr: 难怪 opens the sentence, before the subject 你; 原来 in the second clause reveals the newly-discovered reason.

examples.target: 怪不得他不接电话,原来手机没电了。
examples.reading: Guàibude tā bù jiē diànhuà, yuánlái shǒujī méi diàn le.
examples.translation_tr: No wonder he's not answering the phone — it turns out his phone is dead.
examples.note_tr: 怪不得 is the more colloquial, spoken-language choice here; fully interchangeable with 难怪 in this sentence.

examples.target: 原来今天是她的生日,难怪大家都送她礼物。
examples.reading: Yuánlái jīntiān shì tā de shēngrì, nánguài dàjiā dōu sòng tā lǐwù.
examples.translation_tr: So today is her birthday — no wonder everyone is giving her gifts.
examples.note_tr: Reason clause (with 原来) comes first, result clause (with 难怪) follows — the reverse order of examples 1-2.

examples.target: 外面下雨呢,怪不得这么潮湿。
examples.reading: Wàimiàn xià yǔ ne, guàibude zhème cháoshī.
examples.translation_tr: It's raining outside — no wonder it's so humid.
examples.note_tr: 原来 is optional and can be dropped when the reason is obvious from context.

examples.target: 这件事不能怪你,是他自己不小心。
examples.reading: Zhè jiàn shì bù néng guài nǐ, shì tā zìjǐ bù xiǎoxīn.
examples.translation_tr: This can't be blamed on you — it's his own carelessness.
examples.note_tr: Here 怪 is used alone as an ordinary verb 'to blame'; this is the root meaning behind 怪不得's literal sense 'cannot blame'.

examples.target: 这也不能怪不得你,你已经尽力了。
examples.reading: Zhè yě bù néng guài bu dé nǐ, nǐ yǐjīng jìnlì le.
examples.translation_tr: This really can't be blamed on you either — you already did your best.
examples.note_tr: Literal verb-phrase use of 怪不得 = 'cannot blame [someone]', different from its 'no wonder' adverb use — context and tone distinguish them.

examples.target: 难怪他中文说得这么好,原来他在中国留学过三年。
examples.reading: Nánguài tā Zhōngwén shuō de zhème hǎo, yuánlái tā zài Zhōngguó liúxué guo sān nián.
examples.translation_tr: No wonder his Chinese is so good — it turns out he studied abroad in China for three years.
examples.note_tr: 难怪 + subject + predicate is the standard 'no wonder [X does Y]' pattern.

examples.target: 怪不得街上这么热闹,原来今天是春节。
examples.reading: Guàibude jiē shang zhème rènao, yuánlái jīntiān shì Chūnjié.
examples.translation_tr: No wonder the street is so lively — it turns out today is Spring Festival.
examples.note_tr: Very common spoken pattern: observation + 怪不得 + observation, 原来 + explanation.

jianzhi.intro_tr: 简直[jiǎnzhí] is an emphatic adverb meaning "simply, practically, virtually, just about." Native speakers use it to react emotionally to something that feels exaggerated, extreme, or almost unbelievable — it turns an ordinary statement into a heightened, subjective exclamation. It always sits directly before a verb, adjective, or the word 是[shì]/就是[jiùshì], never in front of a bare noun. Because it signals the speaker's strong reaction (surprise, frustration, admiration, disbelief), 简直[jiǎnzhí] pairs naturally with exclamatory endings like 了[le], 极了[jíle], or comparisons with 跟...一样[gēn...yíyàng]. It is very common in spoken Chinese from HSK5 level onward and gives sentences a vivid, hyperbolic flavor similar to English "simply," "practically," or "just plain."

tables.caption_tr: Core Sentence Patterns with 简直[jiǎnzhí]
rows: 简直太好了[jiǎnzhí tài hǎo le]
这简直是奇迹[zhè jiǎnzhí shì qíjì]
他简直就是个天才[tā jiǎnzhí jiùshì ge tiāncái]
简直不敢相信[jiǎnzhí bùgǎn xiāngxìn]
简直 + 像/跟 + NP + 一样
他简直像个孩子一样[tā jiǎnzhí xiàng ge háizi yíyàng]
He is simply just like a child.

tables.caption_tr: Typical Collocations & Intensifiers
rows: 简直太贵了![jiǎnzhí tài guì le]
这里简直美极了[zhèlǐ jiǎnzhí měi jíle]
我简直不敢相信[wǒ jiǎnzhí bùgǎn xiāngxìn]
这简直是个笑话嘛[zhè jiǎnzhí shì ge xiàohuà ma]

tables.caption_tr: 简直[jiǎnzhí] vs Similar Adverbs
rows: Expresses the speaker's strong emotional reaction; borders on hyperbole/unbelievable.
他简直是疯了![tā jiǎnzhí shì fēng le]
States near-completeness objectively; no exaggeration or emotion.
我几乎忘了这件事[wǒ jīhū wàng le zhè jiàn shì]
States a total degree factually, without emotional coloring.
这完全不一样[zhè wánquán bù yíyàng]
Confirms sincerity/truth of a statement; not about exaggeration.
我真的很累[wǒ zhēnde hěn lèi]

tables.caption_tr: Position & Usage Rules
rows: 简直 always comes directly before the verb, adjective, or 是/就是.
简直不敢相信[jiǎnzhí bùgǎn xiāngxìn], not 不简直敢相信
The normal sentence order keeps 简直 right after the subject.
他简直不敢相信[tā jiǎnzhí bùgǎn xiāngxìn]
简直 needs 是/就是 inserted before a plain noun phrase.
简直是个笑话[jiǎnzhí shì ge xiàohuà], not 简直个笑话
Often combined with 了/极了/啊 at the end for extra emphasis.

tables.caption_tr: Common Fixed Expressions with 简直[jiǎnzhí]
rows: it's simply a waste of time
there's simply nothing to be done

examples.target: 这个消息简直太让人震惊了。
examples.reading: Zhège xiāoxi jiǎnzhí tài ràng rén zhènjīng le.
examples.translation_tr: This news is simply so shocking.

examples.target: 他说的话简直是胡说八道。
examples.reading: Tā shuō de huà jiǎnzhí shì húshuō bādào.
examples.translation_tr: What he said is simply nonsense.

examples.target: 这里的风景简直美极了。
examples.reading: Zhèlǐ de fēngjǐng jiǎnzhí měi jíle.
examples.translation_tr: The scenery here is simply gorgeous.

examples.target: 我简直不敢相信自己的眼睛。
examples.reading: Wǒ jiǎnzhí bùgǎn xiāngxìn zìjǐ de yǎnjing.
examples.translation_tr: I simply can't believe my own eyes.

examples.target: 这道题太难了,我简直一点都不会。
examples.reading: Zhè dào tí tài nán le, wǒ jiǎnzhí yìdiǎn dōu bú huì.
examples.translation_tr: This problem is so hard that I simply don't know any of it.

examples.target: 他的中文说得简直跟中国人一样。
examples.reading: Tā de Zhōngwén shuō de jiǎnzhí gēn Zhōngguórén yíyàng.
examples.translation_tr: His Chinese sounds simply just like a native speaker's.

examples.target: 你简直就是个天才!
examples.reading: Nǐ jiǎnzhí jiùshì ge tiāncái!
examples.translation_tr: You are simply a genius!

examples.target: 这简直是浪费时间。
examples.reading: Zhè jiǎnzhí shì làngfèi shíjiān.
examples.translation_tr: This is simply a waste of time.

weibi.intro_tr: 未必[wèibì] is a formal adverb meaning "not necessarily" or "not always the case." It softens a statement into a partial or uncertain denial, rather than a flat "no." Unlike 不[bù], which flatly negates a verb or adjective, 未必[wèibì] challenges an assumption, implying "it might be true, but it might also not be" — a hedge often used to politely disagree or cast doubt on someone else's claim. It always appears directly before the verb/adjective/modal being qualified, and is common in written Chinese, debates, and thoughtful spoken remarks. It can also stand alone as a one-word reply meaning "Not necessarily so."

tables.caption_tr: Core structure of 未必[wèibì]
rows: 未必[wèibì]. (alone as a full response)
A: 他很厉害吧? B: 未必。
A: Tā hěn lìhai ba? B: Wèibì.
A: He's quite skilled, right? B: Not necessarily.

tables.caption_tr: 未必[wèibì] vs. 不[bù] vs. 一定不[yídìng bù]: degree of negation
rows: He doesn't necessarily know (he might or might not).
Leaves possibility open toward the positive
It's not necessarily the case that he doesn't know (he might know).

tables.caption_tr: 未必[wèibì] compared to similar hedging adverbs
rows: Casts doubt on a claim/assumption; 'not necessarily'
这未必是坏事。 (This isn't necessarily a bad thing.)
Similar meaning, more common/neutral, used in speech
这不一定是坏事。 (This isn't necessarily a bad thing.)
恐怕他不会来。 (I'm afraid he won't come.)
他也许不知道。 (Maybe he doesn't know.)

tables.caption_tr: Common collocations and fixed patterns with 未必[wèibì]
rows: What he said isn't necessarily fact.
Rich people aren't necessarily all happy.
He might well agree (it's not certain he disagrees).

examples.target: 他未必知道这件事。
examples.reading: Tā wèibì zhīdào zhè jiàn shì.
examples.translation_tr: He doesn't necessarily know about this matter.

examples.target: 这个方法未必有效。
examples.reading: Zhège fāngfǎ wèibì yǒuxiào.
examples.translation_tr: This method isn't necessarily effective.

examples.target: 贵的东西未必好。
examples.reading: Guì de dōngxi wèibì hǎo.
examples.translation_tr: Expensive things aren't necessarily good.

examples.target: 他这么说,未必是真心的。
examples.reading: Tā zhème shuō, wèibì shì zhēnxīn de.
examples.translation_tr: Just because he said so doesn't mean he really meant it.

examples.target: A: 他一定会来吧? B: 未必。
examples.reading: A: Tā yídìng huì lái ba? B: Wèibì.
examples.translation_tr: A: He's definitely coming, right? B: Not necessarily.

examples.target: 多吃未必对身体好。
examples.reading: Duō chī wèibì duì shēntǐ hǎo.
examples.translation_tr: Eating more isn't necessarily good for your health.

examples.target: 她未必不知道,只是不想说。
examples.reading: Tā wèibì bù zhīdào, zhǐshì bù xiǎng shuō.
examples.translation_tr: It's not that she necessarily doesn't know — she just doesn't want to say.

examples.target: 聪明的人未必都成功。
examples.reading: Cōngmíng de rén wèibì dōu chénggōng.
examples.translation_tr: Smart people don't all necessarily succeed.

written-vs-spoken.title_tr: Written Language vs Spoken Language (书面语 / 口语)
written-vs-spoken.intro_tr: Chinese has two distinct registers: 口语[kǒuyǔ] ("spoken language") used in everyday conversation, chat, and casual speech, and 书面语[shūmiànyǔ] ("written language") used in news reports, essays, official documents, and formal writing. The two registers share the same core grammar but differ heavily in vocabulary, connectives, pronouns, and sentence structure — written Chinese favors shorter, denser, often literary-flavored words (many originating from Classical Chinese), while spoken Chinese favors longer, more explicit phrases and colloquial particles (啊, 呢, 吧, 呀). Using written-style words in casual conversation sounds stiff or pompous; using spoken-style words in a formal essay sounds unpolished or unprofessional. Since this contrast spans the entire language rather than being one single grammar rule, this page works as a reference map: it pairs up common spoken words/patterns with their written equivalents so you can recognize and eventually produce the correct register for the context. At HSK5 level, learners are expected to start recognizing these written-register forms in newspapers, formal essays, and news broadcasts.

tables.caption_tr: Core vocabulary: spoken (口语) vs written (书面语) equivalents
Connectives and correlative patterns: spoken vs written
Particles, pronouns, and function words: spoken vs written
rows: 啊[a] / 呀[ya] / 呢[ne] / 吧[ba] / 啦[la]
rarely used; formal texts drop these entirely

tables.caption_tr: Register comparison: where and how each style is used
rows: daily conversation, chat apps, phone calls, casual interviews
shorter clauses, sentence-final particles (啊/吧/呢), colloquial vocabulary, looser word order, repetition and filler words
news reports, official documents, academic essays, literature, formal speeches
denser vocabulary (often 2-character words from Classical Chinese roots), four-character set phrases (四字格), parallel/balanced clause structure, connectives like 之/而/则/故, no tone particles
textbooks, most modern novels, blog posts, TV news scripts read aloud
blends both: written-style connectives with spoken-accessible vocabulary; typical of HSK5-6 reading passages
footnotes_tr: Native speakers constantly switch registers depending on context — using written-style vocabulary in casual chat can sound overly formal or even sarcastic, while spoken-style words in an essay can sound unpolished.

examples.target: 我因为很忙，所以没去。
examples.reading: Wǒ yīnwèi hěn máng, suǒyǐ méi qù.
examples.translation_tr: I didn't go because I was busy. (spoken register — everyday conversation)
examples.note_tr: Spoken version: uses 因为...所以, casual and direct.

examples.target: 我因工作繁忙，故未能前往。
examples.reading: Wǒ yīn gōngzuò fánmáng, gù wèi néng qiánwǎng.
examples.translation_tr: I was unable to attend due to being occupied with work. (written register — formal report/letter)
examples.note_tr: Written version: uses 因...故, more formal vocabulary (繁忙, 未能, 前往).

examples.target: 这个问题挺重要的。
examples.reading: Zhège wèntí tǐng zhòngyào de.
examples.translation_tr: This issue is pretty important. (spoken register)
examples.note_tr: Spoken version: 挺...的 pattern, casual intensifier.

examples.target: 此问题十分重要。
examples.reading: Cǐ wèntí shífēn zhòngyào.
examples.translation_tr: This issue is of great importance. (written register)
examples.note_tr: Written version: literary demonstrative 此 replaces 这个, formal intensifier 十分.

examples.target: 他说他明天要来。
examples.reading: Tā shuō tā míngtiān yào lái.
examples.translation_tr: He said he'll come tomorrow. (spoken register)
examples.note_tr: Spoken version: simple 说 + subordinate clause.

examples.target: 他称其明日将至。
examples.reading: Tā chēng qí míngrì jiāng zhì.
examples.translation_tr: He stated that he would arrive the following day. (written/news register)
examples.note_tr: Written version: 称 instead of 说, 其 instead of 他, 明日 instead of 明天, 将至 instead of 要来 — heavily literary.

examples.target: 越来越多的人喜欢这个。
examples.reading: Yuè lái yuè duō de rén xǐhuan zhège.
examples.translation_tr: More and more people like this. (spoken register)
examples.note_tr: Spoken version: common 越来越 pattern.

examples.target: 喜欢此物者日益增多。
examples.reading: Xǐhuan cǐ wù zhě rìyì zēngduō.
examples.translation_tr: Those who like this item are increasing day by day. (written register)
examples.note_tr: Written version: 者 marks 'those who...', 日益 replaces 越来越, inverted topic-first structure typical of essays.

tangruo.intro_tr: 倘若 (tǎngruò) is a literary/formal conjunction meaning "if, supposing, in the event that." It introduces a hypothetical or counterfactual condition and belongs to written Chinese — essays, speeches, literature, news commentary — rather than everyday conversation, where 如果 or 要是 are used instead. Structurally it behaves exactly like 如果: 倘若 + condition clause, followed optionally by 就/便/则/那么 + result clause. Because it signals a formal or literary register, using 倘若 in casual speech can sound stiff or bookish, so learners should reserve it for writing, formal presentations, or reading comprehension (it is a favorite of HSK6 reading passages). It belongs to a small family of classical-flavored conditionals (倘, 倘若, 倘使, 倘或) that all translate roughly as "if."

tables.caption_tr: 倘若 Compared with Other Conditional Conjunctions (Register Scale)
rows: Most casual; almost never in formal writing
Slightly more literary than 如果, still common
footnotes_tr: For HSK6 reading and writing tasks, 倘若 is interchangeable with 如果/假如 in meaning but signals a more literary tone.

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Structure Patterns with 倘若
rows: 倘若 + S + V(O)，(就/便/则/那么) + S + V(O)
If you come, I'll go pick you up.
倘若可能的话，就早点出发。
这个计划，倘若失败，损失很大。
This plan — if it fails, the losses will be great.
倘若失败了，也不要灰心。
Even if it fails, don't lose heart (concessive nuance).
倘若当初听你的话，就不会有今天的麻烦。
If I had listened to you back then, there wouldn't be today's trouble.

tables.caption_tr: Correlative Adverbs Used in the Result Clause
rows: More literary than 就; typical in essays
Makes the conditional link explicit and clear
Common when the relationship is already obvious

tables.caption_tr: The 倘 Family of Literary Conditional Words
rows: Rare alone; mostly in fixed expressions
Found in older written works; rare today
footnotes_tr: All four are mutually substitutable in meaning; 倘若 is by far the one most likely to appear on HSK6.

tables.caption_tr: Common Errors When Using 倘若
rows: 倘若你吃了吗？(as a casual chat opener)
你吃了吗？ / 如果你吃了...
倘若 is reserved for formal/written condition clauses, not small talk
倘若 must introduce a full clause stating the condition
倘若中彩票（描述一般假设）
万一中彩票 (for a very unlikely lucky event) / 倘若下雨 (for a plausible scenario)
万一 stresses unlikely/undesirable events; 倘若 is register-neutral about likelihood
倘若你来... / 如果你来...
Do not stack two conditional conjunctions together

examples.target: 倘若明天下雨，运动会就取消。
examples.reading: Tǎngruò míngtiān xiàyǔ, yùndònghuì jiù qǔxiāo.
examples.translation_tr: If it rains tomorrow, the sports meet will be canceled.
examples.note_tr: Basic pattern: 倘若 + condition, 就 + result.

examples.target: 倘若没有他的帮助，我们不可能成功。
examples.reading: Tǎngruò méiyǒu tā de bāngzhù, wǒmen bù kěnéng chénggōng.
examples.translation_tr: If it weren't for his help, we could not have succeeded.
examples.note_tr: Counterfactual use — the condition did not actually happen.

examples.target: 倘若你早一点告诉我，我就能想办法解决。
examples.reading: Tǎngruò nǐ zǎo yìdiǎn gàosu wǒ, wǒ jiù néng xiǎng bànfǎ jiějué.
examples.translation_tr: If you had told me a little earlier, I could have found a way to solve it.
examples.note_tr: Also works as a hypothetical about the past, similar to English 'had ... would have'.

examples.target: 人生倘若没有理想，便如同行尸走肉。
examples.reading: Rénshēng tǎngruò méiyǒu lǐxiǎng, biàn rútóng xíngshī zǒuròu.
examples.translation_tr: If life has no ideals, it is just like a walking corpse.
examples.note_tr: 便 (biàn) is a literary substitute for 就, common in essayistic writing alongside 倘若.

examples.target: 倘若事情真的如此，那么后果不堪设想。
examples.reading: Tǎngruò shìqing zhēn de rúcǐ, nàme hòuguǒ bùkān shèxiǎng.
examples.translation_tr: If things really are like this, then the consequences would be unimaginable.
examples.note_tr: 那么 explicitly marks the following clause as the consequence.

examples.target: 倘若你不同意，我们可以再商量。
examples.reading: Tǎngruò nǐ bù tóngyì, wǒmen kěyǐ zài shāngliang.
examples.translation_tr: If you don't agree, we can discuss it further.
examples.note_tr: No correlative adverb is required in the second clause; it can be omitted.

examples.target: 倘若失败了，也不要灰心。
examples.reading: Tǎngruò shībài le, yě búyào huīxīn.
examples.translation_tr: Even if you fail, don't lose heart.
examples.note_tr: 倘若 + 也 gives a concessive-conditional flavor ('even if').

examples.target: 这份工作，倘若给你，你愿意接受吗？
examples.reading: Zhè fèn gōngzuò, tǎngruò gěi nǐ, nǐ yuànyì jiēshòu ma?
examples.translation_tr: This job — if it were given to you, would you be willing to accept it?
examples.note_tr: Topic-comment order: the topic can precede 倘若, moving the clause after the subject.

guran.title_tr: 固然[gùrán]...但是[dànshì]... ("It's true that... but...")
guran.intro_tr: 固然[gùrán] is a formal, written-style conjunction meaning "it is true that / granted that / admittedly." It first concedes that a statement is a genuine, undeniable fact, and then a second clause introduced by 但是[dànshì], 可是[kěshì], 却[què], 不过[búguò] or 然而[rán'ér] pivots to a more important, often contrasting, point. Unlike casual concessive words, 固然 signals that the speaker fully accepts clause A as true — it is not hypothetical or in doubt — which makes the "but" that follows feel more persuasive and rhetorically forceful. It appears mainly in essays, speeches, news articles and formal argumentation rather than everyday chat. A secondary, non-contrastive use pairs 固然 with 也[yě]/还[hái] to mean "A is indeed true, and B is equally true," stacking two valid points rather than opposing them.

tables.caption_tr: Core sentence patterns with 固然[gùrán]
rows: Clause A (固然) + Clause B (但是/可是/却/不过)
这本书固然有趣，但是太贵了。[Zhè běn shū gùrán yǒuqù, dànshì tài guì le.]
This book / granted / interesting / but / too expensive
The book is interesting, granted, but it's too expensive.
Subject + 固然 + Predicate A, 但是 + Predicate B (same subject)
他固然努力，但是方法不对。[Tā gùrán nǔlì, dànshì fāngfǎ bú duì.]
He / granted / works hard / but / method / not right
He works hard, granted, but his method is wrong.
固然 + Subject A + Predicate A, 但是 + Subject B + Predicate B (different subjects)
固然天气很好，但是我们还是决定不出门。[Gùrán tiānqì hěn hǎo, dànshì wǒmen háishi juédìng bù chūmén.]
Granted / weather / very good / but / we / still / decide / not go out
Granted the weather is nice, we still decided not to go out.
固然 + A，也/还 + B (additive, not contrastive)
读书固然重要，也要注意身体。[Dúshū gùrán zhòngyào, yě yào zhùyì shēntǐ.]
Studying / granted / important / also / must / pay attention / health
Studying is certainly important, but you must also take care of your health.

tables.caption_tr: 固然[gùrán] vs 虽然[suīrán]: how they differ
rows: Formal, written (书面语[shūmiànyǔ]); rare in casual speech
Neutral; used in both speech and writing
Only facts the speaker personally accepts as indisputably true
Any circumstance, real or assumed, true or hypothetical-sounding
Stronger — implies 'I fully grant this point, BUT...' (used to strengthen an argument)
Yes — 'A is true, and B is equally true' (no real contrast)
No — 虽然 always signals contrast, never simple addition
但是, 可是, 不过, 却, 然而
但是, 可是, 不过, 还是
Can start the sentence before the subject

tables.caption_tr: Contrast words that pair with 固然[gùrán]
rows: Slightly more conversational than 但是
Literary, places extra stress on the twist, often mid-clause after the subject
...固然便宜，质量却...[...gùrán piányi, zhìliàng què...]

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes with 固然[gùrán]
rows: Using 固然 for a hypothetical situation: *如果固然...
固然 concedes an accepted FACT, not a hypothesis; it cannot follow 如果[rúguǒ]
Use 虽然[suīrán] or 即使[jíshǐ] instead for hypothetical/conditional concession
Dropping the second clause entirely: *这个方法固然好。 (stopping there)
固然 grammatically requires a following contrastive or additive clause; leaving it off sounds incomplete in formal writing
这个方法固然好，但是成本太高。[Zhège fāngfǎ gùrán hǎo, dànshì chéngběn tài gāo.]
Using it in casual spoken requests: *你固然想去，我们走吧。
固然 is bookish; sounds unnatural/stilted in everyday spoken commands
Replace with 虽然...但是... or just drop the concessive structure in casual speech
Pairing with 因为/所以 instead of a contrast word
固然's second clause must show contrast or addition, not cause-effect

yimian-miande.title_tr: 以便 / 以免 / 免得 ('so that / so as not to')
yimian-miande.intro_tr: 以便[yǐbiàn], 以免[yǐmiǎn], and 免得[miǎndé] are purpose connectors that join two clauses: the first clause states an action or method, and the second clause (introduced by one of these words) states the goal. 以便[yǐbiàn] introduces a positive purpose — something you want to make possible or easier. 以免[yǐmiǎn] and 免得[miǎndé] introduce a negative purpose — an unwanted result you want to avoid — and the clause after them normally does NOT contain 不[bù] or 别[bié], because the undesired event itself is already the thing being avoided. 以免[yǐmiǎn] belongs to formal/written style, while 免得[miǎndé] is common and neutral in everyday spoken Chinese. All three words sit at the start of the second clause, right after the comma, and the subject of that second clause is usually dropped when it is the same as the subject of the first clause.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of the three purpose connectors
rows: so that; in order to (make X possible/easier)
Start of clause 2, right after the comma
so as not to; in order to avoid
Start of clause 2, right after the comma
so as not to; to avoid
Neutral / spoken, common in daily conversation
Start of clause 2, right after the comma

tables.caption_tr: Sentence structure pattern
rows: 我们提前出发[Wǒmen tíqián chūfā] — We set off early
以便[yǐbiàn] / 以免[yǐmiǎn] / 免得[miǎndé]
Purpose to achieve (with 以便) or bad result to avoid (with 以免/免得); subject usually omitted
赶上火车[gǎnshàng huǒchē] — catch the train
Clause 1 + 以便/以免/免得 + Clause 2
我们提前出发，以便赶上火车。[Wǒmen tíqián chūfā, yǐbiàn gǎnshàng huǒchē.] — We set off early so that we could catch the train.

tables.caption_tr: Polarity contrast: 以便 vs. 以免 / 免得
rows: Usually a bad/undesired situation (already negative in meaning)
Need for 不[bù] before the verb?
Normally NOT added — the bad event itself is the thing being avoided, e.g. 以免迟到[yǐmiǎn chídào] 'so as not to be late', not 以免不迟到

tables.caption_tr: Nuance between 以免 and 免得
rows: Neutral to colloquial, common in speech
Yes, but sounds more casual/friendly than 以免
请系好安全带，以免发生意外。[Qǐng jì hǎo ānquándài, yǐmiǎn fāshēng yìwài.]
多穿点儿，免得感冒。[Duō chuān diǎnr, miǎndé gǎnmào.]

tables.caption_tr: Common collocations after 以免 / 免得
rows: so as to avoid accidents happening
so as not to cause misunderstanding
so as to avoid causing losses
so as not to be late

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes
rows: Adding 不 reverses the meaning to the illogical 'avoid not being late'; 迟到 is already the bad thing to avoid
以免迟到 [yǐmiǎn chídào] — so as not to be late
用以便表示要避免的坏事 (using 以便 to express something bad to be avoided)
以便 only expresses a positive purpose, never an avoidance
Use 以免 or 免得 instead for negative purposes
以便 / 以免 / 免得 单独放在句首引出整句 (treating them like 因为 that can head an independent reason clause)
They connect two related clauses; the first clause (the means) must be stated first
Clause 1 (action), 以便/以免/免得 + Clause 2 (purpose)
重复主语：他早点儿出门，以便他赶上火车 (repeating the same subject in clause 2)
When the subject is identical to clause 1, it is normally dropped for natural flow
他早点儿出门，以便赶上火车。[Tā zǎo diǎnr chūmén, yǐbiàn gǎnshàng huǒchē.]

examples.target: 我们应该提前预订房间，以便旅行时不用担心住宿问题。

examples.target: 出门带把伞，免得下雨淋湿了。

yizhi-yizhi.title_tr: 以至 / 以致 (yǐzhì): "to such an extent that... / as a result..."
yizhi-yizhi.intro_tr: 以至 [yǐzhì] and 以致 [yǐzhì] are formal, written-style conjunctions that connect a cause/degree clause to a resulting clause, roughly meaning "to such an extent that..." or "as a result...". They are pronounced identically, which is why learners often confuse them, but their usage differs in one crucial way: 以至 [yǐzhì] is neutral and can introduce a result that is positive, neutral, or negative — it often simply marks an extreme degree ("so much so that..."). 以致 [yǐzhì] is reserved almost exclusively for negative, undesirable, or unfortunate outcomes — it carries a built-in sense of "and unfortunately this bad thing happened." Both appear at the start of the second clause in a sentence, never at the very beginning of a sentence, and both belong to formal/written Chinese (书面语[shūmiànyǔ]) rather than everyday spoken conversation. A common extended form, 以至于 [yǐzhìyú], is used only with 以至 (not with 以致) to add emphasis, often paired with 连...都/也 [lián...dōu/yě] ("even...").

tables.caption_tr: Core meaning and tone comparison: 以至 vs 以致
rows: "to such an extent that", "so much that", "(even) up to"
Neutral, positive, OR negative — just marks an extreme degree
Can also mean a range "down to / up to"
Yes, e.g. 从大到小，以至最小的 [cóng dà dào xiǎo, yǐzhì zuì xiǎo de] "from big to small, down to the smallest"
No, 以致 never expresses a range
太...了[tài...le], 越来越[yuèláiyuè], 非常[fēicháng], 甚至[shènzhì]
由于[yóuyú], 因为[yīnwèi], 不小心[bù xiǎoxīn], 不注意[bú zhùyì]
Can extend to 以至于/以致于?
Yes — 以至于[yǐzhìyú] is common and adds emphasis
No — adding 于 after 以致 is a common learner mistake
footnotes_tr: When the result is clearly bad and caused by a mistake or negligence, 以致 is the safer, more natural choice.
When in doubt and the result is not negative, always choose 以至, never 以致.

tables.caption_tr: Sentence structure and patterns
rows: 他学习很努力，以至（于）成绩提高得很快。[Tā xuéxí hěn nǔlì, yǐzhì(yú) chéngjì tígāo de hěn kuài.]
He studied so hard that his grades improved very quickly.
他不小心，以致摔倒了。[Tā bù xiǎoxīn, yǐzhì shuāidǎo le.]
He was careless, resulting in a fall.
..., 以至于 + 连 + Noun + 都/也 + V
他忙得很，以至于连饭都忘了吃。[Tā máng de hěn, yǐzhìyú lián fàn dōu wàng le chī.]
He was so busy that he even forgot to eat.
由于...以致... formal cause-effect pair
由于 + Cause, 以致 + Bad Result
由于疏忽，以致造成重大损失。[Yóuyú shūhu, yǐzhì zàochéng zhòngdà sǔnshī.]
Due to negligence, it resulted in major losses.
参加会议的有校长、老师，以至学生。[Cānjiā huìyì de yǒu xiàozhǎng, lǎoshī, yǐzhì xuésheng.]
Attendees included the principal, teachers, and even (down to) students.

tables.caption_tr: 以至于 vs 以致于: which form actually exists?
rows: Extended, more emphatic version of 以至; very common in speech-adjacent formal writing
Standalone form only; used strictly for negative results
Native speakers do NOT add 于 after 以致; if you want the emphatic form with a negative result, just keep 以致 alone or restructure with 以至于 if the result can be framed neutrally
footnotes_tr: This is one of the most frequent mistakes intermediate-to-advanced learners make — memorize that 于 only ever attaches to 以至, never to 以致.

tables.caption_tr: 以至 / 以致 vs similar cause-result connectors
rows: Marks an extreme degree, not just any result
Cannot be used for good news or neutral outcomes
Followed directly by a noun/noun phrase, not a full independent clause with subject repeated the same way as 以致
Emphasizes a purposeful, often planned, follow-up result — opposite feel from 以致
General-purpose "therefore/so", no built-in extreme-degree or negativity nuance
footnotes_tr: If the second clause simply states a logical consequence with no strong emotional coloring, prefer 因此/于是 rather than 以至/以致.
If you want to stress that a goal was achieved thanks to the first action, 从而 is usually more natural than 以至.

tables.caption_tr: Common learner mistakes with 以至 / 以致
rows: Using 以致 for a good outcome
他努力学习，以致取得了好成绩。[Tā nǔlì xuéxí, yǐzhì qǔdé le hǎo chéngjì.] (✗)
他努力学习，以至（于）取得了好成绩。[Tā nǔlì xuéxí, yǐzhì(yú) qǔdé le hǎo chéngjì.] (✓)
取得好成绩 (getting good grades) is positive, so 以致 is wrong; use 以至 instead.
他不小心，以致于摔倒了。[...] (✗ non-standard)
他不小心，以致摔倒了。[Tā bù xiǎoxīn, yǐzhì shuāidǎo le.] (✓)
以致 never takes 于; only 以至 can become 以至于.
Starting a sentence with 以至/以致
以至他失眠了，他压力太大。(✗ wrong order)
他压力太大，以至他失眠了。[Tā yālì tài dà, yǐzhì tā shīmián le.] (✓)
以至/以致 always introduce the SECOND (result) clause, never the first.
他不小心以致机器（direct noun with no clause）(⚠ awkward)
他不小心，导致机器损坏。[Tā bù xiǎoxīn, dǎozhì jīqì sǔnhuài.] (✓ with 导致) / 他不小心，以致机器损坏了。[...] (✓ with 以致 + clause)
导致 directly governs a noun/result as a transitive verb; 以致/以至 are conjunctions connecting two full clauses.

examples.target: 他学习很努力，以至（于）成绩提高得很快。
examples.reading: Tā xuéxí hěn nǔlì, yǐzhì(yú) chéngjì tígāo de hěn kuài.
examples.translation_tr: He studied so hard that his grades improved very quickly.
examples.note_tr: 以至 here introduces a positive/neutral extreme result — perfectly fine, unlike 以致.

examples.target: 他上课不认真听讲，以致考试没有及格。
examples.reading: Tā shàngkè bù rènzhēn tīngjiǎng, yǐzhì kǎoshì méiyǒu jígé.
examples.translation_tr: He didn't listen carefully in class, and as a result he failed the exam.
examples.note_tr: Classic 以致 pattern: careless cause → undesirable, negative outcome.

examples.target: 她太紧张了，以至说话都结巴了。
examples.reading: Tā tài jǐnzhāng le, yǐzhì shuōhuà dōu jiēbā le.
examples.translation_tr: She was so nervous that she even started stuttering when speaking.
examples.note_tr: 以至 can express a natural, non-blameworthy extreme degree, not necessarily 'bad' in a moral sense.

examples.target: 大家讨论得非常热烈，以至忘记了时间。
examples.reading: Dàjiā tǎolùn de fēicháng rèliè, yǐzhì wàngjì le shíjiān.
examples.translation_tr: Everyone discussed so animatedly that they forgot about the time.
examples.note_tr: Result is neutral/mildly negative but not caused by fault — 以至 fits better than 以致.

examples.target: 由于操作不当，以致机器损坏了。
examples.reading: Yóuyú cāozuò bùdàng, yǐzhì jīqì sǔnhuài le.
examples.translation_tr: Because of improper operation, the machine ended up being damaged.
examples.note_tr: 由于...以致... is a very common formal cause-and-bad-result pairing.

examples.target: 工作压力太大，以至他每天都失眠。
examples.reading: Gōngzuò yālì tài dà, yǐzhì tā měitiān dōu shīmián.
examples.translation_tr: The work pressure was so great that he couldn't sleep every night.
examples.note_tr: Negative result caused by an external circumstance — both 以至 and 以致 are acceptable here.

examples.target: 这个问题太复杂了，以至于专家们也难以达成一致。
examples.reading: Zhège wèntí tài fùzá le, yǐzhìyú zhuānjiāmen yě nányǐ dáchéng yízhì.
examples.translation_tr: The problem was so complicated that even the experts found it hard to reach agreement.
examples.note_tr: 以至于 + 连/也/都 structures emphasize an extreme, almost surprising degree.

examples.target: 他喝多了酒，以致站不稳，摔倒在地上。
examples.reading: Tā hē duō le jiǔ, yǐzhì zhàn bù wěn, shuāi dǎo zài dìshang.
examples.translation_tr: He drank too much, so that he couldn't stand steadily and fell to the ground.
examples.note_tr: 以致 strongly signals a bad, often physically harmful, consequence of one's own action.

fanshi-dou.intro_tr: 凡是[fánshì]...都[dōu]... is a formal, written-register pattern used to state a universal rule: it introduces a category of people, things, or situations, and 都[dōu] (or its stricter formal cousins 一律[yílǜ] and 均[jūn]) in the second clause confirms that the rule applies to every single member of that category without exception. Unlike English "whoever," 凡是[fánshì] is not really a question word — it works more like "any and all cases where..." It is extremely common in regulations, announcements, contracts, and formal writing (school rules, legal notices, official statements), and is rarely used in casual spoken conversation, where 所有[suǒyǒu]...都[dōu]... or 只要[zhǐyào]...就[jiù]... are more natural. A key trap for learners is confusing 凡是[fánshì] (a declarative generalization: "all X are Y") with 只要[zhǐyào] (a conditional: "if X, then Y") — they look similar in translation but express different logical relationships.

tables.caption_tr: Core Structure of 凡是...都...
rows: Introduces the category — 'whoever/whatever fits this description'
凡是[fánshì]学过汉语的人[xuéguo Hànyǔ de rén] — 'whoever has studied Chinese'
States what is universally true for every member of that category — the adverb is mandatory
都[dōu]会说几句[huì shuō jǐ jù] — 'can all say a few phrases'

tables.caption_tr: 凡是...都... vs. Similar Universal-Quantifier Patterns
rows: Declarative generalization: 'every member of category X is/does Y'
凡是[fánshì]会员都[dōu]可以享受优惠。[Huìyuán dōu kěyǐ xiǎngshòu yōuhuì.] — 'Every member can enjoy the discount.'
Neutral factual listing: 'all (of) X are Y'
所有[suǒyǒu]学生都[dōu]到齐了。[Xuésheng dōu dào qí le.] — 'All the students have arrived.'
Concessive: 'no matter which/what X, Y still holds' — X is usually a range or question word
无论[wúlùn]多难都[dōu]要坚持。[Duō nán dōu yào jiānchí.] — 'No matter how hard, must persist.'
Same meaning as 无论[wúlùn], more colloquial
不管[bùguǎn]你去不去都[dōu]行。[Nǐ qù bu qù dōu xíng.] — 'Whether you go or not is fine.'
Sufficient condition: 'as long as X happens, Y follows' — a real if-then
只要[zhǐyào]努力就[jiù]能成功。[Nǔlì jiù néng chénggōng.] — 'As long as you try hard, you'll succeed.'

tables.caption_tr: Adverbs Pairing with 凡是 in the Second Clause
rows: 凡是[fánshì]错误都[dōu]要改正。[Cuòwù dōu yào gǎizhèng.] — 'Every mistake must be corrected.'
'Without any exception' — stricter, typical of rules/regulations/announcements
凡是[fánshì]迟到者一律[yílǜ]扣分。[Chídào zhě yílǜ kòu fēn.] — 'Anyone late will have points deducted, no exceptions.'
Very formal written equivalent of 都[dōu], common in official documents
凡是[fánshì]申请者均[jūn]需提交材料。[Shēnqǐngzhě jūn xū tíjiāo cáiliào.] — 'All applicants must submit materials.'

tables.caption_tr: What Can Follow 凡是
rows: 凡是[fánshì]他说过的话[tā shuōguo de huà]
凡是[fánshì]不符合要求的[bù fúhé yāoqiú de]都不能通过
'whatever doesn't meet the requirements can't pass'

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: The second clause is missing the mandatory 都[dōu]/均[jūn]/一律[yílǜ]; 凡是[fánshì] cannot stand alone
凡是[fánshì]学生都[dōu]要努力学习。
凡是[fánshì] is being used as a conditional 'if,' which is not its function — that job belongs to 只要[zhǐyào]
凡是[fánshì] must be followed directly by a noun phrase or a nominalized clause with 的[de] before the noun — it cannot itself be marked with 的[de] right after it with nothing in between
凡是[fánshì]这个班的学生都很努力。

yuqi-buru.title_tr: 与其[yǔqí]...不如[bùrú]... ('Rather than..., it would be better to...')
yuqi-buru.intro_tr: 与其[yǔqí]...不如[bùrú]... is a formal comparative structure meaning "rather than A, it would be better to B," used when the speaker wants to recommend one option over another. The clause after 与其[yǔqí] always states the LESS desirable option, while the clause after 不如[bùrú] states the PREFERRED alternative — this order can never be swapped without reversing the meaning. If both clauses share the same subject, that subject usually appears once, before 与其[yǔqí]; if the two clauses have different subjects, each subject follows its own conjunction (与其[yǔqí] + S1..., 不如[bùrú] + S2...). Unlike a plain objective comparison, this pattern expresses the speaker's subjective judgment or advice, and it is common in both writing and moderately formal speech. For extra emphasis, 还[hái] or 倒[dào] can be inserted directly before 不如[bùrú] (还不如[hái bùrú] / 倒不如[dào bùrú]).

tables.caption_tr: Core Structure Patterns of 与其[yǔqí]...不如[bùrú]...
rows: Basic — shared subject before 与其[yǔqí]
(S) + 与其[yǔqí] + A, 不如[bùrú] + B
我与其在家等，不如出去找。[Wǒ yǔqí zài jiā děng, bùrú chūqù zhǎo.]
Rather than waiting at home, I'd rather go out and look.
Different subjects — subject after each conjunction
与其[yǔqí] + S1 + A, 不如[bùrú] + S2 + B
与其你去，不如我去。[Yǔqí nǐ qù, bùrú wǒ qù.]
Rather than you going, it's better that I go.
与其[yǔqí] A, 还不如[hái bùrú] B
与其道歉，还不如别做错事。[Yǔqí dàoqiàn, hái bùrú bié zuò cuò shì.]
Rather than apologizing, better not to do wrong in the first place.
与其[yǔqí] A, 倒不如[dào bùrú] B
与其抱怨，倒不如努力改变。[Yǔqí bàoyuàn, dào bùrú nǔlì gǎibiàn.]
Rather than complaining, better to work hard to change things.

tables.caption_tr: 与其[yǔqí]...不如[bùrú]... vs Similar Structures
rows: Rather than A, it's better to B
Subjective recommendation choosing between two explicit options
与其看电视，不如看书。[Yǔqí kàn diànshì, bùrú kàn shū.] — Better to read than watch TV.
I would rather A (even if hard) than B
Emphasizes willingness to endure a hardship (A) in order to avoid an even worse outcome (B); expresses determination, not a simple comparison
宁可累一点，也不要放弃。[Nìngkě lèi yìdiǎn, yě bú yào fàngqì.] — I'd rather be a bit tired than give up.
A is not as good as B
Simple, often objective, comparison of two things; no built-in 'rather' nuance
他的汉语不如你好。[Tā de Hànyǔ bùrú nǐ hǎo.] — His Chinese isn't as good as yours.
A suggestion stated alone, without explicitly comparing two options
你最好早点儿睡。[Nǐ zuìhǎo zǎodiǎnr shuì.] — You'd best sleep early.

tables.caption_tr: Common Collocations and Fixed Patterns
rows: 与其说[yǔqí shuō]...不如说[bùrú shuō]...
Rephrasing: 'rather than saying A, it's more accurate to say B'
与其说他懒，不如说他忙。[Yǔqí shuō tā lǎn, bùrú shuō tā máng.]
Rather than saying he's lazy, it's more accurate to say he's busy.
Emphasizes that B has more of a quality than A, in a comparative sense
与其坐车，不如走路来得快。[Yǔqí zuò chē, bùrú zǒulù láide kuài.]
Rather than taking the car, walking is actually faster.
Refers back to a previously mentioned situation ('rather than being like this')
与其这样浪费时间，不如现在就开始。[Yǔqí zhèyàng làngfèi shíjiān, bùrú xiànzài jiù kāishǐ.]
Rather than wasting time like this, it's better to start right now.

tables.caption_tr: Common Errors and Usage Notes
rows: 与其[yǔqí] alone cannot form the comparison; 不如[bùrú] (or 还不如[hái bùrú] / 倒不如[dào bùrú]) is obligatory in the second clause
✓ 与其在家睡觉，不如出去运动。 ✗ 与其在家睡觉，出去运动。(missing 不如)
The LESS-preferred option must go in the 与其[yǔqí] clause; the preferred one always follows 不如[bùrú]
✓ 与其买新的，不如修一修。[Yǔqí mǎi xīn de, bùrú xiū yi xiū.] ✗ 与其修一修，不如买新的。(reverses the intended meaning)
With one shared subject, place it before 与其[yǔqí]; with two different subjects, repeat the subject after each conjunction
我们与其争吵，不如好好谈谈。[Wǒmen yǔqí zhēngchǎo, bùrú hǎohǎo tántan.]
与其[yǔqí]...不如[bùrú]... is somewhat formal/written; in very casual speech, 还是[háishi]...吧[ba] or 最好[zuìhǎo] often sound more natural
casual: 我们还是走路吧。[Wǒmen háishi zǒulù ba.] vs formal: 与其打车，不如走路。[Yǔqí dǎchē, bùrú zǒulù.]

yidan-jiu.intro_tr: 一旦[yīdàn]...就[jiù]... means "once (something happens), then..." and is used to describe a hypothetical or expected future trigger event, after which a significant, often serious or irreversible consequence follows. It is more formal and dramatic in tone than the simpler 一[yī]...就[jiù]... pattern, and is very common in written Chinese, warnings, rules, contracts, and news reports. 一旦[yīdàn] introduces the triggering condition (clause 1), and 就[jiù] introduces the resulting consequence (clause 2), which appears right before the main verb of the second clause. Because the tone is often cautionary, 一旦[yīdàn]...就[jiù]... frequently appears with negative, risky, or hard-to-reverse outcomes, though it can also describe neutral or positive chain reactions.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure of 一旦[yīdàn]...就[jiù]...
rows: States the trigger event that may or will happen — the 'once' condition
States the consequence that automatically or inevitably follows once the trigger occurs
footnotes_tr: If the subject of both clauses is the same, it is usually placed before 一旦[yīdàn]: 你一旦[nǐ yīdàn]... rather than after it.
If the subjects differ, each subject stays inside its own clause: 一旦[yīdàn] + Subject1 ..., Subject2 + 就[jiù] ...

tables.caption_tr: 一旦[yīdàn]...就[jiù]... vs. Similar 'if/once...then' Patterns
rows: 'Once (a usually serious/irreversible trigger) happens, then...' — formal, dramatic, often written
一旦[yīdàn]决定[juédìng],就[jiù]不再[bùzài]改变[gǎibiàn]。 ('Once decided, it won't change again.')
'As soon as... then immediately...' — neutral, everyday, describes quick succession, not necessarily serious
他一[tā yī]到家[dàojiā]就[jiù]睡觉[shuìjiào]。 ('As soon as he gets home he sleeps.')
'As long as (a sufficient condition) is met, then...' — focuses on minimum requirement, often positive
只要[zhǐyào]努力[nǔlì],就[jiù]会[huì]成功[chénggōng]。 ('As long as you work hard, you'll succeed.')
'If... then...' — plain, general hypothetical, no special sense of irreversibility or seriousness
如果[rúguǒ]下雨[xiàyǔ],就[jiù]别[bié]去[qù]了。 ('If it rains, then don't go.')
footnotes_tr: 一旦[yīdàn] adds a stronger sense of 'the moment this crosses the line, there is no going back' compared to 如果[rúguǒ] or plain 一[yī]...就[jiù]...
只要[zhǐyào] emphasizes sufficiency of a condition, while 一旦[yīdàn] emphasizes the critical turning-point nature of an event.

tables.caption_tr: Typical Contexts Where 一旦[yīdàn]...就[jiù]... Is Used
rows: Common in safety instructions, medical warnings, legal notices
一旦[yīdàn]开始[kāishǐ]下雪[xiàxuě],气温[qìwēn]就[jiù]会[huì]下降[xiàjiàng]。
Can describe neutral natural processes too, not only negative ones

tables.caption_tr: Common Errors and Clarifications
rows: Using 一旦[yīdàn] for routine, repeated daily actions
Use 一[yī]...就[jiù]... instead: 他一[tā yī]起床[qǐchuáng]就[jiù]刷牙[shuāyá]。
一旦[yīdàn] is reserved for significant, often one-time, critical turning points, not everyday habitual sequences
Omitting 就[jiù] in the second clause
一旦[yīdàn]下雨[xiàyǔ],比赛[bǐsài]就[jiù]取消[qǔxiāo]。 (not: ...比赛[bǐsài]取消[qǔxiāo]。)
就[jiù] is required to link the result back to the 一旦[yīdàn] clause; dropping it breaks the pattern
Placing the shared subject after 一旦[yīdàn] when it should come before
你一旦[nǐ yīdàn]... (correct) rather than 一旦你[yīdàn nǐ]...
When both clauses share the same subject, the subject normally precedes 一旦[yīdàn]
Using 一旦[yīdàn] about the past as a completed single event narration
Prefer 一[yī]...就[jiù]... or plain time clauses for simple past sequences; 一旦[yīdàn] usually frames a hypothetical/general 'once X, then Y' rule
一旦[yīdàn] is most natural for hypothetical, habitual-rule, or future-oriented statements, less so for a one-off past narrative

buzhiyu.title_tr: 不至于 (búzhìyú): "Won't Go So Far As To" / "It's Not That Bad"
buzhiyu.intro_tr: 不至于[búzhìyú] is an HSK6 adverbial expression meaning "won't go so far as to," "isn't to the extent of," or "it's not that bad." It is used to judge that a situation, action, or consequence does not reach an extreme or implied degree, often to reassure someone, to push back gently against an exaggeration, or to voice disbelief. It typically sits directly before a verb phrase (S + 不至于 + VP), but it can also stand alone as a short reply, 不至于吧, meaning "surely not that bad!" Do not confuse it with the unrelated topic marker 至于[zhìyú] ("as for"), which drops the negation 不[bù] and has a completely different function.

tables.caption_tr: Core Sentence Patterns with 不至于[búzhìyú]
rows: States the subject won't reach that extreme degree
他不至于生气。[tā búzhìyú shēngqì.] "He won't go so far as to get angry."
"Not yet to that extent" — degree hasn't been reached so far
情况还不至于失控。[qíngkuàng hái búzhìyú shīkòng.] "The situation hasn't gotten out of control yet."
Casts doubt on an exaggerated claim someone just made
A: 他快疯了。 B: 不至于吧。[A: tā kuài fēng le. B: búzhìyú ba.] "A: He's about to lose it. B: Surely not that bad."
Softens a rhetorical doubt, inviting agreement
你不至于连这个都不知道吧。[nǐ búzhìyú lián zhège dōu bù zhīdào ba.] "Surely you're not so clueless as to not even know this."
"Wouldn't go that far either" — adds to a previous negative statement
他再忙,也不至于连电话都不接。[tā zài máng, yě búzhìyú lián diànhuà dōu bù jiē.] "No matter how busy he is, he wouldn't go so far as to not even answer the phone."

tables.caption_tr: 不至于[búzhìyú] vs. Similar-Looking Expressions
rows: won't go so far as to / not that extreme
Judges degree or severity; downplays an implied extreme
不至于这么惨吧。[búzhìyú zhème cǎn ba.] "Surely it's not that miserable."
Topic marker; no negative or degree meaning at all
至于这件事,我们以后再说。[zhìyú zhè jiàn shì, wǒmen yǐhòu zài shuō.] "As for this matter, let's discuss it later."
won't / it's not going to happen
Plain prediction of impossibility, no idea of "extreme degree"
他不会来了。[tā búhuì lái le.] "He's not coming."
Doubts the truth of a claim, not its severity
他未必知道这件事。[tā wèibì zhīdào zhè jiàn shì.] "He doesn't necessarily know about this."
Casts doubt on certainty, more colloquial than 未必
他不见得会同意。[tā bújiànde huì tóngyì.] "He might well not agree."
Negates necessity of an action, not its extremity
用不着担心这个。[yòngbuzháo dānxīn zhège.] "No need to worry about this."

tables.caption_tr: Common Fixed Collocations
rows: won't go so far as to die / it's not fatal
there's no need to go this far / it doesn't have to be like this
surely not! / no way it's that bad
the crime doesn't warrant death (idiomatic, legal/formal register)

tables.caption_tr: Where 不至于[búzhìyú] Sits in the Sentence
rows: Directly before the main verb phrase
他不至于骗你。[tā búzhìyú piàn nǐ.]
He wouldn't go so far as to cheat you.
After a topic subject, often with 还[hái]
事情还不至于那么糟。[shìqing hái búzhìyú nàme zāo.]
Standing alone as a full reply
A: 他快要疯了。B: 不至于吧。
A: He's about to lose it. B: Surely not that bad.
With 吧[ba] at the end for rhetorical softening
你不至于生这么大气吧。[nǐ búzhìyú shēng zhème dà qì ba.]
You wouldn't be THAT angry, would you?

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: 用不至于表达简单的"不想"
不至于[búzhìyú] judges degree/extremity, not plain intention or desire
我不想去。[wǒ bùxiǎng qù.] "I don't want to go." (not 不至于)
把不至于当作事实否定词使用
不至于[búzhìyú] is not used to deny a plain fact
这不是真的。[zhè bú shì zhēnde.] "This isn't true." (not 不至于)
不至于[búzhìyú] ("won't go so far as") and 至于[zhìyú] ("as for") are unrelated in meaning despite looking similar
至于[zhìyú] introduces a new topic; 不至于[búzhìyú] judges degree — keep the 不[bù] only for the degree meaning

examples.target: 他不至于连这点小事都做不好。
