jianyu-benzhe.title_tr: Formal Reason/Basis Prepositions (鉴于, 基于, 本着)
jianyu-benzhe.intro_tr: 鉴于[jiànyú], 基于[jīyú], and 本着[běnzhe] are three formal, written-style prepositions used almost exclusively in official documents, reports, news articles, legal texts, and academic writing to introduce a reason, basis, or guiding principle before stating a conclusion or action. 鉴于 means "in view of / considering" and introduces an observed fact or situation that has prompted a decision. 基于 means "based on / on the basis of" and introduces the logical or factual foundation for a judgment. 本着 means "in the spirit of / guided by" and, unlike the other two, introduces an abstract principle, attitude, or spirit rather than a fact — it almost always requires an abstract noun such as 原则[yuánzé], 精神[jīngshén], or 态度[tàidu]. All three typically stand at the very beginning of the sentence, before the subject, framing the entire clause that follows.

tables.caption_tr: Core meaning and function of each preposition
rows: in view of / considering / in light of
an observed fact, situation, or problem that motivates the following action
official reports, government notices, legal documents
based on / on the basis of
a reason, piece of evidence, data, or logical consideration behind a judgment
academic writing, argumentative essays, formal decisions
in the spirit of / guided by / adhering to
an abstract principle, attitude, spirit, or purpose guiding an action
diplomatic statements, policy documents, formal speeches
footnotes_tr: All three are used almost exclusively in written/formal registers; in everyday spoken Chinese, 因为[yīnwèi] or 由于[yóuyú] are used instead.

tables.caption_tr: Sentence structure patterns
rows: 鉴于 + [situation/fact clause]，+ [(就/特/因此) result clause]
The clause after 鉴于 usually describes a state of affairs, not an abstract value
基于 can also appear inside 是...的[shì...de] to emphasize the basis of an action already stated
本着 + [abstract principle NP] + (的原则/精神/态度) + [action clause]
本着 almost never takes a bare fact; it needs an abstract head noun like 原则/精神/态度/宗旨

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed collocations
rows: Refers back to something already mentioned; very common sentence opener
in light of this / for this reason
More formal variant of 鉴于此, common in speeches and reports
特[tè] signals an official action taken specifically because of the stated situation
Refers to a previously stated reason or piece of data
Introduces the motivating consideration behind a decision
in the spirit of the principle of...
Most common 本着 collocation, used for rules/guidelines
Common in diplomatic/cooperative contexts (友好合作的精神, etc.)

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with related reason/basis words
rows: General causal conjunction; usable anywhere in a sentence, no special formality
More written than 因为 but still far less formal than 鉴于/基于/本着
Introduces an objective rule, law, or piece of evidence, not a subjective consideration
Introduces an observed situation/problem prompting a response
Introduces the logical/factual foundation of a judgment or decision
Introduces an abstract guiding principle or attitude, not a fact or rule

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes to avoid
rows: 鉴于 cannot introduce a concrete physical location
本着[běnzhe]这些[zhèxiē]数据[shùjù]，我们[wǒmen]做出[zuòchū]决定[juédìng]
本着 cannot take concrete data/facts as its object; that role belongs to 基于
基于[jīyú]这些[zhèxiē]数据[shùjù]，我们[wǒmen]做出[zuòchū]决定[juédìng]
鉴于 is far too formal for casual spoken remarks
精神/原则/态度 collocate with 本着, not 基于
他[tā]鉴于[jiànyú]身体[shēntǐ]不好[bù hǎo]决定[juédìng]辞职[cízhí]
鉴于 phrase should generally open the whole sentence, before the subject, in formal style
鉴于[jiànyú]身体[shēntǐ]不好[bù hǎo]，他[tā]决定[juédìng]辞职[cízhí]

examples.target: 鉴于[jiànyú]目前[mùqián]的[de]经济[jīngjì]形势[xíngshì]，政府[zhèngfǔ]决定[juédìng]采取[cǎiqǔ]新[xīn]的[de]措施[cuòshī]。
examples.reading: Jiànyú mùqián de jīngjì xíngshì, zhèngfǔ juédìng cǎiqǔ xīn de cuòshī.
examples.translation_tr: In view of the current economic situation, the government has decided to adopt new measures.
examples.note_tr: 鉴于 introduces an observed situation/fact; the main clause states the resulting action.

examples.target: 鉴于[jiànyú]他[tā]多次[duōcì]迟到[chídào]，公司[gōngsī]对[duì]他[tā]提出[tíchū]了[le]警告[jǐnggào]。
examples.reading: Jiànyú tā duōcì chídào, gōngsī duì tā tíchūle jǐnggào.
examples.translation_tr: In view of his repeated lateness, the company issued him a warning.
examples.note_tr: The clause after 鉴于 describes a repeated behavior/problem, a typical use case.

examples.target: 鉴于[jiànyú]此[cǐ]，我们[wǒmen]决定[juédìng]推迟[tuīchí]会议[huìyì]。
examples.reading: Jiànyú cǐ, wǒmen juédìng tuīchí huìyì.
examples.translation_tr: In view of this, we have decided to postpone the meeting.
examples.note_tr: 鉴于此 ('in view of this') is a fixed formal transition referring back to previously mentioned facts.

examples.target: 基于[jīyú]以上[yǐshàng]原因[yuányīn]，我们[wǒmen]不能[bùnéng]批准[pīzhǔn]这个[zhège]申请[shēnqǐng]。
examples.reading: Jīyú yǐshàng yuányīn, wǒmen bùnéng pīzhǔn zhège shēnqǐng.
examples.translation_tr: Based on the above reasons, we cannot approve this application.
examples.note_tr: 基于以上原因 ('based on the above reasons') is a very common formal opener in official replies.

examples.target: 这个[zhège]理论[lǐlùn]是[shì]基于[jīyú]大量[dàliàng]的[de]实验[shíyàn]数据[shùjù]提出[tíchū]的[de]。
examples.reading: Zhège lǐlùn shì jīyú dàliàng de shíyàn shùjù tíchū de.
examples.translation_tr: This theory was proposed on the basis of a large amount of experimental data.
examples.note_tr: 基于 can also sit inside a 是...的 structure, unlike 鉴于, which is almost always sentence-initial.

examples.target: 我们[wǒmen]应该[yīnggāi]本着[běnzhe]实事求是[shíshìqiúshì]的[de]原则[yuánzé]处理[chǔlǐ]这[zhè]件[jiàn]事[shì]。
examples.reading: Wǒmen yīnggāi běnzhe shíshìqiúshì de yuánzé chǔlǐ zhè jiàn shì.
examples.translation_tr: We should handle this matter in the spirit of the principle of seeking truth from facts.
examples.note_tr: 本着 almost always pairs with an abstract noun like 原则/精神/态度, never with a concrete fact.

examples.target: 双方[shuāngfāng]本着[běnzhe]友好[yǒuhǎo]合作[hézuò]的[de]精神[jīngshén]签署[qiānshǔ]了[le]协议[xiéyì]。
examples.reading: Shuāngfāng běnzhe yǒuhǎo hézuò de jīngshén qiānshǔle xiéyì.
examples.translation_tr: Both parties signed the agreement in the spirit of friendly cooperation.
examples.note_tr: Typical diplomatic/business register: 本着...的精神 + main verb describing a formal action.

examples.target: 我们[wǒmen]是[shì]基于[jīyú]事实[shìshí]，而[ér]不是[búshì]本着[běnzhe]个人[gèrén]喜好[xǐhào]做出[zuòchū]这个[zhège]决定[juédìng]的[de]。
examples.reading: Wǒmen shì jīyú shìshí, ér búshì běnzhe gèrén xǐhào zuòchū zhège juédìng de.
examples.translation_tr: We made this decision based on facts, not guided by personal preference.
examples.note_tr: Contrasts 基于 (factual basis) with 本着 (guiding attitude) in one sentence to highlight the semantic difference.

qi-hechang-rhetorical.intro_tr: 岂[qǐ] and 何尝[hécháng] are advanced, strongly literary rhetorical-question markers used to assert the opposite of what is literally asked — no answer is expected, because the question itself IS the statement. 岂[qǐ] roughly means "how could it possibly be that..." and almost always sets up an implied negation ("there's no way that..."), while 何尝[hécháng] literally asks "when did it ever..." and is used to deny that something happened or, when paired with 不[bù]/没[méi], to strongly affirm that it did. Both belong to formal written Chinese (书面语[shūmiànyǔ]) — essays, speeches, classical-flavored idioms — and are rarely heard in casual spoken conversation, where 难道[nándào] or 怎么[zěnme] would be used instead. Mastering their fixed collocations (岂不, 岂非, 岂能, 岂敢, 岂止 / 何尝不) is essential, since these markers are almost always used in set patterns rather than freely.

tables.caption_tr: Core meaning and function of 岂[qǐ] and 何尝[hécháng]
rows: Sets up a question that literally cannot be true, forcing the listener to reject it
Strongly implies the negative of the clause that follows
Denies that an action/state ever occurred, OR (with 不/没) strongly affirms it
何尝 + V = 'never V'; 何尝不/没 + V = 'certainly did/does V'

tables.caption_tr: Fixed collocations built on 岂[qǐ]
rows: 岂不更好?[Qǐ bù gèng hǎo?] 'Wouldn't that be even better?'
More formal version of 岂不是, 'isn't it the case that...?'
岂非笑话?[Qǐ fēi xiàohua?] 'Isn't that a joke?'
Rejects the possibility of an action: 'how could one possibly...?'
岂能坐视不理?[Qǐ néng zuòshì bùlǐ?] 'How could one just sit back and do nothing?'
Rhetorical/modest refusal: 'how would I dare...'; also a stock polite reply
岂敢岂敢![Qǐ gǎn qǐ gǎn!] 'I wouldn't dare (accept such praise)!'
Rejects a lesser scope/degree, 'it's not just... (it's far more)'
岂止一次?[Qǐ zhǐ yí cì?] 'Not just once! (many times)'
Narrative marker: 'who would have expected that...' (introduces a surprising turn)
岂料半路杀出个程咬金。[Qǐliào bànlù shāchū ge Chéng Yǎojīn.] 'Who would have expected an unexpected obstacle to appear halfway through.'

tables.caption_tr: Patterns built on 何尝[hécháng]
rows: Rhetorically denies the action ever happened = 'never V'
他何尝来过?[Tā hécháng láiguo?] 'When did he ever come? (He never did.)'
Double negative → strong affirmative: 'of course V / how could (I) not V'
我何尝不知道?[Wǒ hécháng bù zhīdào?] 'Of course I know!'
他何尝没努力过?[Tā hécháng méi nǔlìguo?] 'He certainly did try hard!'
Rhetorically denies an identity/quality: 'when is it ever...?'
这何尝是办法?[Zhè hécháng shì bànfǎ?] 'How is this ever a solution? (It isn't.)'

tables.caption_tr: Comparing rhetorical question markers by formality and use
rows: 'how could it possibly be that...' → strong negation
Before the verb/modal (岂能, 岂敢, 岂不)
岂能如此?[Qǐ néng rúcǐ?] 'How can this be so?'
'when did it ever...' → denial, or strong affirmation with 不/没
Before the verb, often with 不/没
何尝不是呢?[Hécháng bú shì ne?] 'Isn't that exactly so?'
'don't tell me that...' → challenges an assumption
Start of clause, often paired with 吗/不成
难道你不知道吗?[Nándào nǐ bù zhīdào ma?] 'Don't tell me you don't know?'
我哪里知道?[Wǒ nǎli zhīdào?] 'How would I know?'
你怎么能这样?[Nǐ zěnme néng zhèyàng?] 'How can you be like this?'
footnotes_tr: 岂 and 何尝 are near-exclusive to written/formal registers; using them in casual speech sounds bookish or dramatic (which can be intentional for emphasis in essays or speeches).
In modern usage 岂 rarely appears alone as a bare question word — it is almost always locked into one of the collocations in the table above (岂不, 岂非, 岂能, 岂敢, 岂止, 岂料).

examples.target: 岂有此理!
examples.reading: Qǐ yǒu cǐ lǐ!
examples.translation_tr: How can there be such logic! (= That's outrageous! / Preposterous!)
examples.note_tr: Fixed idiomatic exclamation with 岂; literally 'how could there be this reasoning'.

examples.target: 他这样做,岂不是自寻烦恼吗?
examples.reading: Tā zhèyàng zuò, qǐ búshì zì xún fánnǎo ma?
examples.translation_tr: Isn't he just asking for trouble by doing this?
examples.note_tr: 岂不是...吗 combines 岂 with 不是...吗 for extra rhetorical force.

examples.target: 你岂能不知道这件事?
examples.reading: Nǐ qǐ néng bù zhīdào zhè jiàn shì?
examples.translation_tr: How could you possibly not know about this matter?
examples.note_tr: 岂能 + negative verb = strong rhetorical accusation that the negative is impossible.

examples.target: 我岂敢跟您争辩?
examples.reading: Wǒ qǐ gǎn gēn nín zhēngbiàn?
examples.translation_tr: How would I dare argue with you?
examples.note_tr: 岂敢 is also used alone as a humble/modest stock reply meaning 'I wouldn't dare (to accept such praise)'.

examples.target: 这个问题岂止复杂,简直无解。
examples.reading: Zhège wèntí qǐzhǐ fùzá, jiǎnzhí wújiě.
examples.translation_tr: This problem isn't just complicated — it's practically unsolvable.
examples.note_tr: 岂止 rejects a lesser description and points to something greater in degree or scope.

examples.target: 我何尝不想早点回家?
examples.reading: Wǒ hécháng bù xiǎng zǎodiǎn huí jiā?
examples.translation_tr: Of course I want to go home early! (How could I not want to?)
examples.note_tr: 何尝 + 不 + V is a double negative that produces a strong affirmative meaning.

examples.target: 他何尝说过这样的话?
examples.reading: Tā hécháng shuōguo zhèyàng de huà?
examples.translation_tr: When did he ever say such a thing? (= He never said that.)
examples.note_tr: 何尝 + V (no 不) rhetorically denies that the action ever happened.

examples.target: 成功何尝是偶然的?
examples.reading: Chénggōng hécháng shì ǒurán de?
examples.translation_tr: When is success ever accidental? (= Success is never accidental.)

double-negation.title_tr: Double Negation (不无 / 未尝不 / 无不)
double-negation.intro_tr: Double negation (双重否定[shuāngchóng fǒudìng]) combines two negative elements to produce a strong — but often deliberately softened or emphasized — positive statement. This is the Chinese equivalent of English litotes ("not uncommon" = "fairly common"). At the advanced level, three fixed literary patterns dominate: 不无[bùwú] ("not without" → "somewhat has"), 未尝不[wèichángbù] ("never not" → "cannot say it isn't, actually is"), and 无不[wúbù] ("none don't" → "all, without exception, do"). These patterns belong mainly to written or formal spoken registers (书面语) and each has its own grammar, collocation habits, and rhetorical flavor, so they must be learned as separate constructions rather than one single formula. Native speakers use them to sound measured, cautious, or emphatic rather than blunt — the double negative softens or intensifies the claim in ways a plain positive sentence cannot.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of the three core double-negation patterns
rows: concedes that something has a certain quality, but only to a modest/partial degree
cautiously affirms something the speaker was reluctant to state directly; softens a claim
"none [is it the case that they] don't"
emphasizes that ALL members of a group do something, with rhetorical force

tables.caption_tr: 不无[bùwú] + abstract noun: common fixed collocations
rows: has some merit / is not entirely wrong
is not unrelated (i.e., is related to some extent)
footnotes_tr: 不无[bùwú] almost always attaches to an ABSTRACT noun (reason, regret, risk, benefit, connection). It sounds odd with concrete nouns like 苹果[píngguǒ] 'apple'.

tables.caption_tr: 未尝不[wèichángbù]: structure and common set phrases
rows: cannot be said to be impermissible → is actually fine/acceptable
very common stand-alone reply meaning "that would work too"
cannot be said to be bad → is actually good
often used to reframe a suggestion positively
cannot be said not to be a good thing → could actually be a good thing
used to find a silver lining
cannot be said to be wrong → is actually right
cannot be said to be unsatisfying → is actually satisfying
footnotes_tr: 未尝不[wèichángbù] is often followed by 是[shì], 可[kě], 好[hǎo], or an adjective; the second 不[bù] negates that following word.
Do not confuse 未尝不[wèichángbù] with 未曾[wèicéng] 'have never (done)' — they look similar but mean very different things.

tables.caption_tr: 无不[wúbù]: structure and usage with collective subjects
rows: (they) were all, without exception, shocked by it
the audience, without exception, applauded and cheered
footnotes_tr: 无不[wúbù] requires a plural or collective subject (人人[rénrén], 大家[dàjiā], 观众[guānzhòng], 听众[tīngzhòng]); it sounds wrong with a single, individual subject.
无不[wúbù] is more emphatic and literary than simply using 都[dōu].

tables.caption_tr: Nuance comparison: double negation vs. the equivalent plain positive statement
rows: double negation = cautious, partial concession ("has SOME merit"); plain form = a flat, confident statement
double negation = reluctant or measured approval, implying earlier doubt; plain form = simple permission
double negation = rhetorically emphatic, literary flavor; plain form = neutral, everyday statement
double negation = a restrained, understated regret; plain form = a direct, stronger statement of regret

tables.caption_tr: Related productive idiom pattern: 无...不... (four-character idioms built on the same logic)
rows: there is no small detail not attended to
meticulous care in every small detail
there is no strangeness that doesn't exist
everything strange/unusual exists (there's nothing you won't find)
there is no crack (it) doesn't enter
to seize every possible opportunity/loophole (often negative)
footnotes_tr: These four-character idioms are not interchangeable with 不无/未尝不/无不 in a sentence, but they show how the same 'no X not Y' double-negative logic is productive across Chinese.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes to avoid
rows: 不无[bùwú] needs an ABSTRACT noun, not a concrete object
use 有[yǒu] instead: 有苹果[yǒu píngguǒ]
confusing 未尝不[wèichángbù] with 未曾[wèicéng]
未曾[wèicéng] means 'have never (done something)', an entirely different meaning (literary past negation)
keep them separate: 未尝不[wèichángbù] = cautious affirmation; 未曾[wèicéng] = 'never yet'
他无不感动 (tā wúbù gǎndòng) with a singular subject
无不[wúbù] requires a plural/collective subject to make sense of "none... don't"
use 大家无不感动[dàjiā wúbù gǎndòng] or simply 他很感动[tā hěn gǎndòng]
using 不无/未尝不/无不 in casual chat with friends
these patterns belong to formal, written, or argumentative registers
in casual speech prefer 挺...的[tǐng...de], 还是[háishi], or plain 都[dōu]

examples.target: 他的话不无道理。
examples.reading: Tā de huà bùwú dàolǐ.
examples.translation_tr: What he said is not without merit (it does have some truth to it).

examples.target: 这件事不无遗憾。
examples.reading: Zhè jiàn shì bùwú yíhàn.
examples.translation_tr: This matter is not without a touch of regret.

examples.target: 你说的未尝不对。
examples.reading: Nǐ shuō de wèicháng bú duì.
examples.translation_tr: What you said can't really be called wrong — it's actually correct.

examples.target: 这未尝不是一个好机会。
examples.reading: Zhè wèicháng búshì yí ge hǎo jīhuì.
examples.translation_tr: This could actually be considered a good opportunity, come to think of it.

examples.target: 听众无不为之感动。
examples.reading: Tīngzhòng wúbù wèi zhī gǎndòng.
examples.translation_tr: The audience were, every single one of them, moved by it.

examples.target: 大家无不称赞他的勇气。
examples.reading: Dàjiā wúbù chēngzàn tā de yǒngqì.
examples.translation_tr: Everyone, without exception, praised his courage.

examples.target: 这种做法不无风险。
examples.reading: Zhè zhǒng zuòfǎ bùwú fēngxiǎn.
examples.translation_tr: This approach is not without risk.

examples.target: 结果未尝不令人满意。
examples.reading: Jiéguǒ wèicháng bú lìng rén mǎnyì.
examples.translation_tr: The result can hardly be said to be unsatisfying — it's actually quite pleasing.

hebi-heku.title_tr: 何必 / 何苦 ("What's the need / Why bother")
hebi-heku.intro_tr: 何必[hébì] and 何苦[hékǔ] are rhetorical-question expressions used to argue that an action is unnecessary or not worth the trouble — they never expect a real answer. 何必 literally means "why must (one)" and questions the necessity of doing something, implying "there's really no need to." 何苦 literally means "why suffer" and goes a step further, implying the action brings needless hardship, pain, or trouble on the doer — closer to "why put yourself through this." Both are placed directly before the verb phrase they criticize and are very often closed with the softening particle 呢[ne]. Because the question is rhetorical, the real meaning is always the opposite of a literal answer: the speaker is telling the listener (or commenting on someone) that the action is pointless, excessive, or self-defeating.

tables.caption_tr: Core meaning: 何必 vs 何苦
rows: There is no need to do this
Neutral to mildly critical — questions necessity
Why put yourself through this trouble/pain — it isn't worth it
Sympathetic or exasperated — highlights self-inflicted hardship

tables.caption_tr: Sentence patterns
rows: 你何必生气呢[Nǐ hébì shēngqì ne]？
The most common and natural pattern; 呢 softens the tone
何必去问他[Hébì qù wèn tā]？
Slightly more abrupt, common in writing
你何苦这样呢[Nǐ hékǔ zhèyàng ne]？
Used alone as a short remark
Subject + 又 + 何必/何苦 + VP
你又何必骗我[Nǐ yòu hébì piàn wǒ]？
既然不爱，又何必在一起[Jìrán bú ài, yòu hébì zài yìqǐ]？

tables.caption_tr: 何必 / 何苦 compared with similar 'no need / not worth it' expressions
rows: 何苦为难自己[hékǔ wéinán zìjǐ]
No need to (plain statement, not a question)
犯不着为这点小事生气[fànbuzháo wèi zhè diǎn xiǎoshì shēngqì]

tables.caption_tr: Fixed expressions and set collocations
rows: "why did it have to be that way at the start" — a regret idiom often used alone
"Had I known it would come to this, why did I do it that way in the first place" — common proverb about regret
Colloquial (Northern/Beijing-flavored) way to say "why bother", used at the end of a complaint
"Why is this even necessary" — emphatic standalone remark, often said with a sigh

tables.caption_tr: Choosing between 何必 and 何苦: quick test
rows: Questioning if an action is simply unnecessary (no strong emotion)
Focuses purely on necessity, e.g. 何必解释[hébì jiěshì] ('no need to explain')
Focuses on self-inflicted suffering, e.g. 何苦熬夜[hékǔ áoyè] ('why stay up all night and suffer for it')
Formal idiom about past regret (何必当初)
何苦 does not appear in this fixed idiom
Either 何必呢 or 何苦呢
Both work; 何苦呢 sounds slightly more sympathetic/resigned

examples.target: 你何必生气呢？
examples.reading: Nǐ hébì shēngqì ne?
examples.translation_tr: Why do you need to get angry? (There's no need to be angry.)
examples.note_tr: Most common pattern: 何必 + VP + 呢, softens the rhetorical question.

examples.target: 他何必这么着急？
examples.reading: Tā hébì zhème zháojí?
examples.translation_tr: Why should he be in such a hurry? (No need to rush.)

examples.target: 你已经道歉了，他何必还不原谅你？
examples.reading: Nǐ yǐjīng dàoqiàn le, tā hébì hái bù yuánliàng nǐ?
examples.translation_tr: You've already apologized — why should he still refuse to forgive you?
examples.note_tr: Shows 何必 questioning the necessity/reasonableness of someone's continued behavior.

examples.target: 你何苦跟一个陌生人计较？
examples.reading: Nǐ hékǔ gēn yí ge mòshēngrén jìjiào?
examples.translation_tr: Why put yourself through the trouble of arguing with a stranger?
examples.note_tr: 何苦 stresses that the action causes unnecessary self-inflicted trouble.

examples.target: 既然不喜欢这份工作，又何必勉强自己做下去？
examples.reading: Jìrán bù xǐhuan zhè fèn gōngzuò, yòu hébì miǎnqiǎng zìjǐ zuò xiàqù?
examples.translation_tr: Since you don't like this job, why force yourself to keep doing it?
examples.note_tr: 既然...又何必... combo: 'since X is true, why bother with Y'.

examples.target: 早知今日，何必当初。
examples.reading: Zǎo zhī jīnrì, hébì dāngchū.
examples.translation_tr: If I'd known it would come to this, why did I do it that way in the first place?
examples.note_tr: Fixed idiom expressing regret; often stands alone as a proverb.

examples.target: 何必呢？大家都是朋友。

examples.translation_tr: What's the point? We're all friends, after all.

henbude-babude.title_tr: 恨不得 / 巴不得 ("Dying to..." Patterns)
henbude-babude.intro_tr: 恨不得[hènbude] and 巴不得[bābude] are two intense HSK6 expressions that both translate roughly as "to be dying to..." or "to wish desperately that...". Both sit directly in front of a verb phrase and describe a strong, urgent inner wish rather than a plain preference. 恨不得 often introduces exaggerated, hyperbolic, or even physically impossible actions, and it can carry a tone of frustration, anxiety, or desperation — the speaker "resents" that the wish isn't already reality. 巴不得 is purely positive and colloquial: it describes an eager, realistic wish for something the speaker would genuinely welcome, and is often used alone as an enthusiastic reply. Neither word ever takes 了/过/着 directly after it, and both must be followed by a verb phrase — never a bare noun.

tables.caption_tr: Core comparison: 恨不得 vs. 巴不得
rows: "hate/resent that (I) cannot..." — the wish isn't already true
to wish desperately (I) could...; to be dying to...
to be dying for...; to just wish that...; would love it if...
often exaggerated, hyperbolic, or physically impossible actions
urgency, desperation, or frustration — can be negative-tinged
Can express a wish for something negative (to hide, cry, disappear)
no — always something the speaker welcomes

tables.caption_tr: Sentence structure patterns
rows: 我恨不得马上见到你。[Wǒ hènbude mǎshàng jiàndào nǐ.]
I wish I could see you right away.
我巴不得马上见到你。[Wǒ bābude mǎshàng jiàndào nǐ.]
I'm dying to see you right away.
Subject1 + 恨不得/巴不得 + Subject2 + VP
妈妈恨不得我每天都打电话。[Māma hènbude wǒ měitiān dōu dǎ diànhuà.]
Mom wishes I'd call every single day.
巴不得 alone as a reply
你请客?巴不得呢![Nǐ qǐngkè? Bābude ne!]

tables.caption_tr: Grammar rules and restrictions
rows: Always followed by a verb phrase
Neither word can be followed directly by a bare noun; a verb (or verb phrase) must come after it.
恨不得马上走[hènbude mǎshàng zǒu] (correct); NOT 恨不得那件事
了, 过, 着 cannot attach to 恨不得/巴不得 themselves.
恨不得见到你 (correct); NOT 恨不得了见到你
The wishing subject and acting subject can differ
The person who is supposed to do the wished-for action can be someone other than the speaker.
老师恨不得学生都考100分。[Lǎoshī hènbude xuésheng dōu kǎo yìbǎi fēn.] — The teacher wishes all students would score 100.
恨不得 frequently combines with 马上/立刻/立即/一下子 to intensify the urgency of the wish.
恨不得立刻[hènbude lìkè] + VP — wish (I) could... immediately
These expressions are almost never negated with 不; the intensity is already built into the word itself.

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed collocations
rows: wish (I) could... all in one go
恨不得找个地缝钻进去[hènbude zhǎo ge dìfèng zuān jìnqù]
wish (I) could find a crack in the ground to hide in (extreme embarrassment)
巴不得你早说[bābude nǐ zǎo shuō]
wish you had said so earlier (would have loved that)
I'd love that! / That's exactly what I want! (used alone as an eager reply)

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with other 'want/wish' expressions
rows: simply 'want very much'; neutral and realistic
'really want to'; emphatic but plain, no hyperbole
'hope'; can be about others or the future, less urgent
urgent, often hyperbolic or impossible; may carry frustration
purely positive; wish for something realistic and welcome
footnotes_tr: 恨不得 and 巴不得 are both stronger and more colloquial/emotionally loaded than 很想, 真想, or 希望, which is why they belong to the HSK6 idiomatic-expression tier rather than basic vocabulary.

bukui-nanmian.title_tr: 不愧 / 难免 ('truly deserving of / unavoidable')
bukui-nanmian.intro_tr: 不愧[bùkuì] and 难免[nánmiǎn] are two common HSK6 written/formal expressions that are grouped together because both add an evaluative or logical "coloring" to a statement, though their meanings are opposite in flavor. 不愧[bùkuì] means "to truly deserve (a title/reputation), to live up to (the name of)" — it is used to praise someone or something as genuinely matching a positive label. 难免[nánmiǎn] means "hard to avoid, unavoidable, inevitably" — it is used to soften a negative statement by framing it as a natural, expected consequence rather than a fault. Both words are placed before the verb phrase they modify (they behave like adverbs), and both frequently combine with 是...的 or 会 to complete the sentence pattern. Mastering these two words lets you sound much more natural when complimenting achievements (不愧) or excusing minor mistakes/problems as normal (难免).

tables.caption_tr: Core meaning comparison: 不愧 vs 难免
rows: truly deserves to be called..., lives up to...
Complimenting a person's ability, quality, reputation, or achievement
Same as 不愧, but followed directly by a noun phrase, more literary
hard to avoid, inevitably, it's only natural that...
Explaining that a mistake, emotion, or problem is a normal, unavoidable result of circumstances
cannot help but..., inevitably (more literary variant of 难免)
Used similarly to 难免 but sounds more bookish; often in narrative writing

tables.caption_tr: 不愧[bùkuì] sentence patterns
rows: Subject + 不愧 + 是 + Noun Phrase
他不愧[bùkuì]是老师[shì lǎoshī] — He truly deserves to be called a teacher.
她不愧为[bùkuìwéi]冠军[guànjūn] — She is truly worthy of the champion title.
More formal/written; 为 replaces 是
他不愧[bùkuì]获得[huòdé]了[le]大奖[dàjiǎng] — He truly deserved winning the big prize.
Directly modifies a verb phrase, no 是 needed
真不愧是高手[zhēn bùkuì shì gāoshǒu]! — Truly a master, as expected!
Adding 真 intensifies admiration, very common in speech

tables.caption_tr: 难免[nánmiǎn] sentence patterns
rows: 他难免[nánmiǎn]紧张[jǐnzhāng] — He can't help feeling nervous.
难免 sits directly before the verb, like an adverb
难免会[nánmiǎn huì]犯错[fàn cuò] — It's inevitable to make mistakes.
会 adds a sense of likely future occurrence
Clause + 是[shì] + 难免的[nánmiǎn de]
犯错[fàn cuò]是难免的[shì nánmiǎn de] — Making mistakes is unavoidable.
Used to state a general truth/conclusion, often sentence-final
在[zài] + Condition + 下[xià], + 难免[nánmiǎn] + V
在压力下[zài yālì xià],难免[nánmiǎn]感到[gǎndào]焦虑[jiāolǜ] — Under pressure, feeling anxious is inevitable.
Sets up the cause/condition before stating the inevitable result

tables.caption_tr: Do not confuse: 难免 vs 未免 vs 不免
rows: 第一次难免会紧张[dì-yī cì nánmiǎn huì jǐnzhāng] — First time, nerves are inevitable.
Describes something unavoidable due to circumstances
你的要求未免太高了[nǐ de yāoqiú wèimiǎn tài gāo le] — Your demands are a bit too high.
Expresses that something goes slightly too far; NOT about avoidability
听到消息,他不免有些激动[tīngdào xiāoxi, tā bùmiǎn yǒuxiē jīdòng] — Hearing the news, he couldn't help feeling excited.
Very close to 难免 in meaning, but more literary/written in tone

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes and corrections
rows: Missing 是 or 为 before the noun
他不愧是老师[tā bùkuì shì lǎoshī]。
不愧 needs 是 or 为 before a plain noun phrase (unless a verb phrase directly follows)
难免会 cannot attach directly before 的
这是难免的[zhè shì nánmiǎn de]。
Use 难免 + 的 for the '...是难免的' pattern; 会 is dropped in this construction
是 wrongly inserted before an adjective/verb after 难免
他难免会紧张[tā nánmiǎn huì jǐnzhāng]。 / 他难免紧张[tā nánmiǎn jǐnzhāng]。
难免 attaches directly to the verb/adjective phrase or with 会, not with 是
confusing 难免 with 未免
Learners often mix up meaning ('unavoidable' vs 'rather too much')
Use 难免 for inevitability, 未免 for 'a bit too much'
See the dedicated comparison table above

wufei-buwaihu.title_tr: 无非 / 不外乎 ("nothing more than / amounts to no more than")
wufei-buwaihu.intro_tr: 无非[wúfēi] and 不外乎[búwàihū] are HSK6 expressions meaning "nothing more than," "is simply," or "amounts to no more than" — they tell the listener that something is limited to a small, unsurprising range of possibilities rather than being complicated or hidden. 无非 usually precedes a single reason, motive, or short clause (often 是[shì] + noun phrase) and frequently ends with 罢了[bàle] or 而已[éryǐ] to add a dismissive, reassuring "that's all" tone. 不外乎 usually introduces a short enumerated list of two or more items or categories, implying nothing exists outside that list — it appears more often in written analysis, essays, and formal speech when summarizing causes, topics, or types. Both expressions let the speaker downplay complexity: essentially saying "it's exactly what you'd expect, nothing extra or surprising." Neither is used for a neutral, purely factual statement — they always carry this evaluative, summarizing flavor.

tables.caption_tr: Core sentence patterns with 无非 and 不外乎
rows: Subject + 无非[wúfēi] + VP / 是 + NP + (罢了[bàle]/而已[éryǐ])
"is nothing more than..., that's all" — adds a dismissive or reassuring tone
他无非是想引起注意罢了。[Tā wúfēi shì xiǎng yǐnqǐ zhùyì bàle.]
States the (limited) full content of what's being discussed
他要的无非是一句道歉。[Tā yào de wúfēi shì yí jù dàoqiàn.]
原因不外乎两个。[Yuányīn búwàihū liǎng ge.]
Slightly more formal way of stating the exhaustive list
内容不外乎是介绍、分析和总结。[Nèiróng búwàihū shì jièshào, fēnxī hé zǒngjié.]

tables.caption_tr: 无非 vs 不外乎 at a glance
rows: 无 (not) + 非 (other than) → "not other than"
不 (not) + 外 (outside) + 乎 (than) → "not outside of / beyond"
A single reason, motive, or short clause
A list of two or more items or categories
Often paired with 罢了[bàle] / 而已[éryǐ] ("that's all")
Rarely takes 罢了; sometimes ends with 等[děng]/等等[děngděng] ("etc.")
Slightly colloquial-literary; common in both speech and writing
Slightly more formal/written; common in essays, reports, analysis
Can sound dismissive, reassuring, or mildly critical
Yes: 不外乎是... (是 is optional)

tables.caption_tr: Common collocations and fixed patterns
rows: 他无非是开玩笑罢了。[Tā wúfēi shì kāi wánxiào bàle.]
Same as above, slightly more literary
这无非是一种巧合而已。[Zhè wúfēi shì yì zhǒng qiǎohé éryǐ.]
"amounts to no more than a few kinds of..."
常见的错误不外乎这几种。[Chángjiàn de cuòwù búwàihū zhè jǐ zhǒng.]
话题不外乎工作、家庭等。[Huàtí búwàihū gōngzuò, jiātíng děng.]
问题无非就是钱不够。[Wèntí wúfēi jiùshì qián bú gòu.]

tables.caption_tr: 无非 / 不外乎 vs similar limiting expressions
column_headers: Key difference from 无非/不外乎
rows: A neutral, everyday limiter; no built-in sense that this is the whole, closed set of possibilities
Softens a statement or downplays its importance; does not imply exhaustiveness of options
Pure identification/emphasis; lacks the "nothing beyond this" evaluative flavor
Judges the matter as unsurprising, usually limited to one obvious reason or motive
Implies an exhaustive, limited list of 2+ categories; common when summarizing causes or types

shibi-weimian.title_tr: 势必 / 未免 ("bound to inevitably / rather too much")
shibi-weimian.intro_tr: 势必[shìbì] and 未免[wèimiǎn] are two formal HSK6 adverbs that look similar but point in opposite directions. 势必[shìbì] means "is bound to / will inevitably," and it announces that a certain result cannot be avoided given the current situation — it points forward to a consequence. 未免[wèimiǎn] means "rather too / a bit too much," and it is used to softly criticize something that has already happened or been said, suggesting it goes a little overboard. Both sit directly before a verb phrase or adjective and belong to written/formal style (书面语), so they show up often in essays, news, and debate-style speech. Because 未免[wèimiǎn] sounds like its cousins 不免[bùmiǎn] and 难免[nánmiǎn] (both meaning "unavoidable"), mixing them up is a very common learner error — this page separates all three clearly.

tables.caption_tr: 势必 vs 未免 at a Glance
rows: "is bound to, will inevitably" — states an unavoidable future consequence
"rather too, a bit too much" — softens a criticism of something already true
未免 + Adjective/Verb Phrase (often + 了/有点儿)

tables.caption_tr: 势必 (shìbì): Expressing an Inevitable Consequence
rows: Doing this will inevitably affect [one's] health.
如果你不注意,势必会出问题。
If you're not careful, problems are bound to occur.
物价上涨,消费势必会下降。
As prices rise, consumption is bound to fall.
势必导致/造成/引起 + Noun
污染势必导致环境恶化。
Pollution will inevitably lead to environmental deterioration.

tables.caption_tr: 未免 (wèimiǎn): Softening a Criticism — "A Bit Too..."
rows: 未免 + Adj (+ 了点儿/了些)
This price is rather too expensive.
His demands are rather too high.
这个决定未免有些草率。
This decision is a bit too hasty.
你这样说未免有点儿武断。
Saying it like that is rather too arbitrary [of you].

tables.caption_tr: Fixed Collocations with 势必
rows: adds modal emphasis to the inevitability
这项政策势必会引起争议。 — This policy is bound to cause controversy.
frames the consequence as a necessary action
公司势必要进行改革。 — The company will inevitably have to reform.
过度开发势必导致资源枯竭。 — Overdevelopment will inevitably lead to resource depletion.
忽视教育势必造成人才短缺。 — Neglecting education will inevitably cause a talent shortage.
这一决定势必引起不满。 — This decision is bound to provoke dissatisfaction.

tables.caption_tr: Don't Confuse: 未免 vs 不免 vs 难免
rows: "rather too much" — a mild criticism of something excessive
这未免太夸张了。 — That's rather too exaggerated.
"inevitably, cannot help but" — a natural emotional/behavioral reaction occurs
第一次演讲,他不免有点紧张。 — Giving his first speech, he couldn't help but feel a bit nervous.
"hard to avoid, unavoidable" — often used as a predicate with 是...的
犯错误是难免的。 — Making mistakes is unavoidable.
footnotes_tr: Memory tip: 势必[shìbì] looks forward to a future result ("X will surely happen"); 未免[wèimiǎn] looks back at something already said/done and judges it as excessive ("that's a bit much"). 不免[bùmiǎn]/难免[nánmiǎn] are about unavoidable reactions or events, not criticism.

examples.target: 如果继续这样浪费资源,势必会引发严重的环境问题。

examples.target: 只用一次考试成绩来评价学生,未免太片面了。

examples.target: 人口老龄化势必给社会保障体系带来压力。

chengyu-patterns.intro_tr: Chéngyǔ [chéngyǔ] (成语) are fixed, mostly four-character idiomatic expressions drawn from classical Chinese literature, history, fables, and philosophy. Their meaning is almost always figurative and cannot be guessed from the individual characters, so each chengyu must be memorized as a whole unit together with its story and emotional connotation (positive, negative, or neutral). Grammatically, a chengyu is not a separate word class — it simply steps into the slot of a verb, adjective, adverb, noun, or object inside a normal Mandarin sentence, and combines with ordinary particles like 得, 地, 的 just like any other word, though its own four syllables usually cannot be split or internally modified. Because chengyu belong to the formal written register (书面语[shūmiànyǔ]), they are indispensable for HSK6 reading, writing, and sounding educated, but using the wrong one — or using one in casual speech — can sound unnatural or even reverse the intended meaning.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes When Using Chengyu
rows: Adding 很/非常 before a chengyu that already expresses a complete state
Most subject-predicate or verb-object chengyu are not simple gradable adjectives, so degree adverbs sound redundant or ungrammatical (e.g. *很一目了然)
Use the chengyu alone, or check a dictionary for whether it accepts degree adverbs at all
Inserting 了/的/地 inside the four syllables
Chengyu are fixed strings; splitting them breaks the idiom
Attach particles only at the boundary: 不假思索地 (correct), not 不假*思索的索
Many chengyu that seem similar in meaning differ sharply in emotional tone, e.g. 处心积虑[chǔxīnjīlǐ] (negative scheming) vs 殚精竭虑[dānjīngjiélǜ] (positive dedication)
Always check the connotation label in a dictionary before using a new chengyu
Figurative meaning is often unrelated to the literal images, e.g. 守株待兔 is not about farming
Learn the origin story/allusion together with the meaning, not just the characters
Overusing chengyu in casual spoken conversation
Chengyu belong to the formal written register (书面语); heavy use in daily chat can sound stiff or pretentious
Reserve dense chengyu use for essays, speeches, news, and formal writing; use plain words in casual talk

literary-negation.title_tr: Literary Negation (未, 无, 非, 勿)
literary-negation.intro_tr: Classical Chinese negation words — 未[wèi], 无[wú], 非[fēi], and 勿[wù] — survive in modern Mandarin mainly in written language, formal signs, idioms, and set four-character phrases, even though everyday speech uses 没/没有, 不是, and 别/不要 instead. Each one has a specific job: 未 negates completed verbs ('not yet'), 无 negates 有 ('there is not / without'), 非 negates the copula 是 ('is not'), and 勿 negates imperative verbs ('don't'). Recognizing these characters is essential for reading news articles, official notices, proverbs, and HSK6-level texts, and for producing more formal or literary-sounding Chinese. This page maps each literary negator to its everyday equivalent and lists the fixed patterns and idioms you will actually encounter.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of the Four Literary Negators
rows: written language, set phrases, news, history

tables.caption_tr: 未 [wèi]: 'Not Yet' — Patterns and Set Phrases
rows: 尚未解决 [shàngwèi jiějué] = not yet resolved
从未见过 [cóngwèi jiànguò] = have never seen
未曾谋面 [wèicéng móumiàn] = never yet met in person
未必对 [wèibì duì] = not necessarily correct
未免太贵 [wèimiǎn tài guì] = rather too expensive
前所未有的变化 [qiánsuǒwèiyǒu de biànhuà]

tables.caption_tr: 无 [wú]: 'Without / There Is Not' — Patterns and Set Phrases
rows: 无家可归 [wú jiā kě guī] = homeless
unable to V, no way to V
无法解释 [wúfǎ jiěshì] = unable to explain
无论多难都要做 [wúlùn duō nán dōu yào zuò]
无非是钱的问题 [wúfēi shì qián de wèntí]
怎么样都无所谓 [zěnmeyàng dōu wúsuǒwèi]
to have no choice, be helpless (idiom)

tables.caption_tr: 非 [fēi]: 'Is Not' — Patterns and Set Phrases
rows: is by no means, is not actually
并非如此 [bìngfēi rúcǐ] = it is not actually so
除非你去，我才去 [chúfēi nǐ qù, wǒ cái qù]
非去不可 [fēi qù bùkě] = absolutely must go
莫非他忘了 [mòfēi tā wàngle] = could it be he forgot?
right and wrong; a dispute (used as a noun)
惹是非 [rě shìfēi] = to stir up trouble

tables.caption_tr: 勿 [wù]: 'Don't' — Imperative Negation
rows: 请勿吸烟 [qǐngwù xīyān] = No smoking
must not, on no account V
切勿模仿 [qièwù mófǎng] = do not imitate, whatever you do
万勿轻信 [wànwù qīngxìn] = never believe rashly
己所不欲，勿施于人 [jǐ suǒ bú yù, wù shī yú rén]

tables.caption_tr: Literary Negators vs. Everyday Equivalents
rows: 非我所愿 [fēi wǒ suǒ yuàn]
不是我想要的 [búshì wǒ xiǎng yào de]

tables.caption_tr: Common Pitfalls
rows: 未 already carries negation; stacking 没 in front is redundant and wrong
未婚 [wèihūn] or 还没结婚 [hái méi jiéhūn]
无 sounds overly literary in daily conversation; 没有 is the natural choice
Treating 非 like plain 不
非 negates nouns/the copula 是 or appears in fixed patterns like 非...不可; it does not freely negate ordinary verbs the way 不 does
非...不可 [fēi...bùkě] = must; 不去 [bú qù] = not going
勿 belongs to formal signs, warnings, and classical text, not casual conversation
*勿吃 (in a text message to a friend)
别吃 [bié chī] / 不要吃 [búyào chī]
footnotes_tr: These four negators rarely combine directly with aspect particles like 了 or 过; instead they attach straight to the verb or noun they negate.
In modern writing, 未, 无, 非, and 勿 are chosen deliberately for a formal, concise, or literary tone — using them correctly is a strong marker of advanced written Chinese.

qi-zhe-literary.title_tr: Literary Pronouns and Particles (其, 者, 也, 矣)
qi-zhe-literary.intro_tr: 其[qí], 者[zhě], 也[yě], and 矣[yǐ] are four core building blocks of Classical Chinese (文言文[wényánwén]) that still surface constantly in modern formal writing, proverbs, idioms (成语[chéngyǔ]), and elevated speech. 其[qí] works as a third-person possessive/demonstrative pronoun ("his/her/its/their/that"), 者[zhě] nominalizes a verb or adjective into "the one who / that which," 也[yě] is a sentence-final particle marking a formal judgment or definition (completely different from the modern adverb 也 "also"), and 矣[yǐ] is a sentence-final particle marking completed action or a newly arisen state, playing a role close to modern 了[le]. At HSK6 you are not expected to produce new classical sentences with these, but recognizing them is essential for reading idioms, quotations, essay titles, and formal/literary registers. Many everyday modern words (尤其, 其实, 学者, 或者, 再者) are frozen fossils of these classical particles.

tables.caption_tr: Overview — The Four Particles at a Glance
rows: Nominalizer: turns V/Adj into 'the one(s) who / that which'
Sentence-final particle marking a judgment or definition: 'is indeed'
Modal particle (classical; NOT the modern adverb 也 'also')
Sentence-final particle marking completion or a new state

tables.caption_tr: 其 (qí) — Detailed Usage
rows: 其言不虚[qí yán bù xū]
原因有二:其一...其二...[yuányīn yǒu èr: qí yī... qí èr...]

其实我不知道[qíshí wǒ bù zhīdào]

Nominalize an adjective → 'one who is X'

记者[jìzhě], 作者[zuòzhě], 患者[huànzhě]
再者,这也不便宜[zàizhě, zhè yě bù piányi]

tables.caption_tr: 也 (yě) — Sentence-Final Particle of Judgment
rows: 此乃吾家也[cǐ nǎi wú jiā yě]
仁者,爱人也[rén zhě, ài rén yě]
不学者,无以成才也[bù xué zhě, wú yǐ chéng cái yě]

classical 也 always stands at the very end of the sentence, never before the verb

tables.caption_tr: 矣 (yǐ) — Sentence-Final Particle of Completion/Change

矣 corresponds to modern 了[le]
矣 is simply the literary-register version of 了

it's too late to regret it now
rén zhě jiàn rén, zhì zhě jiàn zhì

yi-wei-literary.intro_tr: 以...为... (yǐ...wéi...) is a classical/literary structure meaning "to take X as Y" or "to regard X as Y." It comes from Classical Chinese but survives heavily in Modern Standard Chinese formal writing, news reports, slogans, academic prose, and set four-character-style collocations (以...为主, 以...为例, 以...为荣, etc.). Here 以 functions as a preposition meaning "with, by means of, using," while 为 acts as a literary verb meaning "to be, to serve as, to count as." The whole frame lets a writer assign a role, status, standard, or value to something in one compact, elegant clause instead of using a full verb like 当作 or 看作. Because it belongs to 书面语 (written register), it sounds stiff or unnatural in casual spoken conversation, where 把...当作/看作 is preferred instead.

tables.caption_tr: Core structure of 以...为...
rows: preposition introducing the item being evaluated/used
the thing that receives a role or status
literary verb linking X to its assigned role
to be / to serve as / to count as
the role, standard, or value assigned to X

tables.caption_tr: Overall pattern and basic meaning
rows: 以他为榜样[yǐ tā wéi bǎngyàng] — 'take him as a role model'
S + 以 X 为 Y (+ verb)
the whole phrase can act as an adverbial modifying the main verb
这本书以历史为背景写成。[Zhè běn shū yǐ lìshǐ wéi bèijǐng xiěchéng.] — 'This book was written with history as its backdrop.'

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed collocations with 以...为...
rows: 工作以质量为主。[Gōngzuò yǐ zhìliàng wéi zhǔ.] — 'Work prioritizes quality.'
一切以合同为准。[Yíqiè yǐ hétong wéi zhǔn.] — 'Everything is subject to the contract.'
他以自己的祖国为荣。[Tā yǐ zìjǐ de zǔguó wéi róng.] — 'He is proud of his homeland.'
以撒谎为耻。[Yǐ sāhuǎng wéi chǐ.] — 'To regard lying as shameful.'
以中国为例。[Yǐ Zhōngguó wéi lì.] — 'Take China as an example.'
以事实为基础。[Yǐ shìshí wéi jīchǔ.] — 'Based on facts.'
以学生为中心。[Yǐ xuésheng wéi zhōngxīn.] — 'Student-centered.'
以赚钱为目的。[Yǐ zhuànqián wéi mùdì.] — 'With making money as the goal.'
以战争为背景。[Yǐ zhànzhēng wéi bèijǐng.] — 'Set against the backdrop of war.'
以人为本。[Yǐ rén wéi běn.] — 'People-oriented / put people first.'

tables.caption_tr: 以...为... versus similar 'regard as / treat as' structures
rows: Cannot naturally stand as the main predicate of a casual spoken sentence by itself; often works as a modifier before another verb.
Most common everyday equivalent; uses 把 to front the object.
Slightly more literary than 当作 but far more common in speech than 以...为...
Near-synonym of 以...为...; both belong to 书面语 and often appear in the same texts.
Simple identity statement; no nuance of 'assigning a role/value', which 以...为... always carries.

tables.caption_tr: Common learner mistakes
rows: 为 is missing — 以 alone cannot link X directly to Y
以学习为主。[Yǐ xuéxí wéi zhǔ.]
Using 以...为... in casual chat: *我以他为朋友。
Sounds overly formal/stiff for spoken register
把他当作朋友。[Bǎ tā dàngzuò péngyou.] — 'I treat him as a friend.'
以 here means 'taking/using', not 'because'; unrelated to the causal conjunction 因为...所以...
Keep 以...为... strictly to the 'regard as / take as' meaning.
Dropping 为 and using another verb: *以他当作榜样
为 is the fixed verb slot in this classical pattern; mixing it with 当作 is incorrect
以他为榜样。[Yǐ tā wéi bǎngyàng.] OR 把他当作榜样。[Bǎ tā dàngzuò bǎngyàng.]
Treating 为 [wéi] here as 为 [wèi] 'for'
为 has two readings: wéi ('to be/serve as', used here) and wèi ('for the sake of', as in 为了[wèile])
Pronounce as wéi in this pattern: 以...为...[yǐ...wéi...]

examples.target: 我们要以学习为主。
examples.reading: Wǒmen yào yǐ xuéxí wéi zhǔ.
examples.translation_tr: We should treat studying as the top priority.
examples.note_tr: 以...为主 = 'with ... as the main thing' — a very common fixed pattern.

examples.target: 他以诚实为荣。
examples.reading: Tā yǐ chéngshí wéi róng.
examples.translation_tr: He regards honesty as an honor.
examples.note_tr: 以...为荣 = 'to regard ... as a source of pride/honor'.

examples.target: 这家公司以质量为生命。
examples.reading: Zhè jiā gōngsī yǐ zhìliàng wéi shēngmìng.
examples.translation_tr: This company treats quality as its lifeblood.
examples.note_tr: A more vivid, metaphorical use of the pattern: X = 'life itself'.

examples.target: 请以第三课为例。
examples.reading: Qǐng yǐ dì-sān kè wéi lì.
examples.translation_tr: Please take Lesson 3 as an example.
examples.note_tr: 以...为例 is extremely common in textbooks, reports, and lectures.

examples.target: 这部电影以真实故事为背景。
examples.reading: Zhè bù diànyǐng yǐ zhēnshí gùshi wéi bèijǐng.
examples.translation_tr: This film is set against (takes as its background) a true story.
examples.note_tr: 以...为背景 = 'with ... as the backdrop/setting'.

examples.target: 我们应该以他为榜样。
examples.reading: Wǒmen yīnggāi yǐ tā wéi bǎngyàng.
examples.translation_tr: We should take him as a role model.
examples.note_tr: Very common in moral or motivational speech.

examples.target: 中国古代社会以农业为本。
examples.reading: Zhōngguó gǔdài shèhuì yǐ nóngyè wéi běn.
examples.translation_tr: Ancient Chinese society regarded agriculture as its foundation.
examples.note_tr: 以...为本 = 'take ... as the root/foundation', found often in classical and formal texts.

examples.target: 他以浪费时间为耻。
examples.reading: Tā yǐ làngfèi shíjiān wéi chǐ.
examples.translation_tr: He regards wasting time as shameful.
examples.note_tr: 以...为耻 is the direct opposite of 以...为荣; both often appear together in moral discourse.

cengjing-weiceng.title_tr: 曾经 / 未曾 / 不曾 (Literary Past Experience)
cengjing-weiceng.intro_tr: 曾经[céngjīng], 未曾[wèicéng], and 不曾[bùcéng] are formal, mostly written-style (书面语[shūmiànyǔ]) words used to talk about past experience in Chinese — think of them as elevated equivalents of English 'once' and 'have never.' 曾经[céngjīng] goes right before the verb to say that something happened at some point in the past, and it very often teams up with the aspect particle 过[guo] on the verb for extra clarity. 未曾[wèicéng] and 不曾[bùcéng] are its negative counterparts, both meaning 'have never,' and both are simply more formal, literary alternatives to the everyday spoken pattern 没有...过[méiyǒu...guo]. You will meet all three constantly in essays, news reports, novels, and speeches, but rarely in casual daily chat. None of the three can describe the future or a hypothetical — they only ever describe real, completed past experience (or the total absence of it).

tables.caption_tr: Core Forms at a Glance
rows: Affirmative: marks that something happened at some point in the past (an experience)
Formal-leaning, but also common in neutral spoken/written Chinese
Negative: 'have never' — formal equivalent of 没有...过
Negative: 'have never, did not ever' — formal equivalent of 没(有)...过
Aspect particle: marks that a verb's action was experienced at least once
Neutral, used freely in both speech and writing

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Pattern Templates
rows: 我曾经去过法国。[Wǒ céngjīng qùguo Fǎguó.]
I have been to France before (at some point in the past).
我未曾去过法国。[Wǒ wèicéng qùguo Fǎguó.]
I have never been to France.
我不曾去过法国。[Wǒ bùcéng qùguo Fǎguó.]
I have never been to France.
S + 从未/从不曾 + V + 过 + O
我从未去过法国。[Wǒ cóngwèi qùguo Fǎguó.]
I have never once been to France.

tables.caption_tr: 未曾 vs 不曾 vs 没有...过 — Choosing the Right Negative
rows: Slight 'not yet, up to now' flavor — leaves open the idea that it could still happen later
他未曾说过这样的话。[Tā wèicéng shuōguo zhèyàng de huà.] — He has never (so far) said such a thing.
Plain, neutral negation of a past experience; no strong 'not yet' implication
他不曾说过这样的话。[Tā bùcéng shuōguo zhèyàng de huà.] — He never said such a thing.
The standard, default way to negate experience in daily conversation
他没有说过这样的话。[Tā méiyǒu shuōguo zhèyàng de huà.] — He has never said such a thing.
footnotes_tr: In real usage 未曾 and 不曾 are largely interchangeable; the difference is subtle and mainly a matter of literary style, not strict rule.

tables.caption_tr: 曾经 vs 已经 vs 过 — Don't Confuse These
rows: Adverb before the verb; the situation it describes often no longer holds true now
我曾经很胖,现在瘦了。[Wǒ céngjīng hěn pàng, xiànzài shòu le.] — I used to be fat; now I'm thin.
Adverb before the verb; the result of the action usually still holds true now
我已经吃饭了。[Wǒ yǐjīng chīfàn le.] — I have already eaten.
Attached directly after the verb (not before); often paired with 曾经 for emphasis
我吃过中国菜。[Wǒ chīguo Zhōngguó cài.] — I have eaten Chinese food before.

tables.caption_tr: Common Literary Collocations
rows: 'never' (formal, equivalent to 从来没有[cónglái méiyǒu])
idiom: 'it was not long ago that...' (used when lamenting how things have changed)
idiom: 'having seen the vast ocean' — having experienced the greatest, lesser things no longer impress

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: 曾经 is an affirmative-only marker; it cannot be directly negated by placing 没有 in front of it
未曾去过[wèicéng qùguo] / 不曾去过[bùcéng qùguo] / 从未去过[cóngwèi qùguo]
You cannot insert 不 between 曾经 and the verb — 曾经 has no built-in negative form of its own
不曾去过[bùcéng qùguo] (a single fused formal negative)
未曾/不曾 only negate something that did or didn't happen in the PAST — never the future or a possibility
他不会去。[Tā bú huì qù.] — He won't go.

examples.target: 我曾经在北京住过三年。
examples.reading: Wǒ céngjīng zài Běijīng zhùguo sān nián.
examples.translation_tr: I once lived in Beijing for three years.
examples.note_tr: 曾经[céngjīng] pairs naturally with 过[guo] on the verb — this double-marking is very common and simply reinforces the 'past experience' meaning.

examples.target: 他曾经是一名医生,后来当了老师。
examples.reading: Tā céngjīng shì yì míng yīshēng, hòulái dāngle lǎoshī.
examples.translation_tr: He used to be a doctor, and later became a teacher.

examples.target: 我未曾见过如此美丽的风景。
examples.reading: Wǒ wèicéng jiànguo rúcǐ měilì de fēngjǐng.
examples.translation_tr: I have never seen such beautiful scenery.

examples.target: 她不曾放弃自己的梦想。
examples.reading: Tā bùcéng fàngqì zìjǐ de mèngxiǎng.
examples.translation_tr: She has never given up on her own dream.

examples.target: 这个问题我们曾经讨论过好几次。
examples.reading: Zhège wèntí wǒmen céngjīng tǎolùnguo hǎojǐ cì.
examples.translation_tr: We have discussed this problem several times before.

examples.target: 这样荒唐的事,我从未曾听说过。
examples.reading: Zhèyàng huāngtáng de shì, wǒ cóng wèicéng tīngshuōguo.
examples.translation_tr: I had never once heard of such an absurd thing.
examples.note_tr: 从未曾[cóng wèicéng] stacks 从[cóng] + 未曾[wèicéng] for extra emphasis — a very bookish, high-register combination.

examples.target: 曾经沧海难为水。
examples.reading: Céngjīng cānghǎi nán wéi shuǐ.
examples.translation_tr: Once you have seen the vast ocean, mere water no longer impresses you.
examples.note_tr: A classical idiom: after experiencing the very best, lesser things fail to satisfy — often quoted in literary or emotional contexts.

examples.target: 他不曾对任何人提起过这件事。
examples.reading: Tā bùcéng duì rènhé rén tíqǐguo zhè jiàn shì.
examples.translation_tr: He has never mentioned this matter to anyone.

zhiji-zhiyu.title_tr: 之际 / 之余 ("at the juncture of... / besides...")
zhiji-zhiyu.intro_tr: 之际 [zhī jì] and 之余 [zhī yú] are formal, literary (书面语[shūmiànyǔ]) structures built on the classical particle 之[zhī], which here functions like 的[de] but only in a very formal register — so 之 and 的 are never used together in these patterns. 之际[zhī jì] attaches after a noun or verb phrase to mean "at the moment/juncture of...", and is used to mark a significant, often ceremonial or historic occasion — think speeches, news broadcasts, official announcements, and greeting cards. 之余[zhī yú] attaches after a noun, adjective, or verb phrase to mean "besides.../in the time left over from...", describing something done in addition to, or during a break from, a main activity or emotional state. Both structures almost never appear in casual spoken Chinese; using them signals formal or written style, and both are frequently tested at HSK6 level.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Patterns: [Noun/Adj/VP] + 之际 / 之余
rows: 新年之际[xīnnián zhī jì] — at the occasion of the New Year
离开之际[líkāi zhī jì] — at the moment of leaving
besides N / in the time left over from N
工作之余[gōngzuò zhī yú] — besides work
besides being Adj / while also being Adj
高兴之余[gāoxìng zhī yú] — besides being happy
besides V-ing / in addition to V-ing
学习之余[xuéxí zhī yú] — besides studying

tables.caption_tr: 之际 vs 之余: Core Differences
rows: at the (critical/significant) moment or juncture of...
besides... / in the time left over from...
a specific, often historic or important point in time
an additional action or feeling that accompanies a main one
a wish, request, call to action, or description tied to that moment
新年[xīnnián], 毕业[bìyè], 周年[zhōunián], 离别[líbié], 即将[jíjiāng]
工作[gōngzuò], 忙碌[mánglù], 高兴[gāoxìng], 惊讶[jīngyà], 学习[xuéxí]
Can stand alone as full sentence?
no — needs a main clause after it
no — needs a main clause after it

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used Fixed Expressions
rows: at the occasion of the New Year
at the juncture of about to...

tables.caption_tr: 之际 / 之余 Compared to Similar Structures
rows: 吃饭的时候[chīfàn de shíhou] — when eating
毕业之际[bìyè zhī jì] — at the time of graduation
工作以外[gōngzuò yǐwài] — besides work
工作之余[gōngzuò zhī yú] — besides work
毕业之后[bìyè zhī hòu] — after graduation

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: 的[de] and 之[zhī] both used — redundant, since 之 already replaces 的
之际 used for a trivial, non-significant moment — too formal/unnatural here
工作之余。(as a full sentence)
之余 phrase cannot stand alone; it must be followed by a main clause
工作之余,他还学画画。[Gōngzuò zhī yú, tā hái xué huàhuà.]
的[de] incorrectly inserted before 之余
footnotes_tr: Both 之际 and 之余 belong to 书面语[shūmiànyǔ] (written/literary style) and are rarely, if ever, used in casual spoken conversation.

examples.target: 在这辞旧迎新之际,祝大家新年快乐!
examples.reading: Zài zhè cíjiù-yíngxīn zhī jì, zhù dàjiā xīnnián kuàilè!
examples.translation_tr: At this moment of bidding farewell to the old year and welcoming the new, I wish everyone a happy New Year!

examples.target: 毕业之际,同学们都依依不舍。
examples.reading: Bìyè zhī jì, tóngxuémen dōu yīyī-bùshě.
examples.translation_tr: At the time of graduation, the classmates were all reluctant to part.

examples.target: 在这个关键之际,我们更应该团结一致。
examples.reading: Zài zhège guānjiàn zhī jì, wǒmen gèng yīnggāi tuánjié yīzhì.
examples.translation_tr: At this critical juncture, we should unite even more.

examples.target: 他工作之余喜欢画画儿。
examples.reading: Tā gōngzuò zhī yú xǐhuan huà huàr.
examples.translation_tr: Besides his work, he likes to paint.

examples.target: 忙碌之余,别忘了照顾好自己。
examples.reading: Mánglù zhī yú, bié wàngle zhàogù hǎo zìjǐ.
examples.translation_tr: Amid all the busyness, don't forget to take good care of yourself.

examples.target: 惊讶之余,她也感到十分高兴。
examples.reading: Jīngyà zhī yú, tā yě gǎndào shífēn gāoxìng.
examples.translation_tr: Besides being surprised, she also felt very happy.

examples.target: 在两国建交五十周年之际,双方举行了隆重的庆祝活动。
examples.reading: Zài liǎng guó jiànjiāo wǔshí zhōunián zhī jì, shuāngfāng jǔxíngle lóngzhòng de qìngzhù huódòng.
examples.translation_tr: On the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the two countries' diplomatic relations, both sides held a grand celebration.

examples.target: 学习之余,我常常去公园散步。
examples.reading: Xuéxí zhī yú, wǒ chángcháng qù gōngyuán sànbù.
examples.translation_tr: In the time apart from studying, I often go for a walk in the park.

liushuiju-topic-chains.title_tr: Flowing Sentences (流水句[liúshuǐjù]) and Topic Chains
liushuiju-topic-chains.intro_tr: 流水句[liúshuǐjù], literally "flowing-water sentence," is the classic Chinese way of stringing several clauses together with commas instead of English-style conjunctions, relative pronouns, or subordinating connectors. Rather than building a hierarchical tree (main clause + dependent clauses) like English does, Chinese lines clauses up one after another like sections of bamboo, usually sharing a single topic that is named once and then silently carried through the rest of the sentence — a pattern linguists call the topic chain (话题链[huàtí liàn]) with zero anaphora (dropped subject). The order of the clauses is normally fixed by the Principle of Temporal Order (时间顺序原则[shíjiān shùnxù yuánzé]): whatever happens or is understood first in real life is said first in the sentence. Recognizing 流水句 is essential for reading authentic Chinese prose fluently, and producing them yourself is what separates natural-sounding Chinese from "translated English" that overuses 因为/所以, 虽然/但是, and repeated pronouns in every clause.

tables.caption_tr: Core Features: 流水句 (Flowing Sentence) vs. English Sentence Structure
rows: 竹子型[zhúzixíng] 'bamboo-shaped' — clauses chained end to end at the same level
Tree-shaped — one main clause plus nested subordinate clauses
Often none at all; commas (逗号[dòuhào]) alone link the clauses
Requires explicit words: and, then, because, after, which, although...
Stated once at the start of the chain, then silently dropped (zero anaphora)
Pronoun normally repeated in every new clause (he..., he..., he...)
Fixed by real-world time/logic sequence (Principle of Temporal Order)
Flexible — a subordinate clause can be fronted or embedded anywhere
Fuzzy — one comma-chain can run for many clauses, even a short paragraph
Clearly marked by full stops between independent sentences
Implied by context, word order, and adverbs like 就[jiù]/也[yě]/还[hái]
Made explicit with conjunctions, relative pronouns, participles

tables.caption_tr: Topic-Chain Zero Anaphora: How One Subject Threads Through a Whole Chain
rows: Subject 他[tā] stated explicitly — this is the topic for the whole chain
Subject dropped; understood to still be 他[tā] from clause 1
Subject still dropped; action happens after clause 2 in real time
就[jiù] signals 'then, right after' — closes the chain, subject still 他[tā]
footnotes_tr: Ø marks a dropped/understood subject — it is grammatical and expected, not a mistake.

tables.caption_tr: The Principle of Temporal Order (PTO): How Clause Sequence Is Decided
rows: Four sequential daily actions, no connectors at all needed between them
The cause clause simply comes first; no 因为[yīnwèi] is required
Setting/location before the action in it
Where something happens is set up first, then the event follows
An implicit 'if...then' relation, with no 如果[rúguǒ] needed

tables.caption_tr: How English Connectors Are 'Hidden' Inside a Chinese Flowing Sentence
rows: Because it was cold, I wore a coat.
If you're free, come see me.
Although he was tired, he kept working.
Do you know that person (I mentioned)?

tables.caption_tr: Typical Structural Patterns Built From 流水句
rows: 我[wǒ]每天[měitiān]起床[qǐchuáng]，刷牙[shuāyá]，吃[chī]早饭[zǎofàn]，上学[shàngxué]。
昨天[zuótiān]晚上[wǎnshang]，我[wǒ]在[zài]家[jiā]，看[kàn]书[shū]，喝[hē]茶[chá]，很[hěn]舒服[shūfu]。

tables.caption_tr: Common Learner Mistakes: Over-Connecting vs. Natural Flowing Style
rows: Overusing 因为...所以 in every clause
因为[yīnwèi]我[wǒ]很[hěn]累[lèi]，所以[suǒyǐ]我[wǒ]回家[huíjiā]了[le]，所以[suǒyǐ]我[wǒ]睡觉[shuìjiào]了[le]。
Repeating the subject pronoun in every clause
Forcing an English subordinate-clause-first order unnaturally
虽然[suīrán]他[tā]很[hěn]累[lèi]，但是[dànshì]他[tā]还在[hái zài]工作[gōngzuò]。 (grammatical, but heavier/more formal than needed)
他[tā]很[hěn]累[lèi]，还[hái]在[zài]工作[gōngzuò]。 (lighter, more native flowing style)
footnotes_tr: The 'over-connected' versions are not wrong — they are grammatical — but native speakers reserve heavy connectors like 虽然/但是 and 因为/所以 for formal writing or when the logical relation genuinely needs emphasis; everyday narration prefers the bare flowing-chain style.

examples.target: 他[tā]下[xià]了[le]课[kè]，回[huí]家[jiā]，吃[chī]了[le]饭[fàn]，就[jiù]睡[shuì]觉[jiào]了[le]。
examples.translation_tr: He got out of class, went home, ate, and then went to sleep. — One long comma-chain, zero connectors, subject '他' stated only once and silently carried through all four clauses.

examples.target: 天[tiān]冷[lěng]了[le]，路[lù]上[shang]的[de]人[rén]少[shǎo]了[le]，商店[shāngdiàn]也[yě]早[zǎo]关[guān]门[mén]了[le]。
examples.translation_tr: The weather turned cold, fewer people were on the streets, and shops closed early too. — Three mini topic-comment clauses chained together; the cause-effect link is implied, not marked by 因为/所以.

examples.target: 我[wǒ]每天[měitiān]六[liù]点[diǎn]起床[qǐchuáng]，刷牙[shuāyá]，洗脸[xǐliǎn]，吃[chī]早饭[zǎofàn]，然后[ránhòu]去[qù]上班[shàngbān]。
examples.translation_tr: Every day I get up at six, brush my teeth, wash my face, eat breakfast, and then go to work. — A daily routine chain following the real-world time order (PTO); only the last link uses 然后 for extra clarity.

examples.target: 那[nà]件[jiàn]事[shì]，说[shuō]来[lái]话[huà]长[cháng]，你[nǐ]先[xiān]坐[zuò]下[xià]，我[wǒ]慢慢[mànmàn]告诉[gàosu]你[nǐ]。
examples.translation_tr: That matter is a long story — sit down first, and I'll tell you slowly. — The whole sentence hangs off one fronted topic ('that matter'), with several comment clauses trailing after it.

examples.target: 下[xià]雨[yǔ]了[le]，路[lù]很[hěn]滑[huá]，你[nǐ]开车[kāichē]小心[xiǎoxīn]点[diǎn]。
examples.translation_tr: It's raining, the road is slippery, drive carefully. — Cause, resulting state, and advice are simply lined up in the order they occur, with no 'because/so' needed.

examples.target: 你[nǐ]不[bù]去[qù]，我[wǒ]也[yě]不[bù]去[qù]，大家[dàjiā]都[dōu]别[bié]去[qù]了[le]。
examples.translation_tr: If you're not going, I'm not going either — let's just say nobody's going. — An implicit conditional relation ('if...then') expressed purely through clause order and the echoing adverb 也.

examples.target: 他[tā]拿[ná]起[qǐ]书[shū]，翻[fān]了[le]两[liǎng]页[yè]，又[yòu]放[fàng]下[xià]了[le]。
examples.translation_tr: He picked up the book, flipped through two pages, and put it down again. — A tight three-action chain; the subject '他' appears once and every following verb is understood to share it.

four-char-parallelism.intro_tr: 四字格 (sìzìgé) refers to the extremely common Chinese pattern of packing a complete idea into exactly four syllables/characters, producing a compact, rhythmic, and often internally parallel unit of meaning. Many 四字格 are chengyu — fixed idioms with historical or literary origins — but the pattern itself is also a living, productive mold: writers and speakers freely build reduplicated or paired 2+2 phrases (AABB, ABAC, subject-predicate compression, verb-object compression, etc.) to sound more polished and balanced, even without using a 'famous' idiom. Structurally, most 四字格 split into two two-character halves that mirror each other in grammar and tone, creating the '2-2' rhythm that Mandarin ears expect in elevated style. Inside a sentence, a 四字格 behaves just like any ordinary word class — predicate (+得), adverbial (+地), attributive (+的), or a standalone clause paired with another 四字格 — so learning its slot-filling behavior matters more than memorizing every fixed phrase. Because this pattern belongs to written/formal register (书面语), overusing it in casual speech can sound stilted, while a formal essay or news report that avoids it entirely will read as flat and unpolished.

tables.caption_tr: Internal Grammatical Structures Inside 四字格
rows: AB + CD, two parallel 2-char units of equal grammatical status
draw a snake, add feet → ruin by overdoing
peach-blossom land beyond the world → utopia
paint the dragon, dot in the eyes → the finishing touch
footnotes_tr: The hyphen inside the reading (e.g. xīnhuā-nùfàng) marks the natural 2+2 rhythmic break of the phrase; it is not an actual pause required in speech.

tables.caption_tr: Reduplication Formulas Used to Build the Four-Character Rhythm
rows: to look into (something), just a little
positions 1 and 3 share the same character
ten complete, ten beautiful → flawless, perfect
doubled first character + a new 2-char unit
a 2-char unit + a doubled final character
full of vitality, bursting with life

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used Formal-Register 四字格 Expressions
rows: seek truth from facts, be pragmatic
describing a rigorous, realistic approach or method
everyone talking at once, a hubbub of voices
describing emotional defeat after a setback
beat around the bush, speak evasively
each person states their own view
describing an open discussion or debate

tables.caption_tr: Syntactic Roles a 四字格 Can Fill in a Sentence
rows: describes the manner/degree of the action, attached after 得
modifies the following verb, attached before it with 地
这是一次实事求是的分析。
[Zhè shì yí cì shíshì-qiúshì de fēnxī.]
modifies the following noun, attached before it with 的
functions as the main verb-like predicate of the sentence
two 四字格 stand side by side for rhythmic, balanced description

tables.caption_tr: Register Comparison: Plain Phrase vs. 四字格 Equivalent
rows: speaking evasively, not getting to the point
footnotes_tr: The 四字格 column is appropriate for essays, news, and speeches; using the plain column in the same context can sound too casual, while using 四字格 in everyday chat can sound overly formal or bookish.

examples.target: 这里山清水秀,风景优美。
examples.reading: [Zhèlǐ shānqīng-shuǐxiù, fēngjǐng yōuměi.]
examples.translation_tr: This place has clear mountains and clean waters — the scenery is beautiful.
examples.note_tr: Two four-character phrases (山清水秀 + implicit balance) set a formal, descriptive tone typical of travel writing.

examples.target: 他做事总是丢三落四。
examples.reading: [Tā zuòshì zǒngshì diūsān-làsì.]
examples.translation_tr: He's always careless and forgetful when he does things.
examples.note_tr: 丢三落四 sits directly after 是-less 总是 as the sentence's predicate.

examples.target: 大家七嘴八舌地讨论起来。
examples.reading: [Dàjiā qīzuǐ-bāshé de tǎolùn qǐlai.]
examples.translation_tr: Everyone started discussing all at once, talking over one another.
examples.note_tr: 四字格 + 地 marks it as an adverbial modifying the verb 讨论.

examples.target: 经过这场变故,他心灰意冷。
examples.reading: [Jīngguò zhè chǎng biàngù, tā xīnhuī-yìlěng.]
examples.translation_tr: After this setback, he became disheartened and discouraged.
examples.note_tr: 心灰意冷 is a subject-predicate style compression: 'heart-ashes, mind-cold'.

examples.target: 公司的发展蒸蒸日上。
examples.reading: [Gōngsī de fāzhǎn zhēngzhēng-rìshàng.]
examples.translation_tr: The company's growth is thriving more and more every day.
examples.note_tr: Used as the main predicate of the sentence, no 是 needed.

examples.target: 我们应该实事求是地分析问题。
examples.reading: [Wǒmen yīnggāi shíshì-qiúshì de fēnxī wèntí.]
examples.translation_tr: We should analyze problems in a realistic, fact-based manner.
examples.note_tr: 实事求是 + 地 shows the typical formal-register adverbial slot.

examples.target: 这次比赛他们准备得井井有条。
examples.reading: [Zhè cì bǐsài tāmen zhǔnbèi de jǐngjǐng-yǒutiáo.]
examples.translation_tr: For this competition they prepared in a very organized, orderly way.
examples.note_tr: 井井有条 follows 得, functioning as a complement of manner.

chucizhiwai.title_tr: Formal Discourse Transitions (除此之外, 此外, 总而言之)
chucizhiwai.intro_tr: Formal discourse transitions are the "signpost" words that hold together written arguments, reports, speeches, and essays in Chinese — they show a reader or listener where an idea is being added, summarized, or wrapped up. 此外[cǐwài] and 除此之外[chúcǐzhīwài] both mean "besides this / in addition," pointing back to something already mentioned, while 总而言之[zǒng'éryánzhī] and its relatives mean "in short / to sum up," closing an argument. These expressions almost always sit at the very start of a sentence, are followed by a comma, and belong to 书面语[shūmiànyǔ] (written/formal register) rather than everyday chat. Mastering them lets you structure a formal paragraph the way a native writer would: 首先[shǒuxiān]...其次[qícì]...此外[cǐwài]...总而言之[zǒng'éryánzhī]. Below you'll find the full inventory, their register level, and the traps that most easily confuse learners.

tables.caption_tr: Additive Transitions — 'besides / in addition' family
rows: Adds one extra, often minor, point to what was just said
Emphatic/extended form of 此外; explicitly points back to a previously mentioned item or list
Adds a new, sometimes unrelated point; can also shift topic
Links two clauses inside one sentence, often paired with 不但[búdàn]
Links two verb phrases or actions performed together

tables.caption_tr: Summary / Conclusion Transitions — 'in short / to sum up' family
rows: General concluding remark; wraps up an argument or discussion
Slightly lighter version of 总而言之; very common in both writing and speech
Neutral summary, often used before giving an overall evaluation
Refers explicitly back to points already enumerated above; typical of reports/academic writing
Introduces a concise restatement of a more complex point
Literary, slightly archaic flourish meaning 'in a nutshell'

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Position and Punctuation Rules
rows: Discourse transitions occupy the whole-sentence initial slot, not mid-clause
A comma is virtually obligatory right after the transition word
总而言之[zǒng'éryánzhī]，这是个好主意。
除此之外/此外 point backward — they need a prior sentence or list to refer to; they cannot open a passage with no context
(previous sentence about problem A) + 除此之外，还有个问题B。
综上所述 strictly follows an enumerated list of points already given; using it with no prior list sounds odd
Point 1. Point 2. Point 3. 综上所述[zōngshàng suǒshù]，...
(list of 3 reasons) + 综上所述，我们不建议这么做。
总而言之/总之 do NOT require a prior list — they can conclude even a single preceding idea
(any prior statement) + 总之[zǒngzhī]/总而言之[zǒng'éryánzhī]，...
这部电影很长，也很闷。总之，我不推荐。

tables.caption_tr: Formal vs. Colloquial Equivalents
rows: (no natural casual equivalent — rarely appears in speech)

tables.caption_tr: Common Confusions and Mistakes
rows: 除此之外[chúcǐzhīwài] vs 除了...以外[chúle...yǐwài]
除此之外 stands alone and refers anaphorically to something already said; 除了...以外 needs its own object stated right after 除了
除此之外，他还会法语。 (refers back) / 除了英语以外，他还会法语。 (names the excluded item directly)
此外 is purely additive, listing a supplementary point tightly related to what precedes; 另外 can also introduce a loosely related or new topic
此外，价格也不贵。(same topic, extra detail) / 另外，明天几点开会？(topic shift)
总之[zǒngzhī] vs 总而言之[zǒng'éryánzhī]
总之 is common in both speech and writing and feels lighter; 总而言之 is more literary and typically closes formal essays or speeches
总之，我们走吧。(casual, fine in speech) / 总而言之，本次改革取得了显著成效。(formal report style)
总而言之[zǒng'éryánzhī] vs 综上所述[zōngshàng suǒshù]
总而言之 gives a general 'in short' conclusion without needing a prior enumerated list; 综上所述 explicitly summarizes points already listed above
总而言之，这是个好机会。 / 综上所述（after listing 3 reasons），我们决定采纳这个方案。
而且 links two clauses WITHIN one sentence (often with 不但); 此外 starts a NEW sentence adding a separate point
他不但聪明，而且很努力。(one sentence) / 他很聪明。此外，他也很努力。(two sentences)

tables.caption_tr: Typical Formal Paragraph Skeleton
rows: 此外[cǐwài] / 除此之外[chúcǐzhīwài] / 另外[lìngwài]
Adds one more relevant point beyond the main ones
总而言之[zǒng'éryánzhī] / 总之[zǒngzhī] / 综上所述[zōngshàng suǒshù]
Wraps up the argument with an overall conclusion

examples.target: 除此之外，我们还需要考虑成本问题。
examples.reading: Chúcǐzhīwài, wǒmen hái xūyào kǎolǜ chéngběn wèntí.
examples.translation_tr: Besides this, we also need to consider the issue of cost.

examples.target: 此外，这个方案还有一些技术上的困难。
examples.reading: Cǐwài, zhège fāng'àn hái yǒu yìxiē jìshù shàng de kùnnan.
examples.translation_tr: Furthermore, this plan also has some technical difficulties.

examples.target: 首先，价格太贵；其次，质量也不好；此外，服务态度也不好。
examples.reading: Shǒuxiān, jiàgé tài guì; qícì, zhìliàng yě bù hǎo; cǐwài, fúwù tàidù yě bù hǎo.
examples.translation_tr: First, the price is too expensive; second, the quality isn't good either; besides, the service attitude isn't good either.

examples.target: 总而言之，这次会议是非常成功的。
examples.reading: Zǒng'éryánzhī, zhè cì huìyì shì fēicháng chénggōng de.
examples.translation_tr: All things considered, this meeting was very successful.

examples.target: 综上所述，我们建议推迟这个项目。
examples.reading: Zōngshàng suǒshù, wǒmen jiànyì tuīchí zhège xiàngmù.
examples.translation_tr: To sum up the above, we recommend postponing this project.

examples.target: 总之，做任何事情都要坚持到底。
examples.reading: Zǒngzhī, zuò rènhé shìqíng dōu yào jiānchí dàodǐ.
examples.translation_tr: In short, whatever you do, you must persevere to the end.

examples.target: 除此之外，他还精通三门外语。
examples.reading: Chúcǐzhīwài, tā hái jīngtōng sān mén wàiyǔ.
examples.translation_tr: Apart from this, he is also fluent in three foreign languages.

examples.target: 另外，我想提醒大家明天要提前到场。
examples.reading: Lìngwài, wǒ xiǎng tíxǐng dàjiā míngtiān yào tíqián dàochǎng.
examples.translation_tr: Additionally, I'd like to remind everyone to arrive early tomorrow.
